en: The Moon Lamp Samādhi Sūtra, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Northern Qi Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.
He was accompanied by a great assembly of one hundred thousand bhikṣus;
eighty nayutas of bodhisattvas, all of whom were in their final birth before Buddhahood, with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ajita as their leader;

and the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra Devendra, Mahābrahmā the Lord of the Sahā World, along with other gods of superior merit, and asuras, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans of superior majesty and power.
Surrounding him from all sides, they gazed up at the Tathāgata.

At that time, among this assembly there was a bodhisattva named Candraprabha Kumāra—who had already made offerings to various Buddhas in the past, planted many roots of goodness, possessed knowledge of his own past lives, and who, with faith and delight in the Mahāyāna, dwelt securely in the Mahāyāna and was endowed with great compassion—rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I now wish to ask the Buddha about something; I only pray that you will grant me leave to do so, and thus remove the knots of my doubt.
The Buddha said, "Young man!"
According to your inclinations, I shall explain each of your questions for you, so that you may attain joy.
I possess all-knowledge and all-vision; I am empowered and fearless regarding all phenomena, having attained mastery and being endowed with unimpeded knowledge and vision of liberation.
"O youth!

The Tathāgata knows nothing that is not known, sees nothing that is not seen, realizes nothing that is not realized, and makes no choice that is not made; he awakens to and perceives immeasurable and boundless worlds."
“Young man!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are able to answer every question according to its nature, causing all hearts to rejoice.
At that time, the young man asked in verse:
"What kind of practice do the Buddhas perform, that they can act as kinsmen to the world and create illumination?
How can they attain inconceivable wisdom?
I pray that you, O Protector, will explain this."
By what practice does one attain this supreme teaching of the Dharma, become a bull-king among men honored by the devas,
and possess that immeasurable, most excellent wisdom?
I pray that you will explain this well for me.
Out of deep faith I have made this inquiry; my heart is truly free from deceit.
No one else is able to witness my inner state, for only the Honored One among Men can clearly perceive it.
I possess a vast and supreme mind of bliss; the Lion of the Śākya clan knows my practice.
My mind does not act for the sake of words; I only pray that you will teach me the aids to the Path.
What dharma can bring all Buddhas here, causing boundless wisdom to increase,
and reaching that state within all dharmas?
I pray you, please explain this well for me.
I pray that you will explain the dharmas for nurturing my practice, so that I may attain cultivated and sharp wisdom;
with a profound mind, may I uphold the precepts without transgression, and remain far removed from all fears.
How does one not abandon the precepts?
How does one not diminish wisdom?
How does one dwell securely in an araṇya?
How can one cause wisdom to increase?
How can one enter the supreme and wondrous Dharma, delighting in the protection of the precepts without regret?
How can one remain without deficiency in the precepts?
How can one know the nature of the conditioned?
How does one attain this purity of the three karmas, with an undefiled mind proceeding toward the Buddha-way?
How can one attain purity of bodily action?
How can one eliminate the evils of speech and mind?
How can one become free from the defiled mind?
We only pray that the World-Honored One will explain according to our questions.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the youth Candraprabha:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accords with even a single dharma, they will swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and thus fully realize all such dharmas."
What is this one dharma?

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives rise toward sentient beings to a mind of equanimity, a mind of protection, a mind free from obstruction, and a mind free from malice—this is the association with the one dharma that swiftly brings about the realization of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and enables one to obtain such benefits of merit.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If there be one who upholds this single dharma, They will be able to accord with the bodhisattva’s correct practice.
By virtue of the merit of this single dharma, They shall swiftly attain the unsurpassed path."
With a mind unimpeded in all places, such is the conduct possible for a courageous Bodhisattva;
never giving rise to thoughts of hatred or attachment, one thus attains sublime merit.
If one can thus cultivate an even mind, one will then realize the fruit of equality;
when such practice of the Dharma is entirely equal, one attains the mark of level soles beneath the feet.
Cultivating equanimity and abandoning the mind of anger, one is able to remove the veil of all afflictions;
by these causes and conditions, the soles of the feet become level, and thus one obtains the color of a lotus upon the soles of the feet.
He alone can manifest throughout the ten directions, The radiance of his merit pervading the buddha-fields;
Having attained the stage of quiescent extinction, He tames immeasurable sentient beings.

"O Youth! A bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise toward all sentient beings to a mind of equanimity, a mind of protection, a mind free from obstruction, and a mind free from poison; acting as the eye of the world, they realize the samādhi named 'The Equality of the Essential Nature of All Dharmas and Freedom from Proliferation. "
From that samādhi, one accomplishes ten dharmas. What are the ten? First, restraint of the body; second, restraint of speech;

third, restraint of the mind; fourth, purity of action; fifth, crossing over all causal conditions; sixth, awakening to and understanding the aggregates (skandhas); seventh, attaining equanimity regarding the elements (dhātus); eighth, eliminating the characteristics of the sense bases (āyatanas); ninth, severing all craving; tenth, realizing non-arising.

"Furthermore, there are ten dharmas: first, entering into the nature of all phenomena; second, revealing all causes; third, not destroying the fruit; fourth, directly perceiving all phenomena; fifth, cultivating and accumulating the Path; sixth, being born together with the Buddhas; seventh, possessing sharp and keen wisdom; eighth, entering the wisdom that understands the inclinations of all sentient beings; ninth, attaining the wisdom of the Dharma; and tenth, entering the wisdom of unimpeded eloquence."
“Furthermore, there are ten dharmas: first, the wisdom of skillfully knowing syllables;

second, having crossed over all affairs; third, attaining the wisdom of sounds; fourth, equanimity regarding the elements (*dhātu*); fifth, attaining a heart of exultation through equanimity regarding the elements; sixth, attaining the factor of joy; seventh, attaining a non-crooked mind; eighth, the subduing of deportment; ninth, attaining a straightforward mind; tenth, the absence of anger-induced changes in physical appearance.”
"Furthermore, there are ten dharmas: first, a face that is always serene and joyful;

second, speech that is harmonious and elegant; third, always being the first to offer greetings; fourth, constant freedom from indolence; fifth, revering one's elders and superiors; sixth, making offerings to one's elders and superiors; seventh, contentment with one's place of birth; eighth, tireless cultivation of goodness; ninth, purity from wrong livelihood; and tenth, dwelling in an araṇya."
“Furthermore, there are ten dharmas: first, wisdom that abides securely in each stage;

second, right mindfulness without forgetfulness; third, attaining the skillful means of wisdom regarding the aggregates (*skandha*); fourth, the skillful means of wisdom regarding the elements (*dhātu*); fifth, the skillful means of wisdom regarding the sense bases (*āyatana*); sixth, realizing the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); seventh, extinguishing all afflictions (*kleśa*); eighth, severing the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); ninth, the mind being constantly courageous; and tenth, dwelling in the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).”
"Furthermore, there are ten dharmas: first, knowing the methods for transgressions;

second, extinguishing all outflows of existence (*āsrava*); third, severing all fetters (*saṃyojana*); fourth, having already crossed over all states of existence; fifth, skillfully recollecting past lives; sixth, being free from doubt regarding the results of karma; seventh, reflecting upon the Dharma; eighth, seeking extensive learning (*bahuśruta*); ninth, attaining sharp wisdom; and tenth, attaining the stage of self-mastery."

“Furthermore, there are ten dharmas: first, not relying on the observance of precepts; second, not engaging in false conceptualization; third, being free from frivolity; fourth, abiding in the mark of non-retrogression; fifth, giving rise to wholesome dharmas; sixth, feeling weary of and detaching from unwholesome dharmas; seventh, not acting out of afflictions; eighth, not abandoning one's training; ninth, discerning the various dhyānas; and tenth, attaining the wisdom that knows the inclinations and desires of all sentient beings.”
“Furthermore, there are ten dharmas: first, skillfully discerning the places of birth;

second, attaining the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*); third, possessing the wisdom of knowing languages; fourth, relinquishing worldly attachments; fifth, cultivating weary detachment from the three realms; sixth, not giving rise to a lowly mind; seventh, non-attachment to all phenomena; eighth, embracing the true Dharma; ninth, guarding the true Dharma; and tenth, knowing the skillful means of the Vinaya.”
“Furthermore, there are ten dharmas: first, the extinguishing of all disputes;

second, non-opposition; third, not engaging in litigation; fourth, equanimity of patience; fifth, attaining the stage of patience; sixth, self-restraint through patience; seventh, skillful discernment of all dharmas; eighth, a mind that delights in possessing the precepts; ninth, certainty in skillful means regarding questions and answers; and tenth, the wisdom that skillfully distinguishes the meaning of phrases.”
“Furthermore, there are ten dharmas: first, the production of skillful means wisdom regarding the Dharma;

second, the production of wisdom through skillfully knowing what is meaningful and what is meaningless; third, wisdom regarding the past limit; fourth, wisdom regarding the future limit; fifth, wisdom regarding the present; sixth, wisdom regarding the equality of the three periods of time; seventh, wisdom in skillfully understanding the three wheels; eighth, the mind abiding in peace; ninth, the body abiding in peace; and tenth, skillfully guarding one’s deportment.”
“Furthermore, there are ten dharmas: first, not violating dignified deportment;

second, discerning dignified deportment; third, having dignified deportment that is upright and elegant; fourth, being skilled at explaining the meaning; fifth, attaining worldly knowledge; sixth, delighting in giving and being without stinginess; seventh, constantly extending the hand of charity; eighth, giving constantly without ceasing; ninth, giving everything without exception; tenth, possessing a sense of shame.”
“Furthermore, there are ten dharmas: first, having a sense of shame; second, abandoning evil thoughts;

third, not forsaking the dhūta practices; fourth, being unswerving in faith; fifth, constantly practicing the conduct of joy; sixth, relinquishing one’s seat to offer it to elders and superiors; seventh, relinquishing arrogance; eighth, skillfully restraining the mind; ninth, skillfully knowing the association of the mind; and tenth, skillfully knowing the arising of the mind.”

“Furthermore, there are ten dharmas: first, skillful knowledge of the meaning; second, skillful knowledge of the teachings; third, being far removed from ignorance; fourth, skillfully entering the subtle mind; fifth, knowing the self-nature of the mind; sixth, skillfully knowing the expedient means for the coming and going of dharmas; seventh, skillfully knowing the wisdom of all languages; eighth, skillfully attaining the distinctions of unimpeded eloquence; ninth, attaining the wisdom of the expedient means for determining the meaning; tenth, abandoning that which is not the meaning.”
“Furthermore, there are ten dharmas: first, associating with virtuous persons; second, engaging in the same activities as them;

third, listening to and receiving their instructions; fourth, distancing oneself from evil persons; fifth, cultivating dhyāna and giving rise to supernatural powers (*abhijñā*); sixth, not becoming attached to the flavor of dhyāna; seventh, sporting in supernatural powers; eighth, attaining worldly knowledge (*lokajñāna*); ninth, distancing oneself from provisional designations (*prajñapti*); and tenth, not being weary of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).”

“Furthermore, there are ten dharmas: first, not rejoicing when gaining profit; second, not being dejected when encountering decline; third, not being pleased when praised; fourth, not being distressed when criticized; fifth, not increasing in stature when lauded; sixth, not diminishing when disparaged; seventh, neither suffering; eighth, neither delighting; ninth, not associating closely with householders; and tenth, not remaining among the monastic assembly.”
“Furthermore, there are ten dharmas: first, abandoning disrespect; second, practicing respect;

third, being complete in etiquette; fourth, abandoning lack of etiquette; fifth, not defiling the homes of the laity; sixth, protecting the Buddha-dharma; seventh, remaining in quietude and speaking little; eighth, having speech and conduct that are not coarse; ninth, being skillful in means when conversing with others; and tenth, subduing all enemies.”

“Furthermore, there are ten dharmas: first, skillfully knowing the proper seasons; second, maintaining the perception that ordinary worldlings are unknowable; third, not giving rise to a contemptuous mind toward those who are poor and lowly; fourth, bestowing gifts whenever one is asked; fifth, allowing those who are poor to beg as they wish without obstruction; sixth, not giving rise to a mind of aversion toward those who violate the precepts; seventh, being mindful of the desire to rescue them; eighth, skillfully knowing what ought to be done; ninth, upholding the True Dharma; and tenth, relinquishing wealth and food.”
“Furthermore, there are ten dharmas: first, not engaging in the accumulation of possessions;

second, praising the observance of precepts; third, censuring the violation of precepts; fourth, revering those who observe the precepts without any deceitful mind; fifth, being able to give away all that one possesses; sixth, earnestly exhorting and requesting [others to practice]; seventh, acting in accordance with what one says; eighth, serving wise people; ninth, having a firm and profound delight in the practice of all dharmas; and tenth, attaining the wisdom of analogies.”
“Furthermore, there are ten dharmas: first, skillful means regarding the past;

second, taking the cultivation of goodness as primary; third, possessing various skillful means; fourth, severing all signs; fifth, relinquishing all perceptions; sixth, skillfully knowing the characteristics of phenomena; seventh, being able to expound all sutras; eighth, skillfully attaining the means regarding all that is adverse or favorable; ninth, certainty regarding the truths; and tenth, realizing liberation.”
"Furthermore, there are ten dharmas: first, speech that is true and straightforward;

second, manifesting the wisdom of intrinsic nature; third, discourse free from doubt; fourth, fixing the mind upon emptiness; fifth, cultivating the signless; sixth, knowing the nature of wishlessness; seventh, attaining the four fearlessnesses; eighth, being firm in the precepts; ninth, entering into right fulfillment; and tenth, attaining wisdom."
“Furthermore, there are ten dharmas:

first, binding the thoughts to a single object; second, having few acquaintances; third, not giving rise to a turbid mind; fourth, abandoning all views; fifth, attaining *dhāraṇī*; sixth, attaining wisdom; seventh, attaining clarity; eighth, abiding securely; ninth, maintaining stability; and tenth, right exertion.”

“O youth! This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s accomplishment of such benefits and merits from the Samādhi of the Equality of the Essential Nature of All Dharmas and the Absence of Conceptual Proliferation.”

“O youth! This samādhi is called ‘cause,’ it is called ‘conformity,’ it is called ‘instruction,’ it is called ‘gate,’ it is called ‘action,’ it is called ‘path-practice,’ it is called ‘freedom from doubt,’ and it is called ‘guide.’”
It is called the practice of conforming patience; it is called the stage of patience; it is called the removal of impatience; it is called the stage of wisdom;
it is called the distancing from ignorance; it is called the establishment in wisdom; it is called the stage of skillful means;
it is called the wandering of the bodhisattva; it is called drawing near to the Supreme Person; it is called...
It is far removed from evil persons; it is called the Buddha-ground taught by the Tathāgata;
it is called that which the wise rejoice in; it is called that which the foolish abandon; it is called that which is difficult for śrāvakas to know;

it is called that which is not the ground of non-Buddhists; it is called that which is embraced by the Tathāgata; it is called that which is known by those possessing the ten powers; it is called that which is [known by] all...
It is called the offering of the devas; it is called the prostration of the Brahma Kings; it is called the following behind by Śakra;
it is called the bowing of the nāgas and spirits; it is called the sympathetic joy of the yakṣas;
it is called the praise of the kiṃnaras; it is called the eulogy of the mahoragas; it is called the practice of the bodhisattvas; it is called wisdom.
That which is sought is called the attainment of the unsurpassed path; it is called the gift of non-material sustenance;
it is called the medicine that removes the diseases of affliction for all sentient beings; it is called the treasury of wisdom; it is called inexhaustible eloquence;
it is called the source from which all teachings arise; it is called the removal of all suffering and pain; it is called the knowledge of the three [vehicles].
It is called the realm; it is called the raft for crossing over; it is called the boat for crossing the four currents; it is called the source of renown;
it is called the praise and manifestation of the Tathāgata; it is called the benefit of the Tathāgata; it is called the radiant praise of the ten powers;
it is called the source of the bodhisattva’s path of virtue; it is called the compassion that extinguishes anger and rage.
Compassion that eliminates affliction and harm is called joy; tranquility within the mind is called equanimity;
one who pities others is called one who finds rest in the Mahāyāna; one who is able to roar the lion’s roar is called the Buddha-way;
it is called the seal of all dharmas; it is called the guide to omniscience; and it is called the bodhisattva.
They are called: the Garden of Play; the Dispeller of the Hosts of Māra; the Pathway of the Sugata;
the Accomplisher of All Auspicious Meanings; the Defender Against Enemies; the Subduer of Foes through the Dharma; the Reality of Fearlessness;
the Power of Seeking Truthfully Without Deception; and the Eighteen [Great Qualities].
The root of the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) is called the adornment of the *dharmakāya*,
called the majesty of all practices, called the adornment of the Buddha’s wisdom, called the relinquishing of all attachments, called delighting the Buddha’s eldest son,
called the fulfillment of the Buddha’s knowledge, called that which is not the stage of the *pratyekabuddha*, and called purity.
The mind is called the pure body; it is called the accomplishment of liberation; it is called being free from all mixed desires;
it is called being free from all mixed hatreds; it is called the ground beyond delusion; it is called the wisdom of the Āgamas;
it is called that which can give rise to all skillful means; it is called the removal of all ignorance; it is called fulfillment.
Liberation is called the joy of the meditative practitioner; it is called the eye for those who must see; it is called the playful exercise of supernormal powers;
it is called the manifestation of the bases of psychic power; it is called the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining;
it is called mindfulness that never forgets; it is called the empowerment of all Buddhas; and it is called the skillful means of the Teacher.
It is called the wisdom that is subtle and difficult to know, which is without conceptual correspondence; it is called the wisdom that has abandoned words and letters;
it is called the wisdom of profound knowledge of meaning; it is called the wisdom of insight and vision; it is called the wisdom of discernment; it is called the wisdom that is ineffable;
it is called the wisdom that can subdue the non-wisdom; it is called the wisdom of those who are upright and honest.
It is called the wisdom of those with few desires; it is called the upholding of diligence; it is called the ability to maintain mindfulness without forgetfulness;
it is called the ability to dissolve all sufferings; it is called the non-arising of all phenomena;

and it is called the single utterance that explains the knowledge of all realms of birth and death—this is termed the equality of the essential nature of all phenomena, free from conceptual proliferation.

“Discourse on Samādhi. When this Dharma-door was being taught, eighty *nayuta* of humans and devas in the assembly attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); ninety-two *nayuta* of humans and devas attained the patience that follows sound; seventy-six *nayuta* of humans and devas attained the patience of conformity (*ānulomikī-kṣānti*); sixty thousand humans and devas became free from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye; one thousand bhikṣus, having exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), attained liberation of mind; two hundred and fifty bhikṣuṇīs, having exhausted all outflows, attained liberation of mind; five hundred upāsakas attained the fruit of *anāgāmin*; and eight hundred upāsikās attained the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*.
At that time, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways—namely: it moved, moved everywhere, and moved equally everywhere;

it leaped up, leaped up everywhere, and leaped up equally everywhere; it rose, rose everywhere, and rose equally everywhere; it roared, roared everywhere, and roared equally everywhere; it quaked, quaked everywhere, and quaked equally everywhere; it trembled, trembled everywhere, and trembled equally everywhere—it surged in the east and subsided in the west, surged in the west and subsided in the east, surged in the south and subsided in the north, surged in the north and subsided in the south, surged in the center and subsided at the edges, and surged at the edges and subsided in the center.

By the power of the Dharma, there suddenly arose an unprecedented radiance that was able to illuminate all dark and remote regions, such that even the Avīci Hell was not left without great brightness.
At that time, among the dark beings within the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa), they were able to see one another for the first time, and they all cried out in astonishment:
"How is it that there are suddenly people such as these here?"
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"I recall sixty million Buddhas of past kalpas, Whose original births were all upon Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
When I sought the Way in ages long past, I heard this samādhi from those Honored Ones."
At that time, the last of those six hundred million Buddhas,
who acted as a light for the world’s kinsmen and was named Śālarājendra Buddha, I questioned that Honored One regarding this samādhi.
At that time, I was born into the Kṣatriya caste, the most honored and supreme among all kings;
I had five hundred sons, who were fully endowed with every skill and talent.
At that time, for the sake of that Unsurpassed Honored One, I established one hundred million monasteries,
constructed entirely of the most excellent and wondrous great sandalwood, interspersed with gold, silver, and various precious gems.
At that time, I was a king beloved by the people, known as King Viśāṃdhara;
for one hundred and eight billion years, I made extensive offerings to the Buddha.
At that time, the most supreme among two-legged beings, known by the name King of the Śāla Trees,
dwelt in this world for seventy-six million years, propagating the Way and transforming beings.
There are eight billion śrāvakas, Possessing the three knowledges and six supernormal powers, ever in meditative concentration;
Abiding in their final bodies with outflows exhausted— Such a noble assembly is beyond reproach.
I have prepared various kinds of supreme offerings to worship those who cross over the evil realms;
desiring to benefit all humans and devas, I seek this samādhi.
I went forth from home together with my wife;
upholding that Buddha’s teaching, which is beyond compare, for fourteen quadrillion years, I constantly inquired about this samādhi.
With eighty thousand nayutas of verses, and eight billion trillion diverse stanzas, that Buddha taught these to others;
yet he spoke only of this single chapter on meditative concentration.
Head, eyes, hands, and feet, as well as wife and children, various kinds of rare jewels and food and drink—
there is no wealth whatsoever that he did not relinquish, for the sake of seeking this samādhi.
I recall the hundreds of millions of Tathāgatas of the past, as well as Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
all of them dwelt upon Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and proclaimed this supreme, tranquil samādhi.
All share the single name Śākyamuni; the sons of the Buddha all bear the same name Rāhula;
their attendants are all named Ānanda; and the royal cities are all called Kapilavastu.
The foremost pair known throughout the world, both named Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra;
the worlds are all equally named Sahā, and those Buddhas all appeared in an age of turbid evil.
I offer all these various articles of worship to the Honored One among Men, desiring to practice the conduct of enlightenment;
I present every requisite for offering because I wish to recite and uphold this samādhi.
By initiating and cultivating sublime practices, one attains this samādhi; having attained this samādhi, one performs immeasurable kinds of deeds.
For those who dwell securely in all virtuous conduct, attaining this samādhi is not difficult.
Unattached to various flavors and free from agitation, they do not involve themselves in worldly affairs and are without envy.
Abiding securely in great compassion and free from anger, attaining this samādhi will not be difficult;
Keeping far from the mundane and not desiring worldly gain, with livelihood pure and free from afflictions,
With precepts as bright as the moon and without fear, attaining this samādhi will not be difficult.
With courageous diligence that never ceases, delighting in solitude and practicing the dhūtas,
abiding securely in the wondrous patience of non-self— attaining this samādhi is then not difficult.
Skillfully subduing the mind so it is free from conceptual proliferation, and abiding securely in dignified deportment and all such practices.
If one joyfully practices relinquishment and giving without stinginess, attaining this samādhi will not be difficult.
All the marks and signs of a Tathāgata, as well as the eighteen unique qualities,
the powers, and the fearlessnesses, will not be difficult to obtain, because one is able to receive and uphold this concentration.
If all sentient beings seen by the Buddha-eye were to simultaneously attain Buddhahood,
and if each of those Buddhas possessed a lifespan of inconceivable hundreds of thousands of millions of *kalpas*,
and if each of those Buddhas had as many heads as there are grains of sand in the great ocean—
Each head possesses immeasurable tongues, Their number equaling the sands of the great ocean.
If each and every tongue were to praise The merit of upholding a single verse of this samādhi, One could not exhaustively describe even a small fraction of it;
How much more so for those who copy it down or receive and uphold it?
If one possesses the ascetic virtues of meditative concentration, they will be cherished and protected by devas, asuras, and spirits;
they will be constantly obeyed by kings and others, because they uphold the tranquil concentration that is difficult to perceive.
He possesses boundless and unimpeded eloquence, proclaiming immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sutras;
at all times he never ceases, for he upholds this sutra, the treasury of hearing and retention.
If you wish to behold Amitābha Buddha and his Land of Peace and Bliss during the future time of great terror and the evil age, you should hear, uphold, and maintain this samādhi.
I now entrust this to you; I, the Honored One among Men, exhort you myself:
after my parinirvāṇa, in the final age, you should hear, uphold, and maintain this samādhi.
All Buddhas throughout the ten directions, Those of the past as well as those of the present—
All those Buddhas studied this samādhi And attained the unconditioned Buddha-enlightenment.

“O Youth! For this reason, if there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to reveal, explain, and discourse upon the inexhaustible meanings, flavors, names, and titles of the Tathāgata’s true merits, and whose every utterance is recorded by the Buddha, you should now read, recite, uphold, and extensively expound for others such a samādhi.”
“O Youth! What are the names of the Tathāgata’s true virtues?

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in a forest hermitage, beneath a tree, in a secluded and quiet place, sitting alone in silence, he should train himself thus: ‘The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. Having accumulated the supreme and wondrous merits of a Tathāgata, he cultivates all roots of goodness without ever losing them; through the power of great patience, he attains the flowers of the primary marks and the secondary signs to adorn himself, becoming the most preeminent among those of lovely form.”

Those who behold him never tire; they revere, believe in, and delight in him. No one is able to deprive him of his wisdom. With indestructible power, he transforms all sentient beings. He is the father of bodhisattvas, the king of the worthy and holy ones, and the guide toward nirvāṇa. He possesses boundless wisdom and immeasurable eloquence.

His Brahma-voice is pure and elegant, his speech is eloquent and fluent, and his marks and signs are rare and extraordinary; those with eyes who gaze upon him cannot bear to look away wherever they behold him.

He has attained an incomparable body, unstained by the realm of desire and unstained by the realm of form, having transcended the formless realm, being far removed from all suffering and having relinquished all dharmas.

Liberated from the realms, they are no longer associated with the sense bases; having severed all fetters and exhausted all craving, they have crossed over the four floods, fulfilled their wisdom, and dwell securely in nirvāṇa at the limit of reality.

“O Youth! This reveals the true merits of the Tathāgata; this is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva abiding in that samādhi being able to obtain the true merits of the Tathāgata. To expound upon names and meanings is inexhaustible, and all that is spoken is recorded by all Buddhas.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Throughout immeasurable thousands of kalpas, One could not fully describe the virtues of the Tathāgata;
Having long accumulated all roots of sublime goodness, It was for the sake of seeking such a supreme samādhi."
Adorned with the exquisite form of a beautiful woman, possessing a most supreme, rare, and delightful complexion—
I originally resolved to give her away without regret, for the sake of seeking such a sublime concentration;
I relinquished my most cherished wealth and servants, as well as mani-jewels, gold, and silver.
With a most supreme mind he gave to them, for the sake of seeking such a samādhi;
with mani-jewels, necklaces, celestial crowns, armlets, and golden cords,
he once offered these to his venerable teachers, for the sake of seeking such a sublime concentration.
All these exquisite fragrant flowers and immeasurable fruits are the Gandharvas’ perfumes;
with these flowers I scatter upon the Buddha’s stūpa, increasing my superior, pure, and most sublime mind.
I bestow the gift of the immeasurable Dharma, joyfully guiding and instructing all sentient beings;
regarding fame and gain, I never give rise to such thoughts as:
"I have originally accumulated the virtues of dhūta."
He dwells alone beneath a tree, silent and without speech, out of immeasurable compassion for sentient beings, seeking the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi.
He abides with others in shared precepts without conflict; his loving words flow as a constant, moistening sound, and his speech is so gentle that people delight in hearing it;
all who see him never grow weary of or abandon him.
Dwelling in the homes of others, he was free from the stinginess of a householder; for immeasurable billions of births he was without envy.
Always joyfully going forth to beg for food himself, he renounced all invitations to feasts.
If one who is learned is able to receive and uphold even a four-line verse of this samādhi,
they thereby perform an offering to me, honoring me with a most excellent mind.
In the past, I practiced various kinds of giving; throughout the long night, I did not transgress the precepts;
I made offerings to the Buddhas in immeasurable ways—all for the sake of seeking such tranquil concentration as this.
If one were to fill immeasurable worlds with mani jewels and give them away as extensive alms,
yet hear this samādhi and uphold even a single verse of it, this merit would surpass that former one beyond measure.
With all manner of diverse flowers, And various rare and exquisite incenses,
I make offerings to all the Tathāgatas, Delighting to cultivate roots of goodness for immeasurable eons.
With all the music and dance of the world, supreme and wondrous food and drink, and precious garments,
they have for immeasurable eons maintained a superior resolve, constantly making offerings to those of Ten Powers.
If a person gives rise to the aspiration for enlightenment, they shall attain the state of the Unsurpassed Great Dharma King;
yet if one hears even a single verse of this Samādhi Sūtra being preached, their merit shall exceed that [of the former].
Even if one were to speak of their benefits for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River,
one could not exhaustively describe those virtues, for they uphold immeasurable merit and meditative concentration.

“O Youth! For this reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should, with a sincere mind, receive, uphold, read, recite, explain to others, analyze, and reveal this samādhi, and extensively transform sentient beings so that they may practice this samādhi.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Having heard such supreme and wondrous benefits from that Buddha,
I shall now, for your sake, expound this sublime samādhi as taught by all the Buddhas."
In the presence of seven hundred and thirty million Buddhas, I have made offerings in the past;
all those Tathāgatas likewise preached this very sūtra.
By this, one is able to enter the mind of great compassion; therefore, I have clearly expounded this samādhi.
If there are those who practice and study with extensive learning, it will not be difficult for them to attain the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
If, during that final age of the Dharma’s decline, after the Teacher of the World has passed into parinirvāṇa,
there should be wicked bhikṣus who disparage the Dharma and take no delight in extensive learning;
Though they preach the Dharma of the precepts to sustain their lives, they themselves take no pleasure in practicing them;
though they preach meditative concentration to sustain their lives, they themselves take no pleasure in practicing it;
though they preach wisdom to sustain their lives, they themselves take no pleasure in practicing it.
Though they speak of liberation and thereby sustain themselves, they do not personally delight in practicing liberation;
though they speak of knowledge and vision and thereby sustain themselves, they do not personally delight in practicing knowledge and vision.
As people say:
"Sandalwood fragrance is the most supreme among all fragrances.
Someone asked that person who spoke of the fragrance:
"Do you yourself possess any fragrance?
He replied:
"I truly do not perceive any fragrance; I merely sustain my life by speaking of fragrance."
In the final evil age after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there will be bhikṣus who do not conform to the proper rules;
though they live by reciting the precepts, they are unable to practice them themselves.
In the final evil age after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there will be bhikṣus who do not conform to the proper rules.
Though they preach the Dharma of concentration and thereby sustain their lives, they are unable to practice the Dharma of concentration themselves;
in the final evil age after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there will be bhikṣus who do not conform to the proper rules,
who though preaching the Dharma of wisdom and thereby sustain their lives, are unable to practice the Dharma of wisdom themselves.
In the final evil age after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there will be monks who act contrary to the rules;
though they preach liberation as their livelihood, they are unable to practice the dharma of liberation themselves.
In the final evil age after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there will be monks who act contrary to the rules.
Though one may live by professing knowledge and vision, If one cannot personally practice the Dharma of knowledge and vision,
One is like a poor and lowly person who is deceived by others, Until later, when becoming wealthy and noble,
they are honored by all. Humans, devas, nāgas, ghosts, and kumbhāṇḍas Will never make offerings to one who lacks steadfastness.
If one attains the subtle stage of samādhi, the wise person then gains a vast treasury of knowledge;
revered by gods and humans alike, they are able to bestow supreme gifts upon sentient beings.
Having heard such benefits as these, which were expounded by the most supreme Buddha,
I have renounced both my kinsmen and all my wealth, desiring to hear this samādhi being taught.
The youth Candraprabha, his heart filled with joy, joined his palms toward the Buddha and spoke these words:
“After the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha-Sage, I shall protect and uphold this supreme Dharma of the Buddha.”
One should be able to renounce one’s own life and all the various pleasures of the world;
in the future, during times of fear in the degenerate age, one shall uphold this supreme and wondrous samādhi.
Seeing the immeasurable sufferings in the world, I gave rise to great compassion and desired to rescue them;
toward them I further gave rise to great loving-kindness, and thus I have expounded this supreme samādhi.
Five hundred people in the assembly all rose, vowing likewise to protect and uphold this samādhi.
The youth was their leader therein, and together they maintained this supreme samādhi.
At that time, the youth Candraprabha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what is called ‘samādhi,’ what is it?”
The Buddha said:
"Young man, listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall explain it for you."
Namely: first, the ability to pacify the mind; second, the absence of arising; third, non-conceptualizing wisdom;
fourth, the casting off of the heavy burden; fifth, the attainment of the Tathāgata’s wisdom; sixth, the majestic power of a Buddha.
1. Power; 2. Governing one's desires and attachments; 3. Eliminating hatred and anger; 4. Severing and departing from ignorance;
5. Abiding in mental correspondence; 6. Relinquishing the non-abiding mind;
7. Delighting in wholesome dharmas; 8. Desiring to transcend conditioned existence; 9. Abiding securely in the Right [Path].
15. Faith; 16. Constant vigilance at night; 17. Not abandoning meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*);
18. Increasing wholesome states already arisen; 19. Having no delight in rebirth; 20. Not creating various karmas; 21.
Not reckoning the internal sense bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*); 22. Not reckoning the external sense bases (*bāhyāyatana*).
12. Not praising oneself; 23. Not disparaging others; 24.
Not staying in the homes of laypeople; 25. Having matured one’s ethical conduct; 26.
Being incapable of being slighted or deceived; 27. Possessing great merit and virtue; 28. Self-awareness.
29. Not being flighty; 30. Abiding in dignified deportment; 31.
Abandoning coarse and harsh speech; 32. Being free from anger and resentment; 33.
Providing protection and rescue for others; 34. Guarding one's spiritual friends; 35. Safeguarding secret teachings.
36. Not giving rise to thoughts of harm toward sentient beings;
37. Not vexing those who uphold the precepts; 38. Always speaking with gentle words; 39. Not relying on the triple world; 40.
Attaining patient compliance regarding all-knowledge.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"I have opened the gate of the Deathless; I have explained the intrinsic nature of all phenomena;
I have shown the faults of birth and death; I have revealed the benefit of Nirvāṇa."
I have already taught you to distance yourself from evil associates, And to always draw near to virtuous friends;
To leave behind all clamorous crowds and dwell in tranquility, To constantly cultivate a mind of loving-kindness without ceasing,
To always guard and uphold the pure precepts, And to joyfully delight in the dhūta ascetic practices.
If one can constantly practice the wisdom of equanimity, attaining this samādhi will not be difficult.
This enables one to reach the stage of quiescence, never falling into the stage of a śrāvaka;
one shall surely realize the Buddha’s wisdom and attain the immeasurable virtues of all Buddhas.
Seeing that sentient beings possess the vessel of wisdom, I preach the Buddha’s insight to reveal it to them;
If they can resolve to seek supreme wisdom, then attaining this samādhi will not be difficult.
If you give rise to envy regarding food, you should contemplate that once consumed, it possesses no purity;
that it was achieved through immeasurable effort; and by deeply contemplating this, one can attain meditative concentration.
No thing can bring forth this concentration; it must arise from pure precepts.
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is eternally quiescent, yet ordinary people, lacking wisdom, cannot realize it.
If one can abide with the mind in tranquil meditative concentration, that person always possesses the Buddha within;
the Honored One among Men constantly beholds all sentient beings as they perpetually cultivate such samādhi of cessation.
By recollecting the Buddha’s physical marks and virtues, one can cause the sense faculties to remain undisturbed;
with a mind free from delusion and in accord with the Dharma, one attains hearing and wisdom as vast as the great ocean.
The wise one dwelling in this samādhi, Gathering mindfulness while walking in the place of circumambulation,
Is able to see thousands of billions of Tathāgatas, And also encounters immeasurable Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
If a person’s mind is deluded, they will grasp at limitations within the Buddha-dharma;
yet within the immeasurable there is no measure, for the virtues of the Tathāgata are inconceivable.
There is nothing in all the worlds that can be compared to you; how much less could there be anyone who surpasses you?
Since all wisdom and all virtues are perfectly integrated within you, one has no doubt that you will certainly attain Buddhahood.
Attaining the Tathāgata’s body, the color of purple gold, Being supremely beautiful and a kinsman to the world,
With the mind dwelling in peace through such conditions— One is then called a Bodhisattva who has attained meditative concentration.
This contemplation of the Buddha’s marks is a conditioned activity;
it can eliminate all perceptions of marks, after which one abides in the signless and is thus able to realize the emptiness of all phenomena.
One is able to dwell securely in the Dharma-body;
knowing that all that exists is non-existent, and having cultivated the mark of non-existence, one then perceives the Buddha as not being the physical body.
I shall now explain this well for you: those who proceed to such a state as this—namely, the realization of all conditioned phenomena—possess immeasurable reflection that never ceases.
If there is one who can give rise to such a mind,
thinking: "I shall recollect the Buddha’s marks and signs,
as well as his wisdom," that person is able to cultivate such mindfulness, single-mindedly advancing toward non-retrogression.
Whether walking, sitting, or practicing walking meditation, they have no doubt regarding the wisdom of all Buddhas.
Having attained freedom from doubt, they make this vow:
"May I attain Buddhahood as the Honored One of the Three Realms."
One shall surely behold all Tathāgatas and, entering into the Buddha-dharma, be able to discern it.
Having arisen from this samādhi, one bows the head in worship to the Buddhas of the ten directions;
with body, speech, and mind all purified, one praises the Buddhas without ceasing.
Constantly cultivating such a mode of mindfulness of the Buddha, one will see all Tathāgatas day and night.
Even when encountering the most grievous illness at the point of death, and being oppressed by pain and distress to the point of utter despondency,
one shall never abandon the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha, so that the intensity of suffering does not seize this mind.
Because that person understands these dharmas for themselves, they know that all dharmas are empty;
by abiding in such gates of teaching, they do not grow weary of the bodhisattva practices.
Having heard of such benefits as these, one should seek the peerless wisdom of the Tathāgata,
lest one later give rise to regret, for supreme enlightenment is difficult to attain.
I have now spoken to you at length; yet if you do not practice this Dharma, it is like a person who, though possessing excellent and wondrous medicine, cannot cure their own illness.

Therefore, one should know how to make this selection: namely, by seeking the supreme samādhi and constantly practicing precepts, learning, and generosity; once these are attained, that samādhi will not be difficult to obtain.
The Moon Lamp Samādhi Sūtra, Volume One;
The Moon Lamp Samādhi Sūtra, Volume Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Northern Qi Dynasty.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the youth Candraprabha, saying:

"In the past, immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable incalculable eons ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Śabdaguṇa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."

“O Youth! At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śabdaguṇa had eight hundred million śrāvakas assembled in his first congregation; all were arhats whose outflows were exhausted, who had attained their own benefit, who had destroyed the fetters of existence, who relied upon the true teaching, whose minds were well-liberated, and who had reached the shore of mastery over all minds.

In his second assembly there were seven hundred million, and in his third assembly six hundred million; all of them were likewise great arhats whose outflows were exhausted, who had attained their own benefit, who had destroyed the fetters of existence, who relied upon the true teaching, whose minds were well-liberated, and who had reached the shore of mastery over all minds.”
“O youth! At that time, the lifespan of that Buddha was forty thousand years; Jambudvīpa was peaceful, prosperous, and joyful, with its population flourishing and everywhere filled.”
“O youth! At that time, there were two great kings in Jambudvīpa:
the first was named Dṛḍhabala, and the second was named Mahābala.”
Each of these two great kings ruled over half of Jambudvīpa; the territories of both kings were peaceful, secure, and prosperous, with a flourishing population that filled them entirely.
At that time, the Tathāgata Ghoṣadatta appeared in the world in the kingdom of Mahābala. “O youth!

At that time, King Mahābala invited the Tathāgata Ghoṣadatta and the community of bhikṣus for a full thousand years, providing them with offerings of all kinds of clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites—everything that was appropriate, pure, and faultless.”
“O youth! That Tathāgata Śabdaguṇa and his community of śrāvakas receive abundant offerings, honor, and praise.

At that time, there were faithful householders and brahmins who, having conceived a resolute intention toward the Tathāgata Śabdaguṇa and his community of śrāvakas, emulated King Mahābala in making offerings—namely, regarding worldly wealth as the supreme offering—but those people did not know how to practice true worship.”
How does one practice making offerings? It is said:

by receiving and upholding the five precepts and the eight precepts; by leaving the household life to go to the Buddha; by personally attending upon him and inquiring after the Dharma; and by seeing the profound patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti).
“O Youth! At that time, the Tathāgata Śabdaguṇa had this thought:

‘These sentient beings are of inferior resolve; they are unable to receive and uphold the five precepts or the eight precepts, go forth to the Buddha to visit and inquire after him, perceive the profound Dharma-patience, cultivate the holy life of tranquility and seclusion, receive full ordination to attain the status of a bhikṣu, or undertake and practice ultimate roots of goodness. Thus, they are entirely devoid of such instruments of the bliss of cessation and the unsurpassed, sublime joy, and instead offer me only worldly wealth.’”
These sentient beings desire only minor pleasures and mistake them for ultimate bliss;
these sentient beings value only the phenomena of the present life and those of future lives, and are unable to cherish or revere the roots of goodness that lead to the ultimate.
What is meant by "valuing the present life"?
It refers to delighting in the five sensual pleasures.
What is meant by "valuing the roots of goodness for future lives"?
That is to say, the joy of being born in heaven.
What is called the ultimate root of goodness?
It refers to ultimate purity, ultimate auspiciousness, the ultimate holy life (*brahmacarya*), ultimate exhaustion, the ultimate finality, and ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
I now teach such a Dharma so that these sentient beings do not regard their practice of giving as the ultimate or most excellent form of worship, but rather worship me through the supreme practice.
"O youth! At that time, the Tathāgata Śabdaguṇa, wishing to awaken King Mahābala and the various elders, brahmins, and others, spoke these verses:
"If a person practices the giving of wealth and food, They cannot be said to mutually respect one another."
Such conduct as this is not to be praised; the Buddhas and the wise have already abandoned it.
If one speaks of the wisdom of non-self, such a superior person should be served and honored.
One whose faith in the Noble Truths is unshakable—honoring and respecting such a person is what the Buddha praises.
If one offers wealth and food as gifts, one obtains only minor benefits in the present life;
if one can distance oneself from such giving, that person accomplishes the practice of renunciation.
If one can give rise to the mind of non-possession, And can further manifest the dharma of non-possession,
And can also possess pure faith in non-possession— Such a person will swiftly accomplish the unsurpassed path.
There is no one dwelling amidst the five desires, nor producing attachment toward wife and children, who—
being an ordinary fool constantly remaining in the household— can attain the exhaustion of outflows;
yet one who feels weary of and renounces the five desires as if they were a pit of fire, and can become free from passionate defilement toward wife and children, [is able to do so].
Fearing the household life and seeking liberation, one will not find it difficult to attain supreme enlightenment.
Among all the Tathāgatas of the past, those of the present, and those of the future, there has never been one who,
while constantly dwelling at home in the realm of desire, was able to obtain the supreme and wondrous path.
Having renounced the royal throne like spittle, dwelling in remote and secluded places,
he severed the afflictions and subdued all Māras, awakening to and realizing the stainless, unconditioned Path.
If one were to make offerings for thousands of millions of billions of years to as many World-Heroes as there are sands in the Ganges,
yet another who is able to feel weary of and renounce the household life— such merit is the most supreme.
Neither food and drink nor clothing, nor various exquisite flowers, incense, and unguents—
such things as these do not constitute an offering to the Buddha that can equal the practice of the Dharma by one who has gone forth from the household life.
If there are those who joyfully seek awakening, who can benefit sentient beings and grow weary of the world,
who proceed toward a secluded place and take seven steps— such a karmic reward is the most supreme.

“O Youth! At that time, when King Mahābala had heard the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śabdaguṇa explain such meanings regarding the benefits of renunciation and spiritual practice, he further thought:

‘As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, the Tathāgata does not teach the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) as being ultimate purity, ultimate auspiciousness, ultimate holy conduct (brahmacarya), ultimate exhaustion, ultimate finality, or ultimate nirvāṇa.’”
That King Mahābala further thought to himself:
"One cannot attain the unsurpassed state, nor realize the purpose and benefit of unsurpassed practice while dwelling as a householder; I shall now distance myself from such conduct."
"I must now shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and leave the household life for the homeless state to go forth into the Way.

"Young man! At that time, King Mahābala, together with eighty thousand of his retinue, surrounded him from front and back as they proceeded to the dwelling of the Buddha Ghoṣadatta. There they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit at one side."

"O Youth! At that time, the Tathāgata Śabdaguṇa, knowing the inclinations and desires in the hearts of King Mahābala and his retinue, immediately proclaimed and analytically revealed for them the Samādhi of the Equality of the Essential Nature of All Dharmas and the Absence of Proliferation."

"O Youth! At that time, King Mahābala, having heard of this samādhi, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; with a heart of deep devotion and delight, he immediately renounced his royal throne in the presence of the Buddha Ghoṣadatta, left the household life out of right faith, shaved off his hair and beard, and donned the three dharma robes."

Having gone forth, he was able to extensively hear, receive, read, recite, memorize, analyze the meaning of, and practice in accordance with this samādhi; by virtue of these roots of goodness, he did not fall into the evil realms for twenty million kalpas.

Subsequently, he encountered two hundred million buddhas, from whose teachings he was always able to go forth as a monk. At the site of each and every buddha, he heard, received, recited, and analyzed the meaning of this samādhi, practicing in accordance with it. By virtue of these roots of goodness, he gradually fulfilled a period of ten billion kalpas and attained the path of Buddhahood, receiving the name Jñānavīra Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. He benefited immeasurable and boundless sentient beings before finally entering parinirvāṇa.
"O youth!
You should observe that this samādhi possesses such supernatural power that it enables a bodhisattva to attract and realize the wisdom of a Buddha. O youth!"

The eighty thousand members of the retinue led by that King Mahābala, upon hearing of this samādhi, leaped for joy with great delight; their hearts were filled with deep affection and they all followed the king in taking genuine faith and leaving the household life, shaving off their hair and beards and donning the dharma robes.

When those who have left the household life hear this samādhi, read and recite it, receive and uphold it, analyze and explain it, and practice in accordance with it, they shall, by virtue of these roots of goodness, not fall into the evil realms for twenty million kalpas. In each and every kalpa, they shall encounter ten million buddhas and always attain renunciation under those buddhas.

Having already left the household life, they hear this samādhi, read and recite it, receive and uphold it, and should cultivate and abide in its practice. By virtue of these roots of goodness, after a full hundred thousand kalpas, they shall each attain the path of Buddhahood in different worlds, all bearing the same title: Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān—named Dṛḍhavīryaparākramakṣama. Having benefited immeasurable sentient beings, they will subsequently enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
“O youth! This samādhi possesses such great power that it enables a bodhisattva to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"I recall in the distant past, through inconceivable eons, a Buddha appeared who was able to bring benefit to sentient beings;
his name was the Great Sage Honored One, Śabdaguṇa."
In the first assembly, the gathering was complete with eight hundred million, all of whom were śrāvaka disciples;
in the second assembly, there were seven hundred million, and in the third, six hundred million arhats—
all of whom had exhausted all outflows, were free from afflictions, and had reached the further shore through their various supernormal powers.
That Buddha’s lifespan was forty thousand years, and his buddha-field was exceedingly magnificent and pure.
At that time, there were two kings in Jambudvīpa named Mahābala and Dṛḍhabala;
the lands inhabited by these two kings each comprised one half of Jambudvīpa.
The Buddha appeared in the kingdom of King Mahābala, where all superior humans and devas made offerings to him;
the king attained pure faith in the Buddha and venerated and made offerings to him for a full thousand years.
Countless people of the land studied under this king, making various offerings to the Tathāgata;
yet, using only worldly wealth rather than the Dharma as their offering, they fully satisfied both the Buddha and his śrāvakas.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"By preaching this Dharma to cause him to renounce desire, I shall surely cause that king to give rise to weary detachment and go forth as a monk within my Dharma."
At that time, the Honored One among Men spoke these verses:

"Abandoning unwholesome dharmas is the teaching of the Buddha; Living at home involves many faults and is fraught with all manner of suffering. To practice according to the Dharma is the true offering to the Buddha."
At that time, having heard these verses spoken, the king went alone to a secluded place and thought:
"I can no longer remain entangled in the household life while performing the most supreme offering of the Dharma."
He immediately renounced his royal throne like nasal mucus or spittle, together with eighty thousand attendants;
they all went at once to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and stood before the Honored One.
The Buddha, knowing their inclinations and desires, taught them the tranquil meditative absorption so difficult to perceive;
hearing it, they felt love, reverence, and joy, and with universal delight, they immediately went forth into homelessness.
Having gone forth, he studied, recited, upheld, and extensively analyzed this samādhi;
throughout the subsequent two hundred million eons, he never fell into the three evil realms.
By means of these various roots of goodness, this person shall behold ten billion Tathāgatas;
within their Buddha-dharma, they will always leave the household life and proclaim such a supreme samādhi.
These shall later attain Buddhahood, all sharing the same name, Firm Great Diligence;
they will benefit immeasurable billions of sentient beings, and later enter nirvana like the extinguishing of a fire.

At that time, the Great Powerful King of old, having long since attained the Way of the Buddha under the name Jñānavīra, benefited immeasurable billions of beings; having established them in Bodhi, he entered Nirvana.
Having heard such supreme benefits, as praised by the Buddha for upholding this sutra in the final age,
those who can reverently uphold the treasury of the Buddha-dharma will swiftly become the most eminent among men.
“O youth! Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who delights in this samādhi should practice that which was first performed. O youth!”
What is the initial practice of a bodhisattva in this samādhi?

Young man, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with great compassion as his foremost motive, constantly and diligently makes offerings—whether the Buddha is in the world or after his parinirvāṇa—namely: flower garlands, powdered incense, unguents, jeweled banners, pennants and canopies, vocal music, song and dance, performances and instrumental music, clothing, food and drink, and medicines for the sick; and if he dedicates all these roots of goodness toward such a samādhi, seeking no other dharmas to offer to the Buddha, nor seeking exquisite forms, nor seeking wealth and resources, nor for the sake of rebirth in heaven, nor seeking a retinue, but thinking only of this Dharma.
This bodhisattva does not perceive even a Buddha within the dharmas, much less perceive a Buddha outside of the dharmas.
Therefore, young man, this is the true worship of the Buddha;
yet one does not perceive a Buddha that can be attained, nor does one grasp at the notion of a self, nor seek for karmic retribution.

This bodhisattva, with the three wheels purified, makes offerings to the Tathāgata with flower garlands, powdered incense, unguents, jeweled banners, flags and canopies, sounds, song and dance, performing music, food and drink, clothing, and medicinal remedies for the sick; dedicating this toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they obtain inconceivable merit and inconceivable retribution through these roots of goodness, and by means of this samādhi, they swiftly achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If a person offers incense to the One of Boundless Wisdom, They shall obtain the immeasurable fruit of fragrance;
For thousands of millions of kalpas, they will remain free from evil realms, Forever devoid of all foul odors and impurities."
Having practiced sublime conduct for ten million kalpas, Making offerings to hundreds of billions of Tathāgatas,
One attains the fragrance of supreme precepts upon becoming a Buddha;
In both the giving of fragrance and the receiving of fragrance, there is nothing at all— If one can give rise to the mind to give in this way, [one attains it].
Then one attains the supple and supreme patient acceptance;
though one's body be cut for others as if it were mere coins, for thousands of millions of billions of Ganges-sands of eons,
the mind remains firm and non-retrogressive.
How is it that one is said to have attained "patience" (kṣānti)?
How, again, is one said to be "conforming" (anuloma)?
And how is one said to be "non-retrogressive" (avaivartika)?
Why, furthermore, is one called a bodhisattva?
Because they are without the notion of self and free from afflictions, and are able to know that all phenomena are utterly extinguished—
for these reasons, it is called patience (kṣānti).
The wise one constantly practices according to the Dharma, knowing all Buddha-dharmas without doubt;
for this reason, they are called "one who accords with [the truth].
If, while practicing, a worldly Māra appears in the form of a Buddha and speaks these words:
"‘The Buddha-way is difficult to attain; one should become a śrāvaka.
To be unwilling to believe and accept this is called non-retrogression.
This alone cannot realize the path to the nectar of immortality; rather, it encourages the abandonment of evil paths and abiding in the happy realms."
For this reason, they are named Bodhisattvas;
by means of the teaching of non-self, they bring about awakening, such that even in their dreams they do not give rise to thoughts or maintain the notions of sentient beings or a life-span.
Even if there were immeasurable Māras, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who manifested in the form of Buddhas and came to his presence, all would say:
"Within the body there is a divine self."
He then said:
"There is no self; you are not a Buddha.
Having realized this, one does not dwell with afflictions; it is only through conceptual proliferation that one speaks of existence."
Having seen that they move through the world in a state of quiescent extinction,
one immediately establishes names for them; yet, when sought throughout all directions, these names cannot be found—
know that these characters have no place from which they come.
A bodhisattva cannot be sought in any direction, nor can they be found even within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*);
one who knows thus is called a bodhisattva.
A bodhisattva never gives rise to the view of a self-identity; such a bodhisattva abides in the first stage of generating the mind of awakening (*prathamacittotpāda*).
All evil views are severed and afflictions are exhausted.
That which is called "sentient beings" and "life-span"— the essence of all phenomena is empty like an illusion—
is something that those non-Buddhists cannot know.
Those who give rise to attachment and stinginess regarding robes and alms bowls, as well as those who are fickle,
playful, and flighty, do not know the Buddha’s bodhi.
Those who are deceitful, treacherous, violent, and lack self-restraint have no pure faith in the Buddhas.
This is not knowing the Buddha’s bodhi;
having no faith or refuge in the Buddha’s Dharma, and showing no respect for fellow practitioners of the holy life—
this is not knowing the Buddha’s bodhi.
Deeply loving and delighting in the Buddha-dharma, and being able to show reverence to fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring—
this is how one knows the supreme enlightenment.
Taking joy as one's bedding and seat, taking dhyāna as food, and taking samādhi as drink;
Thus one is able to know the Buddha’s bodhi.
By practicing right mindfulness in the empty forest, the fragrant flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment are most delightful;
having smelled them, one attains the unsurpassed path.
This is not a ground traversed by others— namely, the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—
who that wise person would not find delight in it?
Even if one were to speak for as many immeasurable kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, one could never exhaust the description of the virtue of a single hair-pore of the Buddha.
Because the Tathāgata’s wisdom is boundless,
the World-Honored One, free from fear, has taught this: if one quickly instructs oneself and others to uphold this samādhi,
unsurpassed bodhi will not be difficult to attain.

“O Youth! Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should skillfully know how to enter the three patiences—namely, knowing those first patience, second patience, and third patience—and within these patiences, they should skillfully know them, and furthermore, they should skillfully know the wisdom regarding them.”
Why is this? If a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses skillful knowledge regarding patience and wisdom, that bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Therefore, young man!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to swiftly seek unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, they should receive and uphold this Dharma-gate of the three kinds of patience.

Having upheld it, they should explain it extensively for others, benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, rescuing the world, and benefiting, bringing peace, and happiness to all devas and humans.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for the sake of the youth Candraprabha, spoke these verses to praise this Dharma-gate of entering the three patiences:
"Having no conflict or contention with any sentient beings, Not uttering words that are not beneficial,
And always being able to abide securely in the Dharma of benefit— This is what is called the first patience."
Knowing that all phenomena are like illusions, one does not grasp at or cling to these very characteristics;
because one can neither increase nor decrease within wisdom, this is called the first supreme patience (*kṣānti*).
Having already studied and practiced all the sūtras, one’s wisdom remains constantly in accord with the well-spoken teachings.
To have no doubt regarding the Buddha’s immeasurable wisdom is called the first supreme patience;
if, upon hearing all well-spoken teachings, one has no doubt as if they were the Buddha’s own words and can believe in all the Buddhas’ dharmas, this is called the first supreme patience.
They constantly expound the sūtras of definitive meaning, preaching exactly as the Buddha has taught;
if they speak of a self, a person, or sentient beings, one should know this is a skillful means for the sake of guiding and receiving others.
Regarding the various heterodox views of the many non-Buddhists, the Bodhisattva’s mind remains undisturbed;
instead, they turn toward those people with deep compassion—this is called the second mark of supreme patience (*kṣānti*).
All *dhāraṇīs* appear before them, and they have no doubt regarding the gates of retention (*dhāraṇīmukha*).
All spoken words are entirely true; this is called the second mark of supreme patience.

Even if the characteristics of the four great elements—namely earth, water, fire, and wind—should undergo transformation, one never regresses from the Buddha’s bodhi; this is called the second mark of supreme patience.
All the various crafts and skills in the world, the Bodhisattva is able to study and master them all;
seeing no one superior to himself, this is called the third mark of supreme patience (kṣānti).
Through the power of śamatha, he attains subduing; through vipaśyanā, he is immovable as a mountain.
No sentient being can deceive them; this is called the third mark of supreme patience.
All their speech is always in meditative concentration; whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, they are constantly in samādhi.
Their samāpatti is firm as they reach the further shore; this is called the third mark of supreme patience.
Abiding in right concentration, one attains supernormal powers; One travels to many Buddha-fields to preach the Dharma.
The power of the wise one’s spiritual feet never diminishes; This is called the third mark of supreme patience.
When practicing such tranquil concentration, All other classes of living beings—
Being unable to know the limits of their mental states— this is called the mark of the third supreme patience;
even if all sentient beings in the world were to simultaneously become Buddhas and expound the Dharma,
this person would be able to fully receive and comprehend it all— this is called the mark of the third supreme patience.
In the east, west, south, north, and the four intermediate directions, as well as in the two directions of above and below—it is thus in all directions that one sees the Buddha;
this is called the third mark of supreme patience (*kṣānti*).
One is able to manifest infinitely many bodies, all of which are made of true golden color.
Traveling to immeasurable lands to preach the Dharma— this is called the third mark of supreme patience;
throughout all the Jambudvīpas of this Buddha-world, everyone beholds the form of the Bodhisattva,
and both gods and humans recognize him— this is called the third mark of supreme patience.

Regarding all Buddha-dharmas and the spheres of the Buddhas' conduct, the wise are able to skillfully train in all the majestic deportments of the Teacher; this is called the third mark of supreme patience.
If all sentient beings throughout the world were to come and praise this bodhisattva,
and the bodhisattva felt joy at that, they would not yet have trained in the Buddha’s wisdom.
If all sentient beings throughout the world were to revile and slander this bodhisattva...
If one gives rise to anger or resentment toward this, know that the Buddha’s wisdom has not yet been cultivated.
If one’s mind does not rejoice upon gaining gain and offerings, and feels no sorrow or distress when they are lost or contrary,
with the mind dwelling as stable as a mountain— this is called the third mark of supreme patience.
The first is called the patience that accords with sounds; the second is called the patience that accords through reflection;
the third is called the patience of non-arising through cultivation. By training in these three patiences, one attains bodhi.
If there are bodhisattvas who are able to attain these three supreme patiences,
when the Sugata beholds those bodhisattvas, he immediately bestows upon them the prediction of unsurpassed enlightenment.
If there are inconceivable numbers of billions of sentient beings who hear this prophecy,
they shall all resolve their minds upon unsurpassed bodhi,
saying: "I must surely become a Honored One among men."
Upon hearing such sounds of prophecy, the great earth immediately shook in six ways;
light universally illuminated the worlds of the ten directions, and an immeasurable variety of sublime flowers rained down.
If there are bodhisattvas who are able to attain these three supreme patiences,
they shall no longer perceive birth or death, nor likewise their arising and ceasing;
if there are bodhisattvas who are able to attain these three kinds of patience...
One sees neither those who have already aged nor those currently aging; by abiding securely within the Dharma, one attains such a state.
The Bodhisattva thoroughly understands that all various phenomena are empty and quiescent in their essential nature, just like an illusion.
This emptiness is likewise neither arising nor ceasing, because the essence of all phenomena is empty and quiescent.
If there are sentient beings who come to show reverence, prostrate, honor, and offer worship,
the Bodhisattva feels no partial affection toward them, for they have deeply penetrated the essential nature of the world;
if there are sentient beings who come to strike or revile them, the Bodhisattva feels no resentment or pride toward them.
He turns toward that person with a heart of compassion, desiring to bring them liberation;
even if they strike him with swords, staves, tiles, or stones, his mind harbors no anger toward them.
Abiding in the dharma of patience regarding selflessness, the Bodhisattva does not fear giving rise to hatred or concealment.
The Bodhisattva thoroughly understands that all various phenomena are empty and quiescent in their essential nature, like an illusion;
if one can abide securely within these dharmas, one will be venerated by all humans and devas.
If someone were to take a sharp adamantine sword and sever each of my limbs and joints one by one, my mind could endure it without malice or resentment;
my increasing compassion would remain undiminished from the start.
When his limbs and joints were being butchered and carved with knives, the Bodhisattva immediately formed this thought:
"If you have not yet attained the state of enlightenment, I vow that I shall not realize nirvana."
Such power of patience is supreme, for it abides in the patience of non-self.
These bodhisattvas of great renown have practiced this for immeasurable nayutas of kalpas,
even exceeding that number as many times as the sands of the Ganges, yet they were still unable to realize awakening.
If one were to practice the conduct of a Buddha for that long, how much more so could their awakened wisdom be described?
Even if one were to speak for inconceivable billions of eons, those various marks of virtue would never be exhausted;
well-established in the patience of non-self, these are the Bodhisattvas of great renown.
If one wishes to be able to know bodhi, one must abide in the accumulation of sublime wisdom;
if one cultivates the patience taught by all Buddhas, attaining supreme bodhi will not be difficult.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the youth Candraprabha, saying:

"In the past, vast, long ago, immeasurable, incalculable, and inconceivable eons beyond asankhyeyas, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Anutpāda (Arising from Non-existence), a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
Why is he named the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Akiṃcanyasamudgata?
Young man, when that Buddha was born, he ascended into the air to the height of seven tala trees, walked seven steps, and spoke these words:
"All dharmas are utterly non-existent; all dharmas are utterly non-existent.
This sound pervaded the entire trichiliocosm.
At that time, the earth deities informed one another in succession until their voices reached the Brahma world, saying:

"In this world, a Buddha has appeared in the world, named Arisen from Non-existence (Anupapāda) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. At the moment of his birth, he walked seven steps through the air and spoke these words:
'All dharmas are entirely non-existent.'"
"O youth! For these reasons, that Buddha is named Arising from Non-existence (Anabhibhūta).
When that Buddha attained perfect enlightenment, all the trees, groves, and medicinal herbs uttered these words:"
"All dharmas are entirely non-existent.
Boy! At that time, all the sounds produced in that world also spoke these words:
"All dharmas are entirely non-existent. "O Youth!
