The Teacher gives rise to great compassion And proclaims the subtle, wondrous, and supreme sound.
In immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas past, you also once inquired about such meanings;
having become the Honored One who is the kinsman of the world’s salvation, now that you have realized the fruit, please explain it to me.
Yakṣas, rākṣasas, nāgas, and pūtanas, gazing up at the Most Victorious Honored One among bipeds,
all stood with palms joined in reverence, wondering for what reason the World-Honored One smiled.
A great multitude of bodhisattvas has gathered like clouds from many billions of lands, endowed with supernatural powers;
these eldest sons born of the Tathāgata’s mind all pay homage with palms joined.
The World-Honored One, the Guide, does not manifest a smile without cause; this Supreme Being has displayed a smile.
With a voice like the sound of a celestial drum and exquisite speech, for what reason and by what cause has he manifested this smile?
The Bodhisattva Gandhahastin comes from the east, From that world of Akṣobhya Buddha, surrounded by a multitude of nayutas of bodhisattvas; He has come here for the sake of questioning Śākyamuni.
Furthermore, from the world of Sukhāvatī, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and Mahāsthāmaprāpta,
surrounded by a host of nayutas of bodhisattvas, have come to question the Lion of the Śākyas, the Two-legged One.
In the past, at the abodes of immeasurable billions of Buddhas, he made offerings to boundless Tathāgatas,
as numerous as the sands within the great ocean, in order to practice the unsurpassed, supreme Bodhi.
Praised by all the Buddhas, having perfected the virtues of a bodhisattva,
and known and heard throughout the worlds of the ten directions— Mañjuśrī stands with palms joined.
They travel through nayutas of Buddha-fields; such excellent disciples are difficult to behold.
These sons of the Buddha, having well-mastered their merits, all stand with palms joined in reverent worship.

With faculties most excellent and peerless, such as you who are disciplined and gentle, are able to uphold the entire treasury of the Buddha’s teachings; we pray that you will speak with words of harmony and kindness.
The World-Honored One, the Guide, does not manifest a smile without cause; O Supreme among Men, you have shown a smile.
With a voice like a subtle drum, we pray that you explain: by what causes and conditions was this smile manifested?
The cries of the *kokila*, the myna, the goose, and the peacock, And the thundering roar of the king of bulls—may these sounds issue forth as the exquisite melodies of celestial music.
I pray that you will proclaim words that increase joy;
May you perfectly gather compassion and be free from all faults, So that wisdom may manifest and sever ignorance.
Revealing the true meaning beyond words, having practiced and maintained it for hundreds of thousands of kalpas,
you have realized the certainty of emptiness and stillness regarding all existences, and have manifested the meanings of all phrases concerning the cessation of suffering.
Able to destroy all the wisdom of external paths, Emptiness wherein there is no sentient being nor life-span;
The Buddhas practice hundreds of thousands of deeds, Adorned by hundreds of thousands of kinds of merit.
Hundreds of thousands of devas all offer praise, and hundreds of thousands of Brahmās do likewise;
the yakṣas and rākṣasas purify their minds, while the mahoragas, garuḍas, and nāgas rejoice.
His mouth constantly proclaims without obstruction, arising from pure and wondrous karmic fruits.
Regarding all Buddhas who have entered parinirvāṇa, as well as those of the present and future worlds, he knows them all without hindrance;
this arises from the production of all meritorious virtues.
The great ocean, the earth, and all the mountains— All of them trembled in six ways.
Devas, asuras, nāgas, and mahoragas Scattered various sublime and excellent fragrant flowers;
Having severed greed, hatred, and delusion, Their ethical discipline and minds were entirely pure.
The tranquil voice is called "non-conceptual"; thus does the Great Sage roar his lion’s roar.
Possessing eloquence and wide renown, he is perfectly equanimous toward both the eye and all phenomena.
Peerless in the world and beyond reproach, I pray that out of great compassion you will explain the meaning of your smile.
The exquisite voices of the *kokila*, the *kalaviṅka*, the peacock, and the *jīvañjīvaka* birds, all sounding together at once, are most lovely;
yet they cannot serve as a metaphor for even a small portion of the Buddha’s voice.
So too the great drums, the gongs, the various kettledrums, the conch shells, the flutes, the *zhu*, the lutes, and the *konghou*.
A thousand kinds of music played simultaneously are no match for even a slight sound of the Buddha;
The thousand kinds of exquisite musical instruments of the devas, And the wondrous singing voices of the celestial maidens,
blending together to produce delight for all who hear— These are no match for even a slight sound of the Buddha.
The World-Honored Guide, with a single voice, Elicits various understandings according to their faith;
Everyone says that the Buddha speaks for them alone— We pray that the Great Śramaṇa will explain the cause of his smile.
The wondrous voices of the devas and nāgas, the garuḍas, gandharvas, and piśācas—none of these can extinguish afflictions; only the voice of the Buddha can sever them.
Though one gives rise to the mind of love, it remains unstained; by practicing loving-kindness, one can leave behind the fault of hatred;
by being able to generate wisdom, one leaves behind delusion. One who can act in this way is free from all defilements.
The Buddha’s voice does not issue from outside the assembly; it can sever all manner of hundreds of doubts.
Within that sound there is no high or low; the Sage’s wondrous voice is tranquil and equal.
Even if the trichiliocosm were to disintegrate, The great ocean were to dry up entirely in a single thought,
And the sun and moon were to fall to the earth, The Hero of the World would never speak a word that is not true.
Your sixty kinds of pure speech are profound and beautiful, like a lion’s roar, free from all fear.
Tathāgata, we pray that you explain your Brahma-voice; for what reason does this serene smile appear?
All classes of beings within the three realms of existence— You can fully comprehend their every conduct In the past, present, and future;
O Honored One among Men, we pray that you will explain the cause of your smile.
All Tathāgatas, the Greatly Compassionate Ones, have attained ultimate perfection among all powers;
with faces like the pure, full moon, the Tathāgatas never manifest a smile without cause.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on that very occasion, replied to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya with these verses:
"This youth Candraprabha thus praised the Tathāgata’s incomparable love;
having thus praised the Tathāgata, he shall later be celebrated by the world."
In the past, in this city of Rājagṛha, I have already beheld many billions of Buddhas;
in the presence of those Buddhas, I constantly inquired about such a supreme and wondrous samādhi of tranquil extinction.
While practicing the path to enlightenment, may you be my son throughout all worlds;
may you always possess unimpeded eloquence and remain eternally established in pure conduct.
In that most fearsome age of the final dharma, this alone shall be witnessed and known by Maitreya;
having dwelt in pure conduct at all times, he will be able to extensively analyze and expound this samādhi.
If one desires to seek this supreme samādhi, one will attain it by practicing according to the Way;
one will be sustained by immeasurable billions of Buddhas and make offerings to the most excellent Great Teacher.
Abiding within wisdom, I have thus prophesied: regarding these supreme and wondrous practices of Candraprabha, in the final age there shall be no obstacles.
Concerning his holy life and lifespan, he will know of billions of Tathāgatas as clearly as one gazes at an amra fruit in the palm of one's hand.
Furthermore, beyond those as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
there are eight hundred million devas and nāgas, and seven thousand billion hosts of yakṣas,
who will be able to practice offerings in the future; they shall all assist the Two-legged Honored One in making offerings in the future.
Having heard such a prophecy, he was filled with joy and delight;
Candra-prabha leaped into the air to the height of seven *tāla* trees and, abiding in space, uttered these words of wonder:
"Aho! How marvelous!"
The Buddha is said to be most unsurpassed; Abiding in the wisdom and supernormal powers of liberation, And abiding in definitive, supreme wisdom, No heterodox arguments can ever destroy him.
Far removed from the two extremes, they realize liberation; observing phenomena, they do not cling to them.
Their wisdom is unimpeded within the three realms, and they are entirely free from all conceptual proliferation.

Untainted by all conceptual proliferations, having completely severed all views, discursive thoughts, and mental investigations, one skillfully cultivates the Path without dependence; neither destroyed by others nor in conflict with others.
Furthermore, having no dependence within the three realms, he has severed all fetters and his conduct is pure;
having completely abandoned the creeping vines of the bonds of craving, the continuity of all modes of existence is utterly extinguished.
Realizing that there is no intrinsic nature, and thoroughly understanding all teachings that transcend words—
for those who are ignorant and deluded, he destroys them like a lion’s roar crushing jackals.
The Buddha now reveals for us the treasury of the sublime Dharma; I have now obtained a collection of exquisite jewels.
Having severed all evil destinies, I have now attained Buddhahood, without a doubt.
With hands adorned with the golden hue of a hundred blessings, may this precious palm touch my crown;
before the great assembly of devas and humans, I pray that the Honored One among Men shall consecrate my head.
"I recall when I was practicing in the past, during the era of the Buddha Siṃhadhvaja,
there was a monk of great wisdom named Bhadradatta who served as a Dharma teacher."
When I was a prince named Prajñāvat, my body was afflicted by a severe and grievous illness;
at that time, Bhadra-datta was my teacher, gentle, pure, upright, and endowed with the virtues of a scholar.
Five hundred excellent physicians, none lacking, have all come to treat me;
yet they were unable to eliminate my illness, leaving my kinsmen and relatives filled with grief and distress.
At that time, the Great Teacher, hearing of my affliction, came to where I was to offer his consolation;
the Worthy One, Śiṣya, immediately gave rise to a heart of compassion and expounded this samādhi for me.
Having heard this samādhi, I disregarded wealth and treasures with a heart full of joy;
because I thoroughly understood the essential nature of all phenomena, my illness and suffering were immediately healed.
The bhikṣu practiced the bodhisattva path and attained buddhahood under the name Dīpaṃkara;
when I was formerly the wise prince, I used this samādhi to eliminate suffering and affliction.
For these reasons, young man,
I now entrust this matter to you as I recall it:
you must be able to endure insults, abuse, and humiliation, and you must uphold, maintain, read, and recite this samādhi.
In the final age, there will be immeasurable bhikṣus, Who are negligent, violate the precepts, and are full of stinginess;
Firmly attached to robes and bowls, they delight in doing evil, And thus give rise to slander against this samādhi;
Envious, fickle, and unrestrained in their senses, They dwell in secular homes for the sake of greed and profit.
Constantly living off the profits from lending and borrowing, these people shall slander this samādhi.
With hands outstretched and legs sprawled, they are dissolute and unrestrained; they stride about and laugh while gazing at their own reflections.
Walking along the road with companions and jostling their arms, they manifest strange appearances when entering a village.
Such a person who does not conform to proper conduct, day and night fixes his mind upon young maidens;

he is constantly attached to their forms and sounds. While wandering through villages and towns, he displays a semblance of decorum, yet his heart is always greedily craving fine food, laughter, song, dance, and music.
Constantly seeking profit through trade and commerce, delighting in drinking, feasting, and riding,
and having stored up vast quantities of food and drink, one falls into the three evil realms at the end of life.
Devoted solely to cultivation and plowing, they cherish and guard their own dwellings;
accepting the commands of others and delivering letters, they abandon the precepts and dignified deportment.
Associating with laypeople, they violate the Buddha’s teachings; breaking the prohibitions, they abide in evil paths.
They constantly perform deeds that the Buddha does not praise—namely, various forms of deception such as using false scales and measures.
By committing such evil actions, they fall into the miserable realms.
Though possessing abundant wealth, jewels, gold, and shells, he abandoned his loved ones to go forth;
yet unable to abide securely in the mass of pure precepts, he returned to engage in the base occupation of trade.
Cows and horses, male and female, conceive and nourish their young; you rely solely on wealth and grain for your superior thoughts.
Why have you left the household life to shave your hair and beard, yet fail to protect your precepts and ritual decorum?
In the past, when I practiced for enlightenment, I cultivated ascetic practices for a thousand eons;
seeking such a state of tranquil extinction as this, the foolish, upon hearing of it, gave rise to derision.
Practicing unchaste conduct and delighting in false speech, Constantly craving gain and offerings, they head toward evil realms.
Clad in the robes of holy life as a mere outward sign, They violate the precepts and slander meditative concentration, claiming it is not the Dharma.
They mutually destroy one another, Unable to seek gain and offerings in accordance with the Dharma.
Each seeks to find the faults and shortcomings of others; at the end of their lives, they fall into the three evil realms.
Among hundreds or thousands of people, one is hard to find—namely, one who can abide in patience.
While countless people engage in factionalism and strife, they abandon patience and are constantly angry and contentious.
All praise themselves as bodhisattvas, desiring their fame to spread throughout all lands;
if they rejoice in such empty reputations, they lack even good conduct, let alone the Way.
I have never heard nor seen anyone who, while possessing no pure conduct and delighting in sensual pleasures,
could revile this Dharma without aspiration and yet attain the path to enlightenment.
Many go forth into homelessness for the sake of a livelihood, not seeking the awakening of all Buddhas;
these fools, dwelling within the view of self, are terrified when they hear the teaching of non-self.
They constantly engage in mutual disputes, exalting themselves with pride and looking down upon one another;
claiming their own views to be right and others to be wrong, they perpetually commit unwholesome deeds while falsely rejoicing.
Those who have accomplished the virtues of pure precepts, who dwell securely in a mind of loving-kindness and practice patience,
and who are disciplined, gentle, and pure in goodness— such virtuous people as these are deceived by them.
If there should be those in the future who give rise to evil thoughts, who are exceedingly aggressive and act unwholesomely,
who delight in strife and practice what is contrary to the Dharma— they shall, at that time, receive offerings.
I now offer you this wholesome exhortation: you should give rise to pure faith in me;
regarding the teachings spoken by this Tathāgata, do not associate with those who are evil.
Toward those who are intensely greedy or deeply resentful, those who are greatly deluded, dull-witted, or arrogant,
and those who lack shame, lack remorse, and have undisciplined minds— toward them all, you should swiftly arouse the power of patience.
Regarding the immeasurable virtues I have now proclaimed, a bhikṣu who does not abide therein will not attain bodhi merely by verbal expression;
it must be attained by one who practices with firm resolve.
The Moon Lamp Samādhi Sūtra, Scroll Three;

The Moon Lamp Samādhi Sūtra, Scroll Four. Part Two of the First Chapter, "The Tathāgata’s Departure from the City," translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas during the Northern Qi Dynasty.
At that time, the Bhagavat, having instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened the great assembly, rose from his seat and departed from the city of Rājagṛha.

He proceeded to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, where he spread out his seat and sat down, surrounded before and behind by the community of bhikṣus as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas.

At that time, the youth Candraprabha, together with eight hundred billion people, the eight classes of devas, nāgas, and others, as well as spirits and deities, and ten nayutas of bodhisattvas from other worlds, carrying various jeweled garlands, ointments, powdered incense, robes, banners, flowers, and all kinds of music; having erected standards and canopies and suspended silken streamers, they departed from the city of Rājagṛha and proceeded toward Vulture Peak to the place where the Tathāgata was. There they prostrated themselves at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, and presented a great offering by striking musical instruments and offering the flowers, incense, robes, jeweled canopies, standards, and streamers they had brought.
Having made the offerings, he bowed with reverence and sat to one side to inquire about the Dharma.
At that time, the youth Candraprabha spoke these words:
"I wish to ask something of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; I pray that you will grant me your permission."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the youth, saying:

“Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, I grant you leave to ask whatever you desire. Your inquiry will bring benefit to immeasurable sentient beings; I shall analyze and explain it for you, so as to gladden your heart.”
At that time, having received permission, the youth Candraprabha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By accomplishing how many dharmas can a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain this samādhi of the equality of the essential nature of all phenomena, which is free from conceptual proliferation?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed the youth Candraprabha, saying:
"A bodhisattva mahāsattva who accomplishes four dharmas is able to attain this samādhi of the equality of the essential nature of all phenomena, which is free from conceptual proliferation."
“What are the four?

First, having well trained in gentleness, dwelling in peace and security, reaching the stage of self-mastery, being able to endure insults and humiliation, and seeing the Dharma to eliminate pride—this is the first quality.
If a bodhisattva can achieve such as this, they will be able to attain the Samādhi of the Equality of the Essential Nature of All Dharmas and the Absence of Proliferation.
Furthermore, young man!

O youth! A bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes well-guarded precepts, pure precepts, foremost well-purified precepts, unclouded precepts, unimpaired precepts, unpierced precepts, unmixed precepts, precepts of indeterminate color, sovereign precepts, irreproachable precepts, non-retrogressive precepts, precepts without dependence, precepts without grasping, precepts without attainment, precepts praised by the noble ones, and precepts praised by the wise.
This is the second.
When a bodhisattva is fully endowed with this dharma, they are able to attain the Samādhi of the Equality of the Essential Nature of All Dharmas and the Absence of Proliferation.
Furthermore, young man!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, O youth, give rise to a heart of alarm and fear because they are deeply terrified of the triple world; they give rise to a heart of non-attachment because they feel weary of and seek detachment from the triple world; they give rise to a heart of urgency because they do not cling to the triple world; they give rise to a heart of great compassion for the sake of liberating sentient beings from the suffering of the triple world; and they give rise to a heart of great vigor directed toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. O youth!
This is the third.
When a bodhisattva accomplishes such [qualities], they are able to attain the Samādhi of the Equality of the Essential Nature of All Dharmas and the Absence of Proliferation.
Furthermore, O Youth!

A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva seeks extensive learning without ever feeling weary or satisfied; they value the Dharma rather than seeking wealth and profit, and they value wisdom rather than seeking fame. They receive and uphold what they hear, explain it extensively for others, and reveal its meaning. Out of compassion, they do not act out of partiality toward their own kin. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva reflects:
"How can I cause those sentient beings who have previously heard the Dharma to swiftly attain non-retrogression in unsurpassed Bodhi?"
"This is the fourth.
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these, they are able to attain the samādhi of the equality of all dharmas and the absence of conceptual proliferation.
Young man, you should know this:"

This dharma-gate of samādhi has been expounded by immeasurable Buddhas, praised by immeasurable Buddhas, extolled by immeasurable Buddhas, revealed by immeasurable Buddhas, and practiced by immeasurable Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"I recall inconceivable nayutas of kalpas past, There was a Buddha named Śarīrasvara;
That Honored Tathāgata Śarīrasvara Lived in the world for six thousand years."
Before that Buddha, there was another Buddha, Named Jñāneśvara, beloved by the world;
That Jñāneśvara, the Perfectly Awakened One, Had a lifespan of twelve thousand years.
Before that Buddha, there was a Buddha named Vīryeśvara, of great power and majesty.
That Buddha of majestic power, the Honored One among men, had a lifespan of seventy-six thousand years;
before that Buddha there was another, named Mahesvara-Svayambhujñāna (Great Sovereign, Self-Existent Wisdom);
that Mahesvara, the Teacher of Gods and Men, had a full lifespan of ten million years.
Before that Buddha, there was another Buddha, whose name was Brahma-voice Teacher (Brahmasvara-guru).
That Brahma-voice Buddha, the Honored One among Two-legged Beings, had a lifespan of a full one hundred million years.
Before that Buddha, there was yet another Buddha, named Most Victorious Freedom from the Multitude (Gana-vaśavarti-viśeṣa).
That Lord of the Assembly, the Peerless Honored One, lived for a full sixty million years;
before that Buddha there was another Buddha, whose name was Svaramaheśvara.
That Blessed One, Svaramaheśvara, lived for a full ten million years.
Before that Buddha, there was another Buddha, Named Voice-Surpassing, the Lamp of the World;
That Buddha, the Guide of the World, Voice-Surpassing, Had a lifespan of fourteen thousand years.
Before that Buddha, there was another Buddha, Named Full-Moon Face, Universal Renown.
He whose face was like the full moon and whose fame was universal lived for a single day and night;
before that Buddha, there was another Buddha named Sūryamukhapūrṇa.
That Buddha Sūryamukha, the peerless Honored One, lived for eighteen thousand years.
Before that Buddha, there was another Buddha, whose name was Brahmamukhapriya;
that Brahmamukhapriya, the Honored One among Two-legged Beings, had a lifespan of twenty-three thousand years.
Before that Buddha, there was yet another Buddha, whose name was Brahmavasu.
That Brahmā Vāsava, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, had a lifespan of eighteen thousand years.
Buddhas such as these, all within a single eon, numbering two hundred World-Leaders—listen now as I recite their names; they are all the kinsmen of the world in the three realms.
The Buddha Undestroyed Body, the Buddha Universal Sound, the Buddha Pervasive Majesty, the Buddha Pervasive Voice,
the Buddha Honored by Sound, the Buddha Renowned Name, the Buddha Valiant Body of Sound, the Buddha Pure Body of Sound, the Buddha Arisen from Wisdom,
the Buddha Knowing through Wisdom, the Buddha Virtuous Sage, the Buddha Light of Wisdom Outshining All, and the Buddha Equal Arising of Wisdom.
Jñānārci-skandha Buddha, Jñānaśūra Buddha, Brahmottama, Brahmajīvita,
Brahmasubha Buddha, Brahmasvabhāva Buddha, Brahmaghoṣa-vijaya, Brahmasvara, Brahmadeva,
Brahmadatta Buddha, Tejobala, Tejendra, Sujateja Buddha, Tejovibhu, Tejasaṃbhava Buddha.
The Buddha of Majestic Power and Vision, the Buddha of Excellent Victory, The Buddha of Dreadful Superiority, the Buddha of Dreadful Wisdom, the Well-Dreaded One,
The Buddha of Dreadful Countenance, the Buddha Arisen from Dread, The Buddha of Dreadful and Dreadful Superiority, the Buddha of Seeing Reality, The Buddha of Good Eyes,
the Moon of Supreme Excellence, the Great Guide, The Buddha of Profound and Distant Sound, the Buddha of Boundless Sound.
The Buddha Sovereign of Pure Sound, the Buddha Pure Sound, the Buddha Immeasurable Sound,
the Buddha Good Manifestation Sound, the Buddha Destroyer of Mara’s Power Sound, the Buddha Good Eye, the Buddha Pure Face,
the Buddha Pure Eye, the Buddha Immeasurable Eye, the Buddha Universal Eye, the Buddha Good Universal Eye, and the Buddha Supreme Eye.
Buddha Who Outshines with the Eye, Buddha Without Defiled Eyes; Buddha Supreme in Subduing, Buddha of Subduing, Buddha of Well-Subdued Mind, Buddha of Excellent Subduing;
Buddha of Tranquil Faculties, Tranquil Intent, and Supreme Tranquility;
Buddha of Tranquil Virtue, Utmost Tranquility, and Reaching the Shore of Samādhi; Unsurpassed Tathāgata of Tranquil Mind, the Honored One.
The Buddha Dwelling in the Tranquility of the Extremes, the Well-Regulated Mind, the Buddha of Tranquil Faculties and Concentrated Intent,
the Buddha of Blazing Tranquility, Supreme Tranquility, and Virtue, the Buddha of Valiant Concentration Who Has Crossed to the Other Shore of Tranquility,
the Buddha Who Is the Sovereign King of All Indra-Hordes, the Buddha of Universal Mastery, and the One Who Outshines All.
The Victorious One of Pure Wisdom, Lord of the Assembly; The Heroic Lord of the Assembly, Buddha of the Great Assembly;
Buddha who Sees the Dharma, Banner of Dharma, and Arising of Dharma; Buddha of the Essence of Dharma, Buddha of the Power of Dharma;
Dharma-Buddha, Buddha of Sublime Dharma, and Heroic Buddha; Buddha of the Arising of Self-Nature and Certainty.
Thus, there arose Buddhas of this very nature, numbering eight hundred million, all bearing the same name;
these Buddhas appeared during the second eon, and I made offerings to all such Tathāgatas.
The Buddha who definitively arises from the nature of phenomena— If there are those who hear his name,
and having heard it, uphold it as people of pure karma, They will swiftly be able to attain this samādhi.
The Sage-King whom I have now described— after that Buddha,
there shall be another Buddha after an inconceivable number of kalpas— shall be known as the Buddha Supuṣpavaraghoṣarāja.
The life span of that Honored One, the Tathāgata Supravr̥ṣa, was seventy-six thousand years.
At the time of this Honored Tathāgata’s first assembly, there were thirty billion arhats who possessed the six superknowledges, the three insights, and disciplined faculties;
they were endowed with great majesty and virtue, and the four bases of psychic power.
Dwelling in their final bodies, with all outflows extinguished, they are not defiled by the eight worldly dharmas.
At that time, there was also a multitude of bodhisattvas, numbering ten trillion in all;
having attained the six supernormal powers and being endowed with eloquence, they had reached the ultimate mastery in the study of the emptiness of all phenomena.
By means of supernormal powers, they travel through billions of lands, successively teaching and transforming beings beyond the sands of the Ganges;
having inquired of all Tathāgatas regarding the path they practice, they return once more to their original world.
Thoroughly versed in all the sūtras, you travel through the world as a lamp of light;
O Son of the Buddha!
This is called great supernormal power, as you travel through various lands for the benefit of sentient beings.
Staying far removed from foul conduct, one practices the holy life;
not committing various evils for the sake of desire, one is always cherished by the devas, having no dependence upon any state of existence.
Constantly seeking alms in secluded places, dwelling in emptiness and silence while practicing the dhūtas,
being learned, eloquent, and of great merit, one is able to remain unattached within the three realms.
Delighting in meditative concentration, they are fearless; having attained certainty in the meaning, they have acquired eloquence.
Having thoroughly mastered words, phrases, and meanings, these sons of the Buddha reach the ultimate conclusion with a single question.
Gathering and protecting all virtuous deeds, Fulfilling the practice throughout immeasurable eons,
Constantly praised by all Buddhas, He expounds the words and meanings of the path to liberation.
Their observance of the precepts is pure and free from defilement, like a lotus in water that remains unstained;
they always give rise to weariness toward the three realms and are never defiled by worldly dharmas.
Their minds are pure and their karma is perfectly refined; possessing few desires and being content, they are endowed with majestic virtue.
They dwell securely within the noble qualities of the future, and likewise abide in the supreme path of the three types of higher knowledge.
The essential point lies in practice, not in mere words;
by abiding in the Dharma oneself and teaching it to others, one is well-protected by all Tathāgatas and entrusted with the entire treasury of the Buddha-dharma.
Arousing fear toward the three realms, they constantly cultivate meditative concentration with a tranquil mind;
always protected by the Buddhas, they proclaim billions of kinds of sūtras.
If one were to speak billions of kinds of sūtras, far removed from all worldly teachings,
and believe in the profound meaning of the discourse on emptiness and stillness, one’s immeasurable fame and virtue would be like the ocean.
"O youth!
For immeasurable eons, I have constantly praised him without interval; what I have now spoken is but a small portion, like a single drop of water from the great ocean."
At that time, the Buddha King of Excellent Victorious Sound preached this supreme samādhi of quiescent extinction;
at that moment, the trichiliocosm was entirely filled with devas and humans.
When that Buddha preached this samādhi of tranquility, at that moment the great earth shook in six ways;
a multitude of devas and humans, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, became established in the non-retrogressive path to bodhi.
There was a king, the most supreme among men, Named Guṇabala, of great majesty and spiritual power.
He possessed five hundred sons, Whose countenances were upright and exceedingly beautiful.
He had eighty million excellent ladies, All of whom were the inner retinue of the royal palace.
The daughters born to that King Guṇarāja numbered one thousand four hundred billion.
On the fifteenth day of the eighth month, when the king was about to properly observe the eightfold precepts of the fast,
he went together with eight hundred million nayutas of people to the place where the Tathāgata resided.
He prostrated to the Unsurpassed Honored One among Two-Legged Beings, and sat to one side before the Buddha.
Knowing what his mind delighted in, the Tathāgata immediately preached for him the supreme samādhi.
Having heard of this samādhi, the king cast aside his royal throne like spittle and abandoned all those he held dear,
going forth into homelessness in the presence of that Buddha.
The queen, the ladies of the inner palace, the well-disciplined sons, and all the daughters likewise went forth;
the retinue of the inner palace and their kin numbered seven million six hundred thousand nayutas.
That king, his wife, and their son who had renounced the world, dwelt securely in courageous and constant diligence;
they practiced walking meditation without ceasing for eight full years, and while in the midst of walking meditation, they passed away.
When this Great Holy King had passed away, he was reborn in his original palace;
he manifested suddenly through transformation without the defilement of a womb, at which time the Tathāgata was still in the world.
His father was named Sthāmadhara, and his mother was named Mahāprajñā.
Once born, the prince asked his parents:
"Is the Buddha Jinasvara still dwelling in the world?"
At that time, the Tathāgata King of Supreme Sound preached for me the supreme samādhi:
it is neither through causes and conditions nor without them; among all modes of existence, he taught only this one.
The seal of the essential nature of all dharmas gives rise to thousands of millions of billions of sūtras;
this is the unsurpassed wealth of all bodhisattvas—does the Buddha still teach this samādhi today?
He teaches the Dharma without violating the law of cause and effect, And is able to cultivate the supreme Eightfold Noble Path.
The Tathāgata’s wisdom perceives the world; He fully understands all phenomena and enters the ultimate truth.
His physical and verbal actions are both pure, And his mental action is pure, as is his purity of knowledge and vision.
Having transcended all objects of conceptual attachment, does the Buddha still speak of samādhi?
Knowing that the aggregates and elements are equal, and being far removed from the characteristics of all sense bases,
Realizing the patient acceptance of the unborn and the quiescent cessation— does the Buddha still speak of samādhi?
With unimpeded eloquence entering the wisdom of tranquility, And the wisdom that thoroughly understands the distinctions of letters,
Able to transcend all matters of grasping and attachment— Is this not the Buddha still teaching the samādhi?
Knowing all sounds, one attains joy; having seen all Buddhas, one gives rise to profound delight.
Attaining the noble path that is supple and straight—does the Buddha still speak of this samādhi?
Never giving rise to anger, always disciplined and virtuous; speaking with beautiful words and ever smiling;
seeing sentient beings, first greeting them with comfort—does the Buddha still say that this is samādhi?
Revering elders without weariness, prostrating, making offerings, and constantly gazing upon them;
with a body pure and endowed with wholesome dharmas—does the Dharma King still preach this samādhi?
Never weary of pure dharmas, dwelling in seclusion and free from wrong livelihood,
remembering all stages without forgetfulness— does the Dharma King still teach this samādhi?
Skilled in the aggregates, possessing wisdom and supernormal powers, having distanced himself from afflictions and attained the stage of self-mastery,
able to sever the path of worldly speech— does the Dharma King still preach the samaya?
Always able to cultivate and advance in all supreme practices, Distant from violating the precepts and knowing what is to be observed and transgressed,
And free from all forms of affection for kinsmen— Does the Dharma King still speak of the samaya?
Having transcended all states of birth, He knows his own past lives and is free from doubt;
With a mind reverent toward the Dharma, he has heard this dhāraṇī— Does the Buddha still teach this samādhi?
Having given birth to profound, sharp, and supreme wisdom, with faith and joy as immovable as the king of mountains,
having attained the gates of dhāraṇī and being non-retrogressive— does the World-Honored One still speak of samādhi?
Constantly seeking all pure and white dharmas, Always remaining far removed from unwholesome dharmas,
With a mind that does not wander into the company of afflictions— Does the Tathāgata still teach such a Dharma?
Having reached the ultimate mastery of all trainings, And having fully exhausted all meditative concentrations,
With wisdom that inspires faith and joy— Does the Muni who preaches the Dharma still remain?

The King of Munis has taught this supreme Dharma: the knowledge that arises from the increase of transcendent wisdom, immeasurable wisdom, impartial wisdom, and the knowledge of being born according to the various realms of existence;
having left the mundane world with faith to go forth, one is unattached to the three realms and remains without dependence.
To subdue the mind and cause it to rejoice—this the Buddha calls supreme enlightenment;
to be without attachment toward any phenomena, yet always able to embrace all dharmas;
to have unwavering faith in the results of karma—this is the Dharma taught by the Most Victorious World-Honored One.
The wisdom regarding the karmic results of upholding or violating the precepts extinguishes all disputes;
the Muni among bipeds has taught this Dharma that describes the ground of neither contradiction nor contention.
Having received patience and being free from anger, he is skillful in all questions and answers.
The World-Honored One of Great Compassion has taught this Dharma, the wisdom that knows the distinctions among all dharmas;
He who knows the limits of the past and the future, who can know the Buddha-nature throughout the three periods of time,
And who possesses the wisdom that discerns the divisions of the three periods— this Dharma was spontaneously proclaimed by the World-Honored One.
Always able to bind the mind to a single point, always able to settle the body in the sacred ground,
never altering one’s deportment at any time— this is the Dharma taught by the Bull-King among Men;
adorned with a sense of shame and dread of blame, knowing how to speak to the world according to the proper occasion.
Always extending the hand of generosity, the Unsurpassed Kinsman of the World has taught this Dharma;
always able to restrain the mind with a sense of shame and dread of blame, and likewise always wearying of and detaching from what is evil and unwholesome;
following the dhūta practices and constantly seeking alms—this is the supreme Dharma taught by the Honored King of Munis.
Always harboring a sense of shame and remorse, ever joyful, Constantly making offerings to the Honored One with reverence,
Abandoning arrogance and practicing prostrations— Such is the supreme and wondrous Dharma taught by the Tathāgata;
He restrains the inferior mind and brings it to peace, Enabling one to measure for oneself the limits of one's own wisdom.
Free from the obstacles of ignorance, such a superior person teaches this Dharma;
Able to enter the wisdom of mind and the wisdom of speech, they are certain to understand all expressions.
Far removed from all that is unbeneficial, the Dharma King, the Tathāgata, teaches this Dharma.
May they always draw near to spiritual friends and remain far removed from all who are unwholesome;
may they always have faith in the Buddha and be free from negligence—this is the unsurpassed Dharma taught by the Muni.
Knowing that the world is but a provisional name and mere verbal expression, may they always grow weary of all the sufferings of saṃsāra.
To be without grief or joy regarding gain or loss is what the Muni calls the supreme Dharma;
if one receives honor and the mind is not elated, if one does not receive honor and the mind remains equanimous,
and if one hears true praise and the mind is not delighted— this is the Dharma taught by the Teacher of the World.
Always abandoning all evil paths, Not associating with worldly crowds,
Nor mingling with the ranks of the ordained— The Self-Awakened One teaches this Dharma.
The valiant remain far removed from improper conduct, And always dwell securely in the Buddha’s way.
Perfect in dignified conduct and with a well-disciplined mind— such is the Mother of Dharma spoken by the Buddha;
always remaining far from all the ways of the foolish and ignorant, and likewise far from all ways that defile the household,
while constantly protecting all the teachings of the Buddhas— this is what the one of Great Wisdom has proclaimed.
Speak little that is beautiful and well-composed; speak gentle words toward others.
Subdue all enemies in accordance with the Dharma—this is the teaching of the Great Wisdom Sun.
Know the proper seasons and measure your food and drink; be careful never to place blind trust in the ways of ordinary worldlings.
If one encounters adverse conditions yet the mind does not grieve, this is the Tathāgata’s excellent and supreme teaching;
If one sees a poor person and enables them to obtain wealth, or sees one who has broken the precepts and gives rise to compassionate rescue,
enlightening them with a heart of pity— such is the Tathāgata’s teaching of the supreme Dharma.
Always gathering all sentient beings through the Dharma, And relinquishing all manner of material wealth;
Regarding the eight worldly concerns, he makes no hoard— Such is the teaching spoken by the Great Sage, the Tathāgata.
He praises the upholding of precepts and censures their breaking; Firmly maintaining pure discipline, he is free from deceit and hypocrisy.
Not accumulating wealth and being able to renounce it— this is the Tathāgata’s most excellent teaching;
Deeply entreating all teachers and elders, and being able to practice everything according to their instructions,
Constantly drawing near to all Dharma masters— such is the Tathāgata’s most excellent teaching.
With a mind always joyful and ever-reverent, And constantly abiding in right view, One is able to be decisive regarding all wholesome deeds;
Such is the most supreme teaching of the Tathāgata.
Making the performance of various virtues one's primary concern, One skillfully abandons the perception of signs.
To remain far removed from conceptualization and the characteristics of phenomena—this is the unsurpassed teaching of the Tathāgata;
To be able to understand and know the sūtras, and to skillfully train in the meaning of the words of ultimate truth;
To realize the wisdom of liberation and always possess skillful means—this is the most supreme teaching of the Tathāgata.
Speech that issues from correct words, where mind and object correspond and the phrasing is definitive,
proclaiming what is taught without doubt— this is the Tathāgata’s most supreme teaching.
One should constantly cultivate the emptiness of all phenomena, dwelling securely in the power of the precepts, free from fear.
To wander through all places of tranquil concentration is the Tathāgata’s most excellent teaching;
To seek neither kin nor gain, with a mind free from all guile and crookedness,
And to remain far removed from all evil views— this is the Tathāgata’s most excellent teaching.
Attaining supreme eloquence through dhāraṇīs, with wisdom illuminating vast and boundlessly,
preaching the Dharma without interruption and with pure eloquence— this is the Tathāgata’s most excellent teaching;
having long practiced the four dharma-gates, one is able to enter the most virtuous conduct.
To practice and uphold this teaching of the Buddha is the most supreme instruction of the Tathāgata;
to accord with the patience regarding what the Buddha has taught, to abide in that patience and be free from all faults,
and to distance oneself from non-wisdom while abiding in wisdom— this is the most supreme instruction of the Tathāgata.
Abiding in the stage of skillful means through wisdom, one cultivates the bodhisattva’s skillful practices;
these are the deeds performed by virtuous men, and this is the most supreme teaching of all Buddhas.
Always remaining far from those who lack skillful means, the Tathāgata declares this to be the Buddha-ground.
If one rejoices with wisdom in accordance with the Buddha, this is called the Tathāgata’s most supreme teaching;
the stage of Buddhahood is vast and not for those of the two vehicles—fools and the ignorant, lacking wisdom, give rise to slander, while the wise are embraced by all Buddhas;
this is called the Tathāgata’s most supreme teaching.
The Tathāgata well understands this Dharma-gate, Which the devas revere and offer worship to;
Billion-fold hosts of Brahmās constantly rejoice in it— Does the Tathāgata still preach this samādhi?
Immeasurable thousands of nāgas constantly prostrate, and kinnaras and garuḍas always offer praise;
does the Tathāgata still teach the samādhi attained beneath the Bodhi tree?
That which is constantly sought by the wise is the wealth of this excellent Dharma;
it is not a gift of material riches, but the unsurpassed medicine. Does the Tathāgata not still teach this samādhi?
With a treasury of wisdom and inexhaustible eloquence, you can produce billions of wondrous sūtras;
you well know the knowledge of the three realms as they truly are—does the Tathāgata still speak of samādhi?
It speaks of the raft for crossing to the other shore, so as not to be drifted by the four floods;
it causes the garland of one’s renown to increase, and for this reason, this samādhi-concentration is taught.
Praising the ten kinds of supreme powers, And praising the Great Ox-King among men,
The Bodhisattva’s virtues are supreme and inexhaustible, Precisely because they have attained this samādhi;
It teaches that with a mind of loving-kindness one eliminates anger, And practices great compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
Those who follow the Mahāyāna find relief precisely through the teaching of this supreme samādhi;
it is the lion’s roar that proclaims the sublime practice, the supreme Āgama of the Buddha’s wisdom,
and the seal of the essential nature of all phenomena— such is the samādhi taught by the Buddha.
It can summon the wisdom of all-knowledge and serves as a garden for those seeking enlightenment;
it can destroy the hosts of Māra’s army—this is called the supreme meditative concentration taught by the Buddha.
It can give rise to the merits of perfect awakening and is the seal of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
The seal of the wondrous Dharma of non-arising and quiescent extinction, this supreme samādhi taught by the Teacher;
it acts as a clarifying rite for those who abide in the Dharma, yet does not manifest among enemies.
It subdues all the hosts of Māras according to the Dharma—this supreme samādhi the Teacher has proclaimed.
It reveals the stage of unimpeded eloquence, The various powers, liberations, and faculties, And the most supreme eighteen unique qualities; Through this samādhi, one attains these dharmas.
The true Dharma sought by those who seek the Ten Powers, the fundamental cause of the supreme wisdom of all Buddhas—
the Dharma taught by the Great Beings, the Buddhas, out of compassion to rescue and protect the world.
Upheld by the most excellent sons of the Buddha, and desired by those seeking liberation,
upon hearing of this tranquil concentration so difficult to see, they are beloved by all the sons of the Buddha.
The place where all Buddhas fulfill wisdom—therein the wise Bodhisattvas give rise to the seeking mind;
with minds pure and free from affliction, they should practice such samādhi of cessation.
With physical karma purified and speech likewise pure, the Tathāgata reveals for them the gate of liberation.
Free from the bonds of impure desire, one should diligently cultivate this samādhi;
Without giving rise to greed, attachment, or anger, one can swiftly attain great wisdom;
Able to give rise to clarity and extinguish ignorance, one should therefore practice the meditative concentration of tranquility.
Those seeking liberation shall attain fulfillment; those seeking samādhi will surely achieve it.
With the Tathāgata’s eye, free from blame, praise, or censure, one should practice this samādhi.
Traveling by supernormal power through many Buddha-fields, one’s psychic powers enable the vision of the virtues of all Buddhas.
It is not difficult to attain the gates of dhāraṇī; One should cultivate such a supreme, tranquil samādhi.
By sustaining the faculty of mindfulness, one attains bodhi, And can likewise sustain the vision of many Buddhas.
By explaining non-arising through subtle wisdom, One will not find it difficult to cultivate this samādhi.
That which is not in accordance with the Dharma is difficult to awaken to, for it is far removed from all words;
it cannot be understood through sounds, as one has never heard of such concentration and thus does not know it.
The wise Bodhisattva has already understood; he knows according to what the Dharma King has taught.
He can fathom the peace that is beyond destruction, solely for the sake of delivering the world.
With courageous diligence, you are able to maintain it well; with firm mindfulness, you never lose it.
Do you still say that this samādhi possesses the wisdom that exhausts suffering and the wisdom of cessation?
He proclaims that all phenomena are unborn, yet he also speaks of the birth of all things;
the Tathāgatas possess the most sublime wisdom—does the Buddha still preach this samādhi?
This Dharma was revealed by the Youth; eighty quadrillion nayutas attained the supreme patience of accordant sounds and shall never regress from supreme enlightenment.
King Dṛḍhabala replied to his son,
"This Buddha, the World-Honored One, still remains.
The king then addressed the youth with these words:
"From where did you hear this Dharma?
The son replied,
"Listen to me, O Kṣatriya King!"
I have seen ten billion buddhas and made offerings to them all throughout a single eon, Fully inquiring about this tranquil samādhi.
For ninety-four eons, I have constantly attained the knowledge of past lives;
from now on, I shall not be born from a womb, Precisely through the power of cultivating this samādhi.
I have constantly listened to the Dharma in the presence of those Buddhas; having heard it, I have practiced with deep faith.
I have always maintained this firm conviction that I shall certainly realize Bodhi, without any doubt.
While upholding, reciting, and practicing this samādhi, if anyone comes to question me—even in my dreams—I shall have no net of doubt; I will certainly attain the unsurpassed path.
Since I attained freedom from craving and attachment, I have known for certain that I would surely become a Buddha;
likewise, I have constantly given rise to this aspiration, wondering when I might attain enlightenment.
To study and uphold this supreme samādhi, if there should be a bhikṣu who instructs me,
I shall conceive a heart of reverence toward that person, just as I do for the Buddhas.
When I taught a single verse to that person while practicing the Bodhisattva’s Accordant Patience (anulomikī-kṣānti),
I gazed upon him with a sincere heart as if he were a virtuous teacher, bowing my body in reverence and making offerings to him.
Toward elder, younger, and middle-aged bhikṣus, one should give rise to shame, modesty, and reverence;
by showing such respect, one gains praise in the present life, and merit and reputation will increase in future lives.
I took no delight in contentious disputes; at that time, I dwelt in fewness of affairs.
I was able to know that evil karma leads to the evil realms, and I was able to know that wholesome karma leads to the good realms.
One who speaks unrighteously to the heedless will hear unpleasant words in return;
yet they should reflect upon their own evil karma, for whatever action one performs, it never perishes.
At that time, I felt neither anger nor pride; the Buddha taught that one should diligently practice the power of patience.
All Buddhas constantly praise and speak of patience, for by cultivating patience, one easily attains the path to Bodhi.
I have always maintained the precepts with constant purity, and have likewise caused sentient beings to abide in pure morality;
I have constantly praised the supremacy of the precepts, so that people, by abiding in pure morality, may accept them with faith;
I have constantly praised the forest hermitages, while also personally dwelling in the pure observance of the precepts.
They encourage others to practice the eightfold precepts and fasts, and likewise teach them to study Bodhi;
they encourage others to cultivate pure Brahma-conduct, and likewise teach them to abide in the Dharma and its meaning;
for the sake of others, they reveal the path to Bodhi, and after the end of their lives, they behold many Buddhas.
I recall that in a past eon, there was a Buddha named Wondrous Sound Body;
before that Buddha, I made a great vow, remaining forever steadfast through the power of patience, never wavering.
When I made such a solemn vow as this, eight hundred and forty million years passed;
though Māra came to revile, disparage, and insult me, my mind never wavered from the beginning.
At that time, having already subdued the hosts of Māra, they recognized the power of my firm resolve in compassion and patience;
with pure hearts, they prostrated at my feet, and the assembly of five hundred gave rise to the bodhicitta.
In the past, I was free from stinginess and constantly praised the practice of giving;
possessing great wealth and abundant riches, I was renowned for my fame and served as a patron during times of famine.
If there is a bhikṣu who upholds this samādhi, or is able to practice it and explain it to others, one should constantly make offerings to him; those who form such a resolve shall attain Buddhahood.

At that time, I possessed that unsurpassed karma; seeing the Buddha, the World-Honored One, supreme among men, I was always fully ordained throughout every birth, becoming a bhikṣu and a recipient of the Dharma Master’s teachings.
I always delight in the practice of dhūta, and likewise dwell in empty, silent forest hermitages;
I do not act with flattery for the sake of food or drink, and I am content with whatever little I obtain.
At all times I am free from envy, and I never cling to the household life;
since I neither cling to home nor harbor resentment, I delight in the araṇya without ever falling away.
At that time, I always dwelt in the practice of loving-kindness; even if others reviled me, I felt no anger.
With a mind of compassion, well-tamed and gentle, the garland of my fame filled the ten directions.
Constantly practicing few desires and knowing contentment, Delighting in ascetic practices and dwelling in forest hermitages,
Also always wandering for alms without weariness, With vows firm and unshakable.
Cultivating the practice of faith, one remains ever pure; One’s faith in the Tathāgata becomes ever more profound.
This is because there are great benefits in trusting the Buddha: The faculties remain unimpaired and one is always upright.
Acting exactly as the Buddha has taught, one accomplishes such steadfast practice;
what benefit is there in this steadfast practice?
The devas offer worship and joyfully entreat you.
The virtues I have proclaimed, as well as the supreme virtues in the world and other virtues—
those wise persons who seek to practice the path to bodhi should cultivate and study them.
I now call to mind my difficult practices, which I have constantly cultivated since the distant past;
if I were to recount them now, it would take a long time, so let us go together with you toward the presence of the Buddha.
That Bodhisattva of Great Benefit, Wisdom, and Excellence, having attained the five supernormal powers in their entirety,
traveled to the Buddha by means of his power of psychic travel, accompanied by many thousands of millions of Brahma kings.

King Dṛḍhabala’s heart was filled with joy; together with his retinue of hundreds of millions, he went in person to the presence of the Honored Tathāgata, prostrated at his feet, and stood before the Buddha.
The Buddha, knowing the king’s heart and his aspirations, immediately expounded this samādhi for him;
having heard this samādhi, the king renounced his royal throne and went forth into homelessness.
Having gone forth, he mastered, recited, and explained this samādhi to others;
after six thousand kalpas had passed, he attained buddhahood under the name Padmottara.
The king had six billion followers who, together with him, went to the Buddha;
having heard of such a supreme samādhi, they too rejoiced with leaping joy and went forth into homelessness.
Those who have left the household life will, regarding this samādhi, uphold, recite, and explain it to others;

after sixty nayutas of kalpas have passed, they shall all attain Buddhahood within a single kalpa, named Buddhas of Subduing Wisdom and Supreme Excellence. Immeasurable humans and devas will offer them worship.
Each of these Buddhas of great renown has delivered beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
I am that very King Sthāmadhara, who practiced the supreme and wondrous conduct of bodhi;
those five hundred sons of mine in former times were the final protectors of the Dharma.
Throughout these thousands of billions of kalpas, I have practiced with courageous diligence, free from indolence,
single-mindedly seeking this supreme samādhi solely for the sake of unsurpassed bodhi.
"O youth!

If there are bodhisattvas who wish to attain such a supreme concentration, they should exert themselves with fierce diligence, disregarding even their own lives, and train as I have diligently striven."
The Moon Lamp Samādhi Sūtra, Scroll Four;
The Moon Lamp Samādhi Sūtra, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Northern Qi Dynasty.
The Buddha again addressed the youth Candraprabha, saying:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva receives, maintains, reads, recites, explains to others, and practices according to the teachings of this samādhi sūtra, they shall obtain four merits."
What are the four?
First, the fulfillment of merit; second, not being destroyed by enemies; third, the accomplishment of boundless wisdom; and fourth, the accomplishment of immeasurable eloquence.
"O Youth!

If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, maintain mindfulness of, contemplate, and extensively explain to others this sūtra of samādhi, they shall obtain these four kinds of merit."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Merit and virtue are ever fulfilled, And at all times they never cease;
Because of upholding such a samādhi, One attains the realm of all Tathāgatas.”
Guarded by the merit of heroic vigor, always achieving success at all times,
one who practices such supreme, tranquil concentration will surely attain unsurpassed, sublime enlightenment.
He has no enemies whatsoever, and is never harmed by foes;
his wisdom is fully accomplished and perfected, remaining constant and uninterrupted at all times.
That person accomplishes immeasurable wisdom, And likewise possesses boundless insight;
With immeasurable and boundless supreme eloquence, It is because they maintain such a sublime samādhi.
They accomplish a fulfillment of the mass of merit, And also achieve the most wondrous bodhisattva conduct.
They have no enemies whatsoever, because they maintain this supreme samādhi of quiescence;
their wisdom is vast and boundless, and they likewise achieve infinite, supreme eloquence.
Their voice is exquisite and most delightful, because they preach such a supreme samādhi.
A virtuous friend is beloved by the wise, for they are able to proclaim one's own true welfare;
all people know such a person to be a treasury of merit, for they proclaim this supreme meditative concentration.
One shall obtain excellent gains and fine garments, and likewise acquire superior, exquisite, and delicious food.
His countenance is upright and exceedingly lovely, because he maintains such tranquil concentration;
He frequently beholds the Buddhas, the Kinsmen of the World, because he makes peerless offerings to the Buddhas;
There are no obstacles or difficulties whatsoever, because he maintains such supreme concentration.
Standing before the Buddha, they offered praise, Speaking hundreds of sublime verses with a joyful heart;
Their wisdom remained undiminished, Because they had taught such tranquil concentration.
The World-Honored One of Ten Powers sat before them, His body adorned with the marks and signs, lovely to behold.
Stainless and pure like a mountain of gold, because they have cultivated such a supreme concentration;
their wisdom has never suffered any diminution, and their erudition and insight are likewise abundant,
as they have accomplished the most excellent treasury of the Great Dharma by expounding this samādhi.
Their wisdom is vast and immeasurable; though one were to speak for many hundreds of eons, it could not be exhausted.
Having heard such profound and tranquil concentration, they abide as the Buddha has taught.
Thus, O Son of the Buddha! They will not be born in any of the difficult realms.
He is always a king who governs the country according to the Dharma and remains forever at peace, because he maintains such a supreme samādhi.
Even if those with the Ten Powers were to describe his meritorious benefits for immeasurable and boundless billions of kalpas,
they could not exhaust even a small fraction of them, just as a single drop of water from the great ocean.
At that time, the youth was filled with great joy; suddenly rising from his seat, he adjusted his robes and stood up.
Joining his palms in reverence toward the Buddha, he gave voice to words of praise born of immense delight:
"The World-Honored One, the Great Hero, is most extraordinary; you are able to act as a source of light for the kinsmen of the world."
The Great Muni, the Honored One, has spoken of these merits, Revealing such supreme benefits.
Great Sage, Hero of the World, speak for my sake; I pray you will look upon me with compassion and grant me protection.
Who, in this final age, will be able to hear A sūtra such as this?
With a voice as wondrous as that of the kalaviṅka bird, a deep and far-reaching sound like the roar of thunder,
and endowed with immeasurable, supreme wisdom—
thus he spoke these words to the youth Candraprabha:
"Listen now attentively as I shall explain the unsurpassed, most supreme, and subtle practice:
those who wish to protect and uphold the Dharma should listen to and receive this samādhi sūtra;
with a reverent heart, they should make offerings to all Buddhas and seek the Buddha’s wisdom with a pure mind."
Furthermore, one should cultivate a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, and listen to and receive such sūtras;
Accomplishing the dhūta practices that leave behind transgressions, and cultivating the forest of merit of tranquility;
Abiding securely in the great, supreme, and wondrous wisdom, one listens to and receives such samādhi sūtras.
Those sentient beings who engage in evil conduct, as well as those who violate the precepts—
such wicked bhikṣus as these are unable to hear this samādhi sūtra.
Those who courageously practice all the pure conducts (brahmacarya), whose minds are free from all defilements and turbidity,
and who are constantly protected by the Buddhas— into the hands of such people this sutra shall enter.
If there are those who, toward immeasurable Buddhas, have served them with reverence and cultivated offerings;
Such a person shall be born in the final age, and this sutra shall fall into their hands.
If a person in a past life committed evil deeds while among the followers of external paths,
upon hearing this sūtra, their heart will find no joy and they will give rise to aversion.
Having gone forth within the Buddha-dharma, they do not seek livelihood for the sake of nirvāṇa;
bound by stinginess and envy, they will surely slander the Buddha’s scriptures.
Clinging greedily to the households of others and giving rise to parsimony, they are protected by the Māra Pāpīyān.
Seeking only gain and profit while breaking the prohibitions, they will certainly have no faith in the Buddha-dharma;
having failed to plant roots of goodness in the past, they give rise to arrogance before attaining wisdom;
these foolish worldlings who rely on the view of self will likewise lack faith in the final age.
While dwelling in worldly meditative concentrations, they falsely imagine they have attained the fruits of realization;
claiming for themselves the status of Arhats who consume the offerings of others, they surely slander the supreme enlightenment of the Buddha.
If one were to destroy all the stūpas and temples throughout the entire Jambudvīpa,
or if one were to slander the Buddha’s bodhi, the sin of the latter would be far greater than that of the former;
and if one were to kill an arhat, the sin thereof would be immeasurable and boundless.
If there are those who slander the sūtras, the retribution for their sin shall be even greater than that.
Who could arouse such courageous vigor as to proclaim such a sūtra in this final age of evil,
at a time when right precepts and the true Dharma are being destroyed?
The youth arose from his wailing and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words:
“This morning I have let out a lion’s roar before the most supreme Dharma King.”
After the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, during the time of the final age of evil,
I shall cast away my body and life without begrudging them, and widely propagate such sūtras as these.
One is able to endure the paths of speech of fools— unreal slanders, extreme injury and humiliation,
abuse, contempt, and intimidation— patiently bearing them with courageous diligence.
Having eliminated all evil karmas committed in past lives,
and harboring no anger within, one shall surely abide securely within the Buddha-dharma.
With his pure, exquisite, Jambu-river gold-colored hand, the Tathāgata stroked the crown of the youth Candraprabha’s head and uttered these harmonious and elegant words:
“The youth Candraprabha possesses great majestic power.”
I shall now provide you with my protection, so that during the time of the final age and future lives,
you shall encounter no obstacles or difficulties, no danger to your life, and no hindrances to your holy life.
Furthermore, there were others who arose all at once— eight hundred bhikṣus upholding the Dharma—
who declared:
"In the final age, we shall certainly protect and uphold this sutra."
At that time, many billions of yakṣas and nāgas,
as well as another eight nayutas, immediately rose from their seats and addressed the World-Honored One with these words:
"Regarding this bhikṣu— those of us who have just risen from our seats— "
In the evil world of the final age, I shall certainly protect those bhikṣus.
When such a sūtra as this is being preached, through the empowerment of the Buddha’s supernatural power,
all the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and immeasurable buddha-fields will tremble.
In accordance with all the worlds that are moved, and in accordance with those worlds, many Buddhas are manifested;
all these are transformations of Śākyamuni, who expounds such sūtras as these.
In all the Buddha-fields that exist, And among inconceivable billions of sentient beings,
All shall hear this supreme Dharma And abide in the wisdom of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
Within this Buddha-field in this world, there are nine hundred million hosts of devas;
all have resolved their minds upon bodhi and have scattered exquisite flowers before the Buddha, saying:
"All the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas and upāsikās..."
"Seven hundred and sixty million in number, they have all heard this sūtra.
The Honored Muni King bestowed upon them this prediction:
"They shall surely behold the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and all shall cultivate the practices for awakening."
Making offerings and paying respect to those Buddhas, for the sake of seeking the wisdom of the Tathāgata,
they were all able, in the presence of those Buddhas, to hear such a wondrous sūtra as this.
Throughout the course of more than eight hundred million kalpas, they shall all attain the state of the Honored Tathāgata;
those possessed of such merit will, within a single kalpa, deliver sentient beings and bring them peace and happiness.
In the presence of that Tathāgata Maitreya, they shall offer unsurpassed and supreme worship;
by skillfully upholding that Buddha’s true and wondrous Dharma, they shall all attain rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing.
That honored Tathāgata Vimalaprabhāsa, whose name is Amitābha,
was extensively provided with supreme offerings by him, for the sake of seeking unsurpassed bodhi.
Throughout those seventy asaṃkhyeya kalpas, having fulfilled such a number of eons,
they shall not fall into any of the evil destinies and shall obtain the hearing of such a supreme sūtra.
If there should be those in a future age who hear such a sūtra as this,
and having heard it, weep with falling tears— I have already made offerings to those people.
I now exhort you all:
because of all that I previously possessed and that which I have now, I have attained the path to bodhi; therefore, I entrust this sūtra to you.
"Therefore, young man!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to seek and delight in such a samādhi—the Dharma taught by the inconceivable Buddhas—they should skillfully understand it; they should inquire about the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas, they should have deep faith in the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas, and they should skillfully seek the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas. Upon hearing the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas, they must not harbor alarm, must not increase their fear, and must not be constantly afraid."
At that time, the youth Candraprabha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how should a bodhisattva skillfully understand the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas?”
How should one seek to inquire about the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas?
How should one have deep faith and purity regarding the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas?
How is it that upon hearing of the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas, one does not give rise to alarm, does not increase fear, and does not remain in constant dread?

At that time, there was a son of the gandharvas named Pañcaśikha, who, together with five hundred other sons of the gandharvas of similar kind, followed behind the Buddha carrying various musical instruments, desiring to make offerings to the Buddha.
At that time, Pañcaśikha thought to himself:
"Just as I previously made offerings before Śakra Kauśika and the Thirty-three Gods, I shall now offer this music and song to the Tathāgata, the God among Gods, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
At that time, Pañcaśikha, the son of a gandharva, together with five hundred other sons of gandharvas, simultaneously struck their lapis lazuli lutes and produced exquisite musical sounds.
At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought:

"By means of my effortless, playful supernormal power, I shall cause the youth Candraprabha to attain one-pointed abiding within the inconceivable Buddha-dharma, and further cause the musical instruments and vocal melodies of Pañcaśikha, the son of the Gandharvas, to manifest in exquisite splendor."

At that time, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, those five hundred musical instruments produced sounds that were perfectly harmonious, elegant, and refined; they issued forth sounds of non-desire, sounds in accord with the Dharma, and sounds corresponding to the Dharma—namely, verses on the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas:
“Within the path of a single hair, many Buddhas appear, Their number equal to the sands of the Ganges;
The Buddha-fields and lands are likewise so, Yet the essence of those Buddha-fields is empty and signless.”
Upon a single hair-tip, the five realms of existence appear— namely, the hells, the various animals,
as well as the hungry ghosts, devas, and humans— all of whom are entirely cool and free from crowding;
within that space of a hair-tip, oceans, ponds, along with all rivers and springs appear.
All are neither constrained nor cramped; this is called the inconceivable nature of the Buddha-dharma.
Within the tip of a single hair appear all mountains—Kālaparvata, Sumeru, Munjina, and Mahāmujina;
this is called the inconceivable nature of the Buddha-dharma.
Upon the tip of a single hair, he manifests hells— The Withering Heat, the Cold Ice, the Feces and Urine, and others;
Sentient beings born there undergo immeasurable and extreme suffering.
Upon the tip of that same single hair, he manifests celestial palaces— Sublime palaces, vast and expansive, sixteen *yojanas* in size.
Innumerable devas dwell upon the hairs, fully experiencing the supreme bliss of the heavens;
yet when a Buddha appears in the world within those hair-tips, the Dharma therein flourishes most brilliantly—
those of unwise intellect are unable to behold it, for their past karmic conduct has been impure.
In some places they hear of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, and at other times they hear that the Dharma has been extinguished;
yet in those very same places, they may also hear that the Buddha is now present, expounding the Dharma.
Furthermore, there may be someone who, upon a single hair-tip, believes their own lifespan to be infinite;
or again, one who hears of a short life in that same place on a hair, realizing it perishes as soon as it arises and does not endure for long;
or again, one who forms such a conception regarding the path of the hairs:
"I have attained the vision of the Buddha and made offerings to him.
Yet the Buddha neither appeared nor was he offered to; it was simply through the power of one's own contemplative mind that joy arose.
For example, suppose there is a person who, within a dream, indulges in the five desires and experiences pleasure;
yet upon waking, those objects of desire are no longer seen, for they were only falsely perceived because of the dream.
The phenomena seen, heard, and recollected are like dreams, devoid of reality; if one attains this samādhi,
they will fully comprehend such phenomena as these,
and shall always experience happiness within the world— meaning that they neither crave nor are attached to what is pleasant or unpleasant.
Always able to find joy in mountain forests, one constantly experiences such happiness as that of a śramaṇa.
If a person is free from all attachments and remains far removed from all notions of "mine," wandering through the world like a rhinoceros,
they move like the wind through space without obstruction.
By practicing the Path, one gives rise to true wisdom: that all phenomena are empty and selfless.
If there is anyone who can cultivate such a Dharma, that person’s eloquence will be boundless.
This person constantly experiences happiness; their mind does not cling to the world.
Their mind is like the wind in the sky, grasping at neither the pleasant nor the unpleasant.
It is difficult to dwell with those one dislikes, and difficult to part from those one loves;
abandoning both of these types of friends, the person who seeks the True Dharma alone finds happiness.
If one hears a sound and craving arises, that person will inevitably give rise to anger;
bound by ignorance, delusion, and pride, they undergo suffering and affliction through the power of arrogance.
If one can abide in equanimity, being well-able to humble oneself and free from arrogance,
and skillfully attaining liberation from both the beloved and the unloved, that person is able to dwell constantly in joyful conduct.
Abiding securely in the purity of ethical discipline, With an undefiled mind delighting in meditative concentration,
Always joyfully dwelling amidst mountain forests— Such a person is forever freed from the net of doubt.
If a person harbors delusions and holds perverted views, And out of ignorance constantly delights in various desires,
Like a vulture greedily craving the flesh of a corpse, Such a person will surely follow the power of Māra.
When this verse was spoken, the youth Candraprabha attained one-pointed mental abiding within the inconceivable and profound Buddha-dharma, becoming capable of expounding the sūtras.

At that time, the gandharva Pañcaśikha and others attained the patience of accordant sounds (*anulomikī-kṣānti*); immeasurable and boundless sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; and immeasurable sentient beings obtained peace, happiness, and benefit among humans and devas.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the youth Candraprabha, saying: "A bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding all roots of goodness, merits, and the benefits of the Dharma, should be well-resolved;

should have few affairs; should distance himself from evil associates and rely upon virtuous friends; should constantly consult with virtuous friends; should delight in hearing the Dharma without weariness; should be joyful; should always seek the Dharma and always embrace the Dharma; should preach the true Dharma; should skillfully inquire of bodhisattvas; should conceive of bodhisattvas as teachers; and should respect Dharma-preachers as one would one's own teacher."
"O Youth!

If there is a bodhisattva who can receive and practice this Dharma, that person will attain inconceivable and perfect eloquence; they will gain faith and enter deeply into the ocean of inconceivable Buddha-Dharmas; their mind will reach certainty regarding the inconceivable and profound Buddha-Dharmas; and they will be able to act as a light-bringer among gods and humans."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"In the past, across many billions of kalpas, Incalculable and inconceivable,
There was then a Buddha, the Honored One among two-legged beings, Named King of Indra’s Banner and Pennant."
At that time, the Buddha spoke this samādhi: "There are no sentient beings and no life-span;
They are like foam, bubbles, and a flash of lightning, And all phenomena are like the moon reflected in water."
The life-span of sentient beings cannot be apprehended;
though they pass away from this realm and are born in another world, the karma they have created does not perish, nor do the retributions of black and white deeds ever vanish.
The supreme dharma-gate of the correspondence between cause and effect, A subtle realm of the Buddha difficult to perceive,
Where words, phrases, and meanings cannot be grasped— This is the wondrous bodhi taught by the Buddha.
Accumulating the great wisdom of dhāraṇī, From samādhi emerge billions of nayutas of sūtras;
The path traversed by nayutas of Buddhas— Such is this samādhi taught by the Buddha.
It is well able to extinguish all ailments And gather the wealth of merit of all bodhisattvas.
All Buddhas praise them, and they are honored by billions of nayutas of devas.
They speak words of truth to all ordinary beings and always remain far removed from the teachings of all non-Buddhists.
This supreme wealth of precepts praised by all Buddhas is as difficult to grasp as lightning in the sky.
In the presence of immeasurable billions of Buddhas in the past, the wise practiced the precepts and generosity;
having long distanced themselves from evil associates, they obtained the supreme paternal inheritance.
There was a bhikṣu there, a Dharma teacher, a son of the Sun who practices the holy life;
having heard this Dharma, he followed it and gave rise to the supreme mind of enlightenment.
That Buddha Indraketudhvaja addressed the bhikṣu Dharma-preacher, saying:
