"Bhikṣu! For a bhikṣu, the foremost difficulty is the difficulty of generating the mind toward enlightenment."
Guarding the precepts like a mani jewel, associating with virtuous friends in accordance with bodhi,
and always remaining far removed from evil associates, one will swiftly attain the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi.
In the past, in this Jambudvīpa, two sons of noble families who were free from negligence went forth into homelessness within the Buddha’s Dharma, like rhinoceroses dwelling in mountain forests.
Having attained the four dhyānas and supernormal powers, he is skilled in all verses and treatises and possesses no fear;
knowing fully the characteristics of both the earth and space, he travels through the air like a bird in flight.
While dwelling in the śmaśāna forest, where the woodland flowers were lush and most extraordinary,
and all manner of exotic birds gathered there, the two sons of the elder conversed together.
At that time, there was a king who went out on a hunting excursion; hearing his voice, he went to where he was.
Then the king listened to the Dharma with reverence, and he felt profound love and respect for that Dharma master.
Then the king exchanged greetings with them, and having spoken these words, he sat down before them.
At that time, the king was accompanied by a vast retinue; those who followed him numbered sixty million.
Among them were two individuals, one of whom was a Dharma teacher. Seeing the king, he addressed him, saying:
"Listen well: the appearance of the Buddhas in the world is extremely difficult to encounter; I pray that Your Majesty will not be heedless.
Life is swift and does not linger for long, like a mountain torrent rushing down a river.
Bound and oppressed by old age, sickness, and death, there is no one who can save you from the results of your own karma."
I only pray that Your Majesty will protect the True Dharma and establish the teachings of the ten powers of the Buddhas;
in the future evil age of the final dharma-ending period, you should abide with those who are in accord with the Dharma.
Thus these immeasurable wise ones, out of a heart of loving-kindness, spoke to the king;
the king and his sixty million retinue all gave rise to the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment.
At that time, having heard these words of pure Dharma—these subtle expressions of harmonious tranquility and cessation—the king’s virtuous mind leaped with joy and delight;
he prostrated with his head at the feet [of the Buddha] and took his leave.
At that time, there were countless other bhikṣus who entered the royal palace for the sake of gain and offerings;
the king knew that their conduct was improper and that they showed no respect toward those of virtue.
When the Dharma of the past Guides has come to an end, and in this future age of increasing evil,
those who are vessels of virtue will be exceedingly rare, while those who are heedless will be many and immeasurable.
Those bhikṣus who are stubborn, stingy, and arrogant, seeking gain and sustenance while clinging to various views, lack correct understanding within the Buddha-dharma;
they speak of what is not the Dharma to the king, saying:
"That Dharma teacher should be executed—he was originally one who spoke to the king of emptiness and annihilation."
He exhorted the king and me to cultivate emptiness and sever [defilements], yet he did not show the king true *nirvāṇa*.
He utterly destroyed their karmic retributions by claiming that the aggregates (*skandhas*) are empty and non-existent.
If one can kill such a deceitful Dharma-preacher, it will surely cause the Great Dharma to abide for a long time.
At that time, there was a protective deity of the king, who had been the king’s spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) in the past;
throughout the long night, he protected the king, keeping him away from evil. That deva addressed the king with these words:
“I pray the King be careful not to give rise to such a thought; the words of an evil friend are truly terrifying.”
Do not, on account of the words of wicked men, commit acts of killing against the wise Dharma Master.
Great King, do you not remember what was spoken by the bhikṣu in the forest?
In the future, during the evil age of the final epoch, the king should abide with those who are in accord with the Dharma;
the devas shall speak words of truth to that king, "Do not abandon the teachings of the Buddhas."
At that time, the king had another wicked younger brother stationed in a remote border region to guard the kingdom's frontiers.
A wicked bhikṣu went there to convert him, saying:
"Have him kill the Dharma Master who preaches emptiness and annihilationism; he has exhorted me for a long time in the past to practice, yet he does not wish for me to seek nirvāṇa."
"Great King!
Your elder brother is exceedingly foolish and evil; he does not wish for you to live at all.
There were two bhikṣus who acted as evil teachers, traveling through the air by means of their supernormal powers:
"Because I know this, I have come here; I have now explained everything in detail to the Great King.
You should quickly put the two sorcerers to death; ensure it is done in time so that you do not later regret it."
The king’s younger brother immediately donned his armor and took up his weapons;
following the words of the wicked man, he went there along with the entire host of troops to the place where the bhikṣu was in that forest.
The nāgas and yakṣas dwelling in the forest, knowing that the king’s younger brother had come with an evil intent,
rained down terrifying sand, gravel, and stones, utterly destroying the king and his entire army.
Now one should contemplate the words of evil associates, who have destroyed such a great assembly of kings;
having given rise to a mind of malice toward the Dharma Master, they shall fall into Avīci for sixty births.
At that time, those grasping and wicked bhikṣus will exhort and convert such Kṣatriya kings.
Thereafter, for ten billion births, they shall experience the immeasurable sufferings of the hells.
Those gods who exhorted that king, as well as others who protected the Dharma Master,
shall behold Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, attend upon them, make offerings, and practice the path.
This king’s retinue numbered sixty million; all went together with the king to listen to the Dharma.
Those among them who gave rise to the mind of enlightenment each attained Buddhahood in separate worlds.
The lifespan of that Buddha shall be many billions of years, and his wisdom shall be peerless and inconceivable;
those people shall all cultivate this samādhi, and having taught it, they shall all enter parinirvāṇa.
Having heard such supreme and wondrous wisdom, one is able to gather the dharmas of the merit of śīla;
with courageous diligence and non-negligence, one always remains far removed from all evil associates.
“O youth! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be attached to the body and should be able to relinquish life. Why is this?
"O youth!
If one who is attached to the body performs unwholesome deeds, for this reason a bodhisattva should understand both the physical body and the Dharma-body. Why is that?"
The Buddha-dharmakāya of all Buddhas is what is subsumed therein, not the rūpakāya;
the Buddha manifests by means of the dharmakāya, not the rūpakāya. O Youth!

Therefore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to practice what the Buddhas practice, who wish to seek the body of a Tathāgata, who wish to seek the wisdom of a Tathāgata, who wish to know the body of a Tathāgata, and who wish to know the wisdom of a Tathāgata, should receive, uphold, read, recite, extensively explain to others, and cultivate in accordance with this samādhi sūtra.
“O Youth! That body of the Tathāgata is born from immeasurable merit. The Tathāgata speaks of a single principle, namely:
that all phenomena arise from causes.”
This is because it is free from all marks, owing to its profound depth;
because phenomena are without limit, owing to their lack of boundaries;
and because phenomena have no marks, owing to the nature of marklessness.
Dharmas have no characteristics, for they are free from all characteristics;
dharmas are without movement, for they are well-established;
dharmas are not dual, for they possess only a single characteristic.
The Dharma cannot be seen, for it transcends the realm of the eye;
the Dharma cannot be conceptualized, for it transcends the ground of the mind;
the Dharma is without movement or change, for it is free from discursive proliferation.
The Dharma is ineffable, for it transcends sound;
the Dharma has no dwelling place, for it is free from caves and houses;
the Dharma has no cave or house, for it is free from speech and sound.
The Dharma has no basis, for it transcends all views;
the Dharma is free from outflows, for it transcends all retributions.

Because the mind is firm and detached from all desires, because the indestructible mind is detached from all hatred, and because steadfast and correct wisdom transcends all delusion, there is that which is spoken: namely, the teaching that all dharmas are empty.
It is without arising, because all arising has been severed;
it is impermanent, being merely a verbal designation;
it transcends the realm of sound, for it is the cessation of sound.
There is sound because of mental reflection; there is commonality of thought because of harmonious convergence. It is so because of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) within the conventional;

it is so because it is cool and free from the heat of affliction. The ultimate truth is such because it is speech as it truly is; it is free from the heat of affliction because it is *nirvāṇa*. It is indestructible because it is invincible; it is without grasping because it extinguishes the meaning of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). It is without conceptual proliferation because it is free from objective reference; it is without limit because it explains merit. It is without even a mote of dust because it explains the subtle; it arises from the successive production of great supernormal powers and original karma. It has attained the power of sovereign mastery; it is indestructible because it is solid and real. It is without limit because its names and titles are inexhaustible; it is vast because it explains the original karma of great compassion. This is the body of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If there are those who wish to see the Kinsman of the World, And to know how the Buddha’s body is,
Having practiced this samādhi, They shall immediately be able to know the body of the Tathāgata."
The Buddha is born from merit and virtue; his body is pure and exceedingly radiant.
His marks are as even as space, and no various distinctions can be found.
Since the Bodhi of all Buddhas is thus, its characteristics and appearances are likewise so.
Its characteristics and appearances cannot be apprehended; such is the physical form of the Tathāgata’s body.
The characteristics of awakening and the body itself, as well as the worlds of all Buddhas, are likewise so.
All the powers, the meditative absorptions, and the liberations—all these are identical in their single characteristic.
The essential nature of all Buddhas is exactly like this; the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is likewise so.
There is no one who can perceive the Buddha; how could the fleshly eye see the Perfectly Awakened One?
Countless people have spoken thus:
"I have once beheld the Buddhas, whose golden bodies are subtle, wondrous, and peerless, illuminating all worlds."
Empowered by all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, through their power they possess supernormal faculties;
thus they are able to behold that body, adorned with its various wondrous marks.
It manifests according to its expansive and long characteristics, yet no one in the world can perceive its true form.
If there were anyone who could know the characteristics of this body, the Buddha would be no different from the world;
if there were anyone who could know the measure of that body, they would be what are called all the Tathāgatas.
The Buddha’s body is no-body, without distinction; so it is for humans and asuras alike.
All minds are entirely empty and quiescent; the characteristics of receiving various different retributions are likewise so.
Since name-and-form and physical appearance are thus, they are pure, complete, and luminous.
There is no one capable of knowing this practice of the samādhi of quiescence;
only the Kinsman of the World has cultivated it for inconceivable billions of kalpas.
From this samādhi emerge immeasurable pure and white dharmas.
By the power of the retribution of meditative concentration, others do not see my body.
If such a mind exists, name-and-form is likewise so;
as the types of mind differ from one another, the characteristics of name-and-form are also thus.
If one perceives with coarse and large conceptions, name-and-form likewise follows them;
whether name-and-form is coarse or subtle, it all arises from the arising of recollection.
If a person’s conception is subtle, name-and-form is likewise so.
If name-and-form are not clung to, the mind and body are illuminated by light.
I recall my past lives for seventy asaṃkhyeyas;
these three kinds of evil thoughts have never arisen from the very beginning.
Because they benefit sentient beings with an untainted mind throughout inconceivable billions of eons, others do not see my body.
If there are those who can thus relinquish their minds and intentions through these things, [they shall attain liberation].
This person no longer associates with those objects;
my mind has attained liberation. Among all kinds of things, I am able to realize their nature and give rise to wisdom.
Within thousands of billions of Buddha-fields, I manifest emanations therein to preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings; for this reason, I cannot be seen.
Being without marks and without form, I am like empty space.
My body is ineffable, for the path of speech is severed.
The Great Hero’s Dharma-body is born from the Dharma;
it has never possessed a physical body, yet it is described as the Buddha.
If, upon hearing this teaching concerning this body, one gives rise to joy and delight,
then those Māras, the Pāpīyasas, will be unable to find an opportunity.
Having heard this profound and wondrous Dharma, one does not give rise to fear or alarm.
Not for the sake of livelihood, they slander the Buddha’s bodhi.
Through billions of sūtras, they proclaim the wisdom of reality as it is,
illuminating for sentient beings each and every place they go.
“O youth! This is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
If one wishes to know the characteristics and activities of the Tathāgata’s form-body (rūpakāya), one will ultimately be unable to know them—whether they be blue, or blue...”
Form that is blue-like, or has the appearance of blue; or yellow, or yellow-colored, or yellow-like, or has the appearance of yellow;
or red, or red-colored, or red-like, or has the appearance of red;
or white, or white-colored, or white-like, or has the appearance of white.
As for its appearance: whether it is crimson or purple, or crimson-purple in color, or resembling crimson or purple in appearance;
or whether it is crystal, or crystal-colored, or resembling crystal in appearance;
or whether it is fire, or fire-colored, or resembling fire in appearance.
The appearance is like gold, like the color of gold, like that which resembles gold, like the characteristics of gold;
like lightning, like the color of lightning, like that which resembles lightning, like the characteristics of lightning;
like clarified butter, like the color of clarified butter, like that which resembles clarified butter, like the characteristics of clarified butter; like beryl, like...
The color of lapis lazuli, or resembling lapis lazuli, or having the appearance of lapis lazuli;
or that of a deva, or the color of a deva, or resembling a deva, or having the appearance of a deva;
or that of Brahmā, or the color of Brahmā, or resembling Brahmā, or having the appearance of Brahmā, O youth!
This is the body of the Tathāgata.

All the physical characteristics of the Tathāgata’s body are immeasurable; because they are inconceivable, they are also inexpressible. The form-body (*rūpakāya*) he has accomplished cannot be measured by gods or people of the world.
Likewise, in every respect—whether long or short, broad or narrow—it is without limit or boundary, inconceivable, and beyond all calculation.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"In all worlds, All the atoms that exist,
As well as the springs and pools, And all the waters of the great oceans— "
Even if there were those skilled in calculation, none could know its limit;
nor could they know the number of its atoms, or even the drops of water.
Having drawn this analogy, the Tathāgata, the Guide, [spoke thus].
The drops of water are infinite, and so too are the motes of dust;
I observe that all living beings are more numerous than those particles,
and I know in a single moment their arousal of the mind and their generation of faith.
If, within my own person, the color of the outer skin were to manifest,
there would be no analogy by which sentient beings who desire faith could know it.
Such is the nature of its marks and karma, and such is its form and appearance.
None are able to know the Buddha; the mark of self (*ātman*) is just like this.
The Buddha is far removed from marks and manifests the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which is profoundly deep and immeasurable; this Buddha is inconceivable.
Perfect enlightenment is inconceivable, and the body of the Tathāgata is likewise so;
it is this inconceivable Dharma-body, because it manifests as the Dharma-body.
The activities of the mind cannot know it, and no one is able to conceive of this body.
As for his physical form and its characteristics, there is no one at all who can measure them.
Those dharmas are limitless; through cultivation over billions of kalpas, he has attained this inconceivable body and radiates pure, great light.
Sentient beings have no one who can grasp it;
Since grasping it is impossible, the body of the Tathāgata Is immeasurable and inconceivable.
Regarding all immeasurable dharmas, He nevertheless apprehends them as having measure.
Within the dharma of non-conceptualization, although there is no conceptualization,
it is spoken of as "non-conceptual" in terms of the limits of conceptualization;
this non-conceptuality free from thought is the inconceivable Buddha.
Infinite like space, it cannot be measured;
The Buddha-body is likewise, just like the great void.
If there are sons of the Buddhas who know my body as it truly is, [they shall attain this state].
He shall attain Buddhahood, and the world shall behold his inconceivable [deeds]. "O Youth!
There are four kinds of discourse of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva that are inconceivable; their exposition is likewise inconceivable and difficult to reach its limit."

“O Youth! Furthermore, there are four kinds of cultivation of wisdom for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
What are these four?

First, the inconceivable wisdom of cultivating all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable wisdom of cultivating revulsion toward the conditioned; third, the inconceivable wisdom of cultivating afflictions (*kleśa*); fourth, the inconceivable wisdom of cultivating purification.
These are the four kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are four kinds of knowledge regarding phenomena for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these four?

First, the inconceivable wisdom regarding all conditioned phenomena; second, the inconceivable wisdom regarding the reproof of conditioned phenomena; third, the inconceivable wisdom regarding the phenomena of affliction; fourth, the inconceivable wisdom regarding the phenomena of purification;
these are the four kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are four kinds of knowledge regarding persons (pudgala) for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
What are the four?

First, the inconceivable wisdom regarding the *pudgala* of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable wisdom regarding the *pudgala* who reviles the conditioned; third, the inconceivable wisdom regarding the *pudgala* of afflictions (*kleśa*); fourth, the inconceivable wisdom regarding the *pudgala* of purification.
These are the four kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are four kinds of clinging-knowledge for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
What are the four?

First, the inconceivable wisdom regarding attachment to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); second, the inconceivable wisdom regarding the reproval of attachment to the conditioned; third, the inconceivable wisdom regarding attachment to afflictions (*kleśa*); fourth, the inconceivable wisdom regarding attachment to purity.
These are the four kinds.
"O youth!
These four kinds of wisdom regarding the attachments of bodhisattvas are inconceivable; their exposition is likewise inconceivable and cannot be fully described."
“O youth! Furthermore, there are four kinds of knowledge for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas that lead away from the evil realms.
What are these four?

First, the inconceivable wisdom that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are free from the evil realms; second, the inconceivable wisdom that reproves the conditioned and is free from the evil realms; third, the inconceivable wisdom that afflictions (*kleśa*) are free from the evil realms; fourth, the inconceivable wisdom that purity is free from the evil realms.
These are the four kinds.
“O youth! Furthermore, there are four kinds of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s wisdom that severs ignorance.
What are these four?

First, the inconceivable wisdom of the cessation of all conditioned phenomena; second, the inconceivable wisdom of the cessation through revulsion toward the conditioned; third, the inconceivable wisdom of the cessation of afflictions; fourth, the inconceivable wisdom of the cessation of purification.
These are the four kinds.
"O Youth! Furthermore, there are four kinds of dhāraṇīs of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that are inconceivable; their exposition is likewise inconceivable and cannot be fully recounted."
What are the four? They are:
the discourse on the inconceivable conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), and the wisdom regarding that—this is called the first dhāraṇī;
the discourse on the inconceivable censure of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and the wisdom regarding that—this is called the second dhāraṇī.
The inconceivable discourse on the support of afflictions, and the wisdom regarding it, is called the third dhāraṇī;
the inconceivable discourse on the support of purification, and the wisdom regarding it, is called the fourth dhāraṇī.
In this way, these four kinds of inconceivables, as well as their exposition, are also inconceivable and cannot be fully described.
"Young man,
bodhisattva-mahāsattvas further possess four kinds of dharma-dhāraṇīs."
What are the four? They are:
the wisdom regarding the inconceivable phenomena of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) is called the first dhāraṇī;
the wisdom regarding the inconceivable censure of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) is called the second dhāraṇī.
The inconceivable dharmas of affliction, the wisdom regarding them is called the third dhāraṇī;
the inconceivable dharmas of purification, the wisdom regarding them is called the fourth dhāraṇī.
"O Youth!
These are called the four kinds of inconceivable dhāraṇīs of a bodhisattva; their exposition is likewise inconceivable and cannot be fully described."
“O Youth! Furthermore, there are four kinds of *dhāraṇī* associated with the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
What are these four?
That is to say: the wisdom regarding the inconceivable association with all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is called the first dhāraṇī;
the wisdom regarding the inconceivable association with the censure of the conditioned is called the second dhāraṇī;
the wisdom regarding the inconceivable association with afflictions (*kleśa*) is called the third dhāraṇī.
Inconceivable purity and its corresponding wisdom therein— this is called the fourth dhāraṇī.
Young man,
these four kinds of inconceivable dhāraṇīs, as well as their exposition, are likewise inconceivable and cannot be fully described.
“O Youth! Furthermore, there are four kinds of dhāraṇī-doors for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
What are these four?
That is to say: the inconceivable gateways of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), the wisdom regarding them is called the first dhāraṇī;
the inconceivable gateways of the censure of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), the wisdom regarding them is called the second dhāraṇī;
the inconceivable gateways of afflictions (*kleśa*), the wisdom regarding them is called the third dhāraṇī.
The inconceivable gate of purity—wisdom regarding that is called the fourth dhāraṇī.
Young man!
These four kinds of dhāraṇī gates are inconceivable; their exposition is likewise inconceivable and cannot be fully described.

Up to and including the elimination of ignorance, all wisdom possesses four kinds of inconceivable *dhāraṇīs*, and their exposition is likewise inconceivable and cannot be fully described, as explained above.
“O Youth! This dhāraṇī is itself wisdom. Such wisdom is able to understand that all phenomena exist merely as names; this is called the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (dharmapratisaṃvid).
When such knowledge of phenomena can penetrate their meanings, it is called the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid).”
Such knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) that can discern the distinctions between the verbal expressions of all phenomena is called the unimpededness of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).

If one explains those syllables—whether by revealing them, establishing them, arranging them in uninterrupted succession, elucidating them, expanding upon them, analyzing them, clarifying them so they are easy to understand, or demonstrating them universally and impartially—if one’s speech is not faltering, not mute, and not timid; if one’s discourse is without obstruction, and one’s language flows freely and with supreme ease, this is called the unimpededness of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The designations established by speech and sound, And the sounds that emerge, are likewise so;
Just as the sounds that are produced, So too is the Buddha’s wisdom."
The wisdom of all Buddhas is such, and the designation by sound is likewise;
the phenomena thus designated, and the radiance of sound, are also thus.
This radiance of sound, and even the name of the precepts, is just so.
Just as are the names of the precepts, so too are the names of the Buddhas;
just as are the names of the Buddhas, so too are the virtues of the Buddhas.
Knowing one sentient being, I know all such names.
The Buddha’s immeasurable speech has already been proclaimed by me;
the names of the precepts, the names of the Buddhas, and the names of sentient beings are all equal.
The conditioned is full of many faults, and the virtues of nirvāṇa are likewise so.
The Buddha’s benefit is thus; it is revealed through parables.
For all sentient beings who have resolved their minds, this has been shown;
from a single pore of the Guide, light likewise issues forth.
The names and the inclinations of all sentient beings—
the Tathāgata transcends them all, yet he teaches the Dharma through his voice-body.
The names of all sentient beings are revealed as belonging to a single sentient being.
In this way, the name "One Person" reveals all sentient beings.
That they all enter into equality is what the Perfectly Awakened One has taught;
he spoke of immeasurable names for the sake of the bodhisattvas.
How can I now possibly expound upon billions of inconceivable sūtras?
By upholding this scripture, one manifests without timidity;
possessing unimpeded eloquence in the midst of the assembly, one expounds upon billions of scriptures.
As space is boundless, so too is their eloquence.
These merits of the bodhisattvas are pure as they guide sentient beings;
by upholding this sutra, they achieve inexhaustible wisdom.
"By repeatedly displaying and teaching it,
one who can faithfully accept the Dharma increases their wisdom, just like a tree on the Snowy Mountains. O Youth!"
This bodhisattva practices unimpededness regarding phenomena (dharmas), seeing phenomena within phenomena and thereby attaining stable abiding.
Young man!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice unimpededness regarding phenomena, seeing phenomena within phenomena and thereby attain stable abiding?

"O Youth! This bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that what is not form is not different from form as he teaches the Dharma; he knows that what is not form is not different from form as he is able to practice; he knows that what is not form is not different from form as he seeks awakening; he knows that what is not form is not different from form as he transforms sentient beings; and he knows that what is not form is not different from form as he perceives the Tathāgata. Yet, it is not by destroying form that he perceives the Tathāgata; he does not perceive the Tathāgata as something other than form, nor as something other than the nature of form. Form, the nature of form, and the Tathāgata are equal and without duality."
"If one can perceive all phenomena in this way, it is called practicing the unimpeded dharma;
consciousness, perception, feeling, and mental formations are likewise so.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Manifesting bodhi by means of form, and manifesting form by means of bodhi—
this which is incongruous is what the Most Victorious One has proclaimed.
The characteristics of form that are spoken of are coarse, yet the nature of form is exceedingly profound and mysterious.”
Form and bodhi are equal; no distinction can be found between them.
Just as nirvāṇa is profound and is proclaimed by means of sound, yet nirvāṇa cannot be apprehended, so too is the proclamation by sound.
Sound and that which is spoken—these two are unattainable;
likewise, within this empty dharma, nirvāṇa is unattainable.
Though one speaks of the cessation of nirvāṇa, that cessation itself is unattainable.
All phenomena are unborn; as they were before, so they are afterward.
The essential nature of all phenomena is similar to nirvāṇa.
One who knows this is a true renunciant, in harmony with the Buddha-dharma.
If one beholds the form-body of the Buddha, it is said that one has seen the Tathāgata;
yet my body is not a material image, and there is no one who can see it.
To know the intrinsic nature of form—that the characteristic of form is thus—[is to see the Tathāgata].
One who can know the nature of form manifests the great body.
Thus, regarding these five aggregates, I have already known their characteristics;
having realized the intrinsic nature of phenomena, I abide in the Dharma-body.
Having established himself in the Dharmakāya, he preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings;
the subtle and wondrous Dharma of the Tathāgata cannot be expressed in words.
Its principle is profound and beyond comprehension, yet it is heard through the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One.
Through sounds and speech alone, I have attained the first fruit.
If one eliminates all perceptions and remains far removed from the affairs of conceptual proliferation,
there is no one who maintains such perceptions, yet they behold the Great Teacher of the World.
If a person can know emptiness, they will immediately know the characteristics of form;
there is no teaching of form that is different from emptiness, nor is there a separate intrinsic nature of form.
If one can know form, then one is able to know emptiness.
If one can realize emptiness, one then knows quiescent extinction.
If a person can understand that the characteristics of form are thus,
they will not be disturbed by billions of māras, nor will they retreat from or waver from that bodhi.
Unable to know this path, one who grasps at it incurs loss;
taking what is not a thing to be a thing, one grasps at non-things as things.
Deceived by the pursuit of kin and wealth, one suffers loss regarding the Dharma.
Perceiving what is not the fruit as the fruit, one loses the wealth of a śramaṇa.
Lacking diligence and possessing little vigor, one does not abide in the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*).
To one who is unfit to practice the Dharma, it should be said:
"This was not spoken by the Buddha," or again, some person might say:
"I am practicing for bodhi."
Those who lack wisdom and are difficult to tame do not respect one another.
Longing for a fine reputation, they do not dwell well in the prohibitions and precepts, constantly wondering:
"When will my fame become universally pervasive?"
For the sake of seeking gain and offerings, they gather a great multitude of people;
arrogant and heedless, their minds are solely intent on seeking profit.
They delight in staying at the houses of laypeople for the sake of honor and gain.
Building monasteries and stūpas— these are all for the sake of fame and profit.
Relying on a mind of grasping and attachment, constantly seeking with thirsty craving,
they devote themselves exclusively to worldly affairs and dwell within the realm of Māra.
He says to those laypeople:
"Sensual desire is like a flame.
Yet when he enters the homes of the laity, he defiles their women and wives.
The white-robed laypeople always regard such a person as their great teacher;
they wait for the men to go out so that the women may engage in mutual intimacy.
That household provides this bhikṣu with delicious food.
Returning to his wife’s quarters, he regards her as his own;
even a layman does not give rise to jealousy toward his wife,
yet a renunciant bhikṣu harbors envy and resentment toward another’s wife.
If worldly people living at home can skillfully guard and uphold the five precepts,
how much more so should those who have gone forth renounce all prohibitions?
Even with drums, conchs, and various musical instruments, they offer them to me as an act of worship.
The supreme practice of making offerings cannot be accomplished in the final age.
Having destroyed the various precepts themselves, when seeing others who uphold the Vinaya,
they speak thus to the world:
"He is no different from me.
When hearing praise for those who uphold the precepts, or descriptions of the realms of those who violate the precepts and commit evil;
when hearing the exposition of the true Buddha-dharma, he says:"
"This was not spoken by the Buddha.
Lacking shame and remorse, they have lost the wealth of a śramaṇa;
if one encourages them to speak the truth, they slander what I have taught."
Those whose precepts are incomplete abandon my teachings and revile the True Dharma; Avīci Hell shall be their home.
I have never seen or heard of anyone practicing such conduct.
Even those who dwell in folly and evil can attain the wisdom of the Buddha.
As for those who are flatterers and full of crookedness and deceit—
I know all such people, for my vision of wisdom never ceases.
If, for the duration of an eon, I were to speak of all those faults of those who claim to be bodhisattvas, I could only describe a small fraction of them, O youth!
You should know this:
there is no evil they will not commit during the final age of the Dharma; therefore, be careful never to associate with them as friends.
With an unperturbed and unturbid mind, you may welcome them and engage them in conversation.
One should serve and provide for them for the sake of seeking the Buddha-way.
One should inquire after their years of ordination;
if they are elders, one should offer them support and respect, performing the prostration by touching one's head to their feet.
Do not observe the faults of others; they will surely reach the site of enlightenment.
Do not give rise to thoughts of anger, but always cultivate a mind of loving-kindness and compassion.
If you see their transgressions, do not speak of their failings in their presence.
One should constantly bear in mind that whatever deeds one performs, such fruits will surely be obtained.
Toward both the young and the old, one should always speak with a smile;
when speaking, one should first offer greetings and eliminate one's own arrogance.
With clothing and food and drink, they constantly made offerings;
by giving with such a mind, these individuals all attained Buddhahood.
If one asks questions of those of long standing, it is for the sake of seeking the gift of Dharma.
One should first say:
"My learning is not extensive.
And again, one should say:
"You are all exceedingly wise; how could I dare to speak recklessly before such great beings?
When speaking, do not be hasty; you must discern who is a worthy vessel and who is not.
Once you have observed their spiritual capacities, you may explain it even without being asked."
If, within a great assembly, you see one who violates the prohibitions, do not praise the virtue of their observance of precepts;
instead, you should praise their practice of giving and other such deeds.
If you see one who has few desires, provided they are in accord with the observance of precepts, [you should likewise praise them].
Arousing a mind of great compassion, one should praise those with few desires who uphold the precepts;
if those who violate the prohibitions are few and those who maintain pure precepts are many,
having obtained such a superior assembly of companions, one may then extol the upholding of the precepts.
First, he observed the great assembly, seeing that all were delighted in various wholesome dharmas;
all those who possessed such wholesome dharmas, he praised them all.
Generosity, precepts, much learning, patience, diligence, as well as fewness of desires—
Practicing contentment and seclusion, he reveals such a Dharma;
praising such a Dharma, he fully explains the path to the next world.
Regarding all things lacking compassion, do not give way to anger, but maintain a heart of loving-kindness.
Dwelling in emptiness and delighting in dhyāna, staying far removed from the clamor of crowds—you should praise those virtues;
this is called the gateway to dhāraṇī.
Always delight in secluded places; do not be solely intent on the practice of giving.
Cultivate meditative seclusion with a single mind; do not say that the precepts alone are supreme.
Having established yourself in the aggregate of pure precepts, you can gather extensive learning and maintain it.
Because you seek this samādhi, you should constantly make offerings to the relics of the Buddha.
They are able to offer canopies, banners, and streamers, flower garlands, ointments, and powdered incense,
seeking this tranquil concentration while making offerings to all Buddhas;
with supreme musical instruments, their exquisite songs harmonize in elegant melody.
To make offerings to the Buddha’s relics, with a courageous and undaunted mind,
they take all flower garlands, every kind of incense, and robes,
and offer them all to the Buddha, seeking the wisdom of the Buddha.
The various portions of merit belonging to all sentient beings, I bestow equally without partiality;
seeking unimpeded wisdom, I call this the unsurpassed state of all Buddhas.
In the presence of former Buddhas, I have presented inconceivable offerings.
Because they seek this tranquil concentration with a mind free from partiality or attachment:
it is extremely difficult for a Buddha to appear; it is difficult to obtain a human body;
it is difficult to have faith in the Buddha’s Dharma; and it is difficult to renounce the household life and take up the precepts.
Now that you have encountered the Buddha and given rise to the bodhicitta,
do not abandon your firm vows, but abide steadfastly in virtuous conduct.
If you uphold this sutra during the final age of the Dharma, [you shall attain the fruit of enlightenment].
One will swiftly attain unimpeded eloquence and uphold [the teachings] without forgetfulness.
If one can maintain even a single verse, the mass of merit is inconceivable;
how much more so for one who can master them all and receive them fully according to their meaning?
If all sentient beings were to become Buddhas, and one were to courageously make offerings to them all with reverence and respect for as many eons as there are sentient beings; yet,
if one can receive and uphold even a single verse of this samādhi, [the latter merit would be far greater].
Compared to those former merits, they do not equal even one-sixteenth.
I know the Buddha’s wisdom and its inconceivable benefits;
by upholding this samādhi, one follows the path practiced by all Buddhas.
The Moon Lamp Samādhi Sūtra, Scroll Five;
The Moon Lamp Samādhi Sūtra, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Northern Qi Dynasty.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the youth Candraprabha, saying:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva should accomplish skillful means. Youth!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva achieve skillful means?

Young man, this bodhisattva mahāsattva conceives the thought of kinship toward all sentient beings; he rejoices in whatever accumulation of merit those sentient beings possess, and throughout the six periods of day and night, he rejoices in that merit.

By taking all-knowledge as their object, they generate merit toward all sentient beings with a mind focused on all-knowledge; through these roots of goodness, this bodhisattva swiftly attains this samādhi and achieves unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Regarding all sentient beings as one's own kin, Whatever mass of merit there may be,
Six times throughout the day and night, One should constantly give rise to the desire for sympathetic joy (anumodanā) in this goodness."
I rejoice in their pure upholding of the precepts, And in their refraining from evil until the end of life;
In the Bodhisattvas who possess pure faith, I rejoice in all their merits whatsoever.
Those who rejoice with faith and delight in all Buddhas, Their faith in the Dharma and the Sangha is likewise;
They rejoice in being able to honor and respect the Tathāgatas, For the sake of seeking unsurpassed bodhi;
They rejoice in those who are free from views of self and other, And are devoid of notions of sentient beings and a life-span.
Rejoicing in being free from all evil views, Hearing the supreme Dharma of emptiness, they love it deeply.
Giving rise to sympathetic joy within the Buddha-dharma, Having left the home life, they receive full ordination.
With few desires and contentment, they dwell in the forest, Cultivating a heart of compassion like a sword.
I rejoice in those who are solitary and peerless, Dwelling in the forest like a sword within its scabbard;
Those of pure livelihood who always possess few desires, Free from flattery and hypocrisy, nor relying on friends;
I rejoice in those who delight in stillness and leave behind clamor, Having no attachment or longing for home or kin.
Constantly fearing the three realms, wandering through the world without attachment;
rejoicing in those who have abandoned conceptual proliferation, and loathing all that undergoes birth and death;
being free from contention and practicing tranquility—if one acts thus, this samādhi will not be difficult to attain.
I rejoice in those who can discern good and evil, Who always remain aloof from all matters of contention,
And who seek noble liberation by resorting to empty groves and beneath trees— true sons of the Buddha.
I rejoice in those who always dwell in seclusion, Who do not praise themselves or disparage others.
Those who follow and delight in meritorious virtues, Abiding in the Buddha-dharma with heedfulness,
All the various virtues that assist the path to enlightenment— Heedfulness is their very root.
If there are bodhisattvas who remain free from heedlessness, It will not be difficult for them to attain this samādhi.
To encounter the Buddha-dharma is the first treasury; Furthermore, to attain renunciation is the second treasury;
Pure faith, untainted, is the third treasury; And to attain this samādhi is the fourth treasury.
Hearing of the Buddha’s realm within the great emptiness, To hear it without slandering is a supreme treasury;
If one attains eloquence, that is the attainment of a treasury, And to attain this samādhi is likewise a supreme treasury.
I have already taught those various wholesome dharmas—namely, ethical discipline, learning, generosity, and patience;
heedfulness is their root, which the Buddha has declared to be the most excellent treasury.
If there is a bodhisattva who is heedful, they will immediately be endowed with all forms of eloquence;
having no doubt regarding the Buddha’s wisdom, it will not be difficult for them to attain this samādhi.
“O youth! For this reason, you should abide in the practice of heedfulness, which is that which all bodhisattvas ought to cultivate and study. Why is this?
If even those who practice heedfulness attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, how much more so this samādhi?
Young man,
how does a bodhisattva abide in heedfulness?
"O youth! This bodhisattva accomplishes the aggregate of well-purified ethical discipline.
O youth!"
How does one accomplish the aggregate of well-purified ethical discipline?
Young man,
it is when this bodhisattva, without abandoning the mind of omniscience, trains in the six perfections.
“O Youth! If a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās without abandoning the mind of omniscience, listen attentively to all the benefits that accrue; I shall explain them to you.”
"O youth!
There are ten kinds of benefits for a bodhisattva who has faith in and delights in the dānapāramitā.
What are these ten?
First, to subdue the affliction of stinginess;
second, to cultivate the continuity of the mind of relinquishment;
third, to share one's assets with all sentient beings, maintaining firm resolve until reaching parinirvāṇa.
Fourth, one is born into a wealthy and noble family;
fifth, the mind of generosity manifests wherever one is born;
sixth, one is always cherished and delighted by the fourfold assembly.
Seventh, when dwelling among the fourfold assembly, he is neither timid nor fearful;
eighth, his excellent reputation spreads throughout all directions;
ninth, his hands and feet are soft and supple, and the soles of his feet are level and even.
Tenth, until reaching the tree of enlightenment, one does not part from spiritual friends— namely, Buddhas, bodhisattvas,
and śrāvaka disciples. Young man,
these are the ten benefits for a bodhisattva who delights in the practice of giving.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Having subdued stinginess, Increasing the mind of giving,
And maintaining firm resolve in generosity, One is born into a family of great wealth."
In whatever place they are born, they are able to give rise to a mind of equanimity;
beloved by all sentient beings, whether lay or ordained,
when they enter among the great assembly, they are fearless and without timidity.
His supreme fame spreads far and wide throughout cities and villages;
his hands and feet are ever supple, and he is endowed with the marks of perfection.
Having encountered spiritual friends—śrāvakas, buddhas, and bodhisattvas—[he attains this state].
Always harboring a mind of generous giving, never having been stingy or parsimonious,
loved by billions of sentient beings— this is the relinquishing of the benefit of stinginess;
born into a wealthy and noble clan, his mind always delights in practicing charity.
Gathering and relinquishing with firm resolve is the benefit of delighting in giving;
Standing among the great multitude, one’s excellent reputation spreads in all directions;
With hands and feet that are soft and beautiful—these are the benefits of delighting in giving.
“Encountering spiritual friends—namely Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others—and seeing them, vying with one another to come and make offerings: this is the benefit of delighting in giving.
‘O Youth!’”
The pure precepts of a bodhisattva have ten benefits.

What are these ten? First, fulfilling all-knowledge; second, training as the Buddha has trained; third, not being disparaged by the wise; fourth, not retreating from one’s vows; fifth, abiding securely in practice; sixth, relinquishing birth and death; seventh, aspiring to and delighting in nirvāṇa; eighth, attaining a mind free from entanglements; ninth, attaining supreme samādhi; and tenth, never lacking the wealth of faith.
"Young man!
These are the ten benefits of pure ethical discipline.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Fulfilling all-encompassing wisdom, training oneself as the Buddha did,
the wise do not disparage this; they are always free from fear,
their vows never regressing, and they are able to abide securely in sublime conduct."
Escaping the realm of birth and death, one joyfully aspires for Nirvāṇa;
dwelling securely free from entanglements and hindrances, one swiftly attains supreme samādhi.
Abiding in the aggregate of pure precepts, one remains far removed from all poverty.
Their wisdom is ever pure, practicing what the Buddhas have taught;
they are not censured by the noble ones because their precepts are pure.
The wise do not retreat from their vows, being courageous and dwelling well in their conduct.
Seeing the manifold faults of the world, one avoids them and proceeds toward the path of cessation.
With a mind free from hindrance, by dwelling in the power of pure precepts, one swiftly attains concentration free from affliction; this is the benefit of pure precepts.
“O youth! There are ten kinds of benefits for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who dwells in loving-kindness and patience.
What are these ten?

First, fire cannot burn them; second, blades cannot cut them; third, poisons cannot affect them; fourth, water cannot sweep them away; fifth, they are protected by non-human beings; sixth, they obtain the adornment of physical marks; seventh, all evil realms are closed to them; eighth, they are reborn in the Brahma Heaven according to their wishes; ninth, they are constantly at peace day and night; and tenth, their bodies are never parted from joy and bliss.
"Young man!
These are the ten benefits of the bodhisattva’s accomplishment of loving-kindness and patience.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"This person is not burned by fire; swords and staves cannot wound them.
They are not struck by poisons, nor can violent waters sweep them away.
They are constantly protected by non-human beings and are endowed with the thirty-two marks."
The closing of all evil realms is entirely the benefit of loving-kindness and patience;
Śakra and Brahmā, if one wishes to attain them, are not difficult to reach.
Abiding forever in a place of peace and bliss, there is inconceivable joy.
Swords and staves do not harm them; fire does not injure them; water and poison likewise do no harm.
Protected by devas, nāgas, and yakṣas, they obtain these benefits by abiding in patience:
the thirty-two marks of a great man, and no fear of falling into the evil realms.
Upon death, one is reborn in the Brahma Heaven; this is the benefit of abiding in loving-kindness and patience.
Day and night one is ever secure, with joy suffusing the entire body;
regarding the pure mind among the multitude, there are no faults or obstructions.
“O youth! There are ten benefits of a bodhisattva’s diligence.
What are these ten?

First, they cannot be subdued by others; second, they are taken into the care of the Buddhas; third, they are protected by non-human beings; fourth, they do not forget the Dharma they have heard; fifth, they are able to hear the Dharma they have not yet heard; sixth, their eloquence increases; seventh, they attain the nature of samādhi; eighth, they have few illnesses and little affliction; ninth, whatever food they receive, they are able to digest after eating; tenth, they are like an utpala flower, which is not crushed by a pestle.
"Young man!
These are the ten benefits of diligence.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
Accomplished and difficult to subdue, their minds free from regret or feverish distress,
they are protected by non-human beings and constantly behold all Buddhas;
with superior eloquence ever increasing, they arrive at inexhaustible wisdom.
Having attained the nature of samādhi, one is no longer afflicted by various illnesses;
whatever food and drink is consumed enters the stomach and is digested,
just as a blue lotus in water gradually grows.
Regarding the Dharma thus heard, having heard it, one is able to increase its growth;
constantly reflecting upon it day and night, it shall never pass in vain.
The Tathāgata, with courageous diligence, donned the armor of progress throughout the accumulation of kalpas.
Having subdued Māra and his hosts, he realized the Way and eliminated all sorrow and fear.
The Bodhisattva rescues those in all realms of existence, disregarding even his own body and life;
through his diligence, he brought forth the treasury of the Dharma—such virtues of his I have now revealed.
Diligence is difficult to overcome; it is that which all Buddhas uphold.
If one can obtain such benefit, one will before long swiftly realize the Way.
What has been heard shall not be forgotten, and what has not yet been heard shall be heard.
Increasing the power of eloquence—this is called the benefit of diligence.
One swiftly attains this samādhi; free from all illness and affliction, whatever food one consumes is digested and brings peace and happiness.
"Day and night increasing wholesome dharmas, always diligent and never regressing,
one will before long attain bodhi because of firm resolve and vigor.
'O Youth!'"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are in union with dhyāna have ten kinds of benefits.

What are these ten? First, abiding securely in ritual protocols; second, practicing within the sphere of loving-kindness; third, being free from all afflictive fevers; fourth, guarding the sense faculties; fifth, attaining the joy and bliss that is independent of food; sixth, remaining far removed from craving and desire; seventh, making the cultivation of dhyāna non-empty; eighth, liberation from the snares of Māra; ninth, abiding securely in the realm of the Buddhas; and tenth, the maturation of liberation.
“Young man!
These are the ten benefits associated with the meditative concentration of a bodhisattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"He does not dwell in what is contrary to the Dharma, but abides securely in proper conduct;
he wanders within the sphere of skillful means, remaining far removed from what is not his domain.
His mind is free from affliction and feverish distress, and he has well disciplined all his faculties."
Experiencing the bliss of supreme meditative concentration, sitting in repose free from all conditions,
far removed from thirsting desire, feasting on the flavor of dhyāna,
liberated from the realm of Māra, and dwelling securely in the sphere of the Buddhas’ conduct.
Delighting in solitude among the forest trees is the supreme skillful means;
by cultivating true liberation, one extinguishes all suffering and affliction.
Settling the mind in the pure Dharma, one remains far removed from improper conduct.
Abiding in distant objects, far from sense-fields, One attains these benefits through meditative concentration;
The mind gives rise to no feverish affliction, Realizing the noble bliss that is free from nutriment.
Body and mind are ever cool and serene— These are the benefits associated with dhyāna.
Dwelling in emptiness with the senses stilled, The mind is free from distraction;
One attains a joy surpassing that of humans, Because of skillful means in departing from desire.
With a mind untainted by the defilement of desire, One always remains far removed from the realm of Māra.
They abide in the sphere of the Buddhas' conduct, and their liberation reaches maturity.
"Young man,
there are ten benefits for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom."

What are these ten? First, to relinquish everything without grasping at the notion of giving; second, to maintain the precepts without flaw yet not rely upon them; third, to abide in the power of patience yet not dwell on the notion of sentient beings; fourth, to practice diligence while remaining detached from body and mind; fifth, to cultivate meditative concentration without any fixed abode; sixth, to be unable to be disturbed by Māra Pāpīyān; seventh, for one’s mind to remain unmoved by the discourses of others; eighth, to be able to reach the bottom of the ocean of birth and death; ninth, to give rise to supreme compassion for all sentient beings; and tenth, to take no pleasure in the paths of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
"O youth!
These are the ten kinds of benefits accomplished by a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Courageous and relinquishing all, yet not conceiving the notion of giving;
upholding the precepts without deficiency, yet having no basis for reliance;
the wise cultivate patience, yet do not perceive a sentient being."
With courageous and diligent perseverance, one remains detached from body and mind;
by cultivating supreme meditative concentration, one does not rely upon the three realms.
No māras can subdue such a person—this is the power of faith and wisdom.
His mind remains unshaken by those various non-Buddhists;
having reached the bottom of birth and death, through the power of faith and wisdom,
he has attained great compassion toward all sentient beings.
One never gives rise to attachment for the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
one neither grasps nor clings to equanimity; one maintains the precepts without dependence;
and one practices patience free from the notion of birth—these are the functions of faith and wisdom.
Through diligence one remains far removed; by practicing meditation without dependence, one is not constrained by Māra—this is the power of faith and wisdom.
Unshaken by the doctrines of others, one reaches the very bottom of birth and death.
To give rise to compassion toward those in birth is the function of faith and wisdom;
to feel no longing for the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
but to study the virtues of the Buddha, is the function of faith and wisdom.
“O youth! There are ten kinds of benefits for a bodhisattva who is well-versed in the teachings.
What are these ten?

First, knowing the aids to affliction; second, knowing the aids to purification; third, being free from doubt and confusion; fourth, establishing upright views; fifth, distancing oneself from non-paths; sixth, abiding securely on the true path; seventh, opening the gate of ambrosia; eighth, drawing near to the Bodhi of the Buddhas; ninth, acting as a light for all sentient beings; and tenth, having no fear of the evil realms.
“Young man!
These are the ten benefits of being learned.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"O youth! These ten benefits, which manifest the state of being well-versed in the teachings, are understood by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, exactly as they truly are."
Afflictions and purification— knowing truly both their conditions,
one is able to abandon afflictions and abide within purification.
With wisdom that removes doubt, one straightens the minds of others’ views.
Always remaining far removed from evil paths, Abiding on the path of true correctness,
Opening wide the gate of ambrosia, Drawing near to the Buddha’s bodhi,
Acting as a light for all beings, And having no fear of the evil realms.
Knowing the provisions for all afflictions, and further understanding the aids to purity,
the courageous one leaves behind delusion and confusion, dwelling in the subtle and pure Dharma.
Dispelling various kinds of doubts, he is able to rectify the views of others.
Abandoning the perilous and evil paths, the learned abide upon the virtuous way.
They can open the gate of the nectar of immortality;
steadfast and close to awakening, they are like a light among the masses, never fearing the evil realms.
“O youth! There are ten kinds of benefits for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the gift of Dharma.
What are these ten?

First, abandoning evil deeds; second, being able to perform virtuous deeds; third, abiding in the dharma of virtuous persons; fourth, purifying buddha-fields; fifth, proceeding to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa); sixth, relinquishing all cherished things; seventh, subduing the afflictions (kleśa); eighth, bestowing a share of merit upon all sentient beings; ninth, cultivating a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings; tenth, attaining joy and bliss through the vision of the Dharma.
“O youth!
These are the ten benefits for a bodhisattva who practices the gift of Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Practicing the most excellent giving, being without stinginess regarding the Dharma—
there are ten benefits for such a person, as the Teacher has already declared.
Abandoning worldly evil deeds, one is always able to perform wholesome actions."
Abiding in the dharmas of virtuous persons, practicing the mind of generosity,
and being able to purify all Buddha-fields as the Buddhas have taught—
proceeding to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is the fruit of the gift of Dharma.
Abandoning all worldly affairs, one trains under the Dharma King;
by subduing all afflictions, the attainment of the Way is not difficult.
With a heart of loving-kindness, one bestows upon sentient beings a share of all merit.
Not giving rise to the fetter of envy, one attains a bliss surpassing that of ordinary men.
The wise person leaves behind remorse and acts with vigor for what is wholesome;
abiding in the dharma of a true man, such is what the giver of the Dharma obtains.
Purifying that Buddha-field, Arising the wholesome dharmas that assist the path,
Approaching the site of enlightenment— This is the benefit of the gift of Dharma;
Being without stinginess or envy regarding material things, One is able to understand the specific characteristics of phenomena.
Liberated from all grasping and attachment, they encounter no obstacles regarding objects of affection.
When the wise give rise to such a mind, they cause all beings to share in merit;
attaining loving-kindness free from envy, they find joy within the wholesome Dharma.
“O youth! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in emptiness, they attain ten kinds of benefits.
What are these ten?

First, dwelling where the Buddhas dwell; second, practicing meditation without dependence; third, taking no delight in any form of rebirth; fourth, not grasping at precepts; fifth, not slandering the worthy and holy ones; sixth, dwelling in non-contention with all sentient beings; seventh, not apprehending the existence of sentient beings; eighth, dwelling in seclusion from all evil deeds; ninth, not slandering the Buddhas; and tenth, embracing all pure and wholesome dharmas.
"Young man!
These are the ten benefits for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who dwells securely in emptiness.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“The abode of the Honored One among Gods and Humans—what is called the World’s Kinsman and Guide—is where the courageous can dwell securely;
namely, that which is devoid of life-span and the like.
Having attained the bliss of that meditative concentration, he has no dependence upon the world.”
The mind does not long for rebirth, because it knows the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
If one does not grasp at precepts, one accomplishes the untainted (anāsrava) precepts;
one is not born in the evil realms and always dwells securely in the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa).
Abiding in non-contention, most gentle in the world,
understanding all matters as they truly are,
and even at the cost of one’s own body and life, never slandering the Tathāgata.
Resolute in the dharma of emptiness, They have realized it bodily and are fearless.
Beloved by all the world, The Buddha-way is inconceivable;
Those who can uphold the Buddha-way Have no doubt regarding the dharma of emptiness.
The dwelling place of the Honored One among Men is not the ground of the non-Buddhists;
he does not rely on the bliss of meditative concentration, for there is no sentient being and no life-span.
He has never had a fixed abode, nor does he rely on the joy of dhyāna.
Knowing that there is no phenomenon of a life-span, one always maintains a mind free from longing.
Skillfully knowing the self-nature of phenomena, one does not rely on any afflictions;
with faith and joy in the Buddha, the Supreme Person, one never possesses a mind of grasping or attachment.
They are always free from strife; observing all things, they cultivate the practice of detachment.
Abiding securely on the path of perfect enlightenment, they are able to uphold the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
"Young man!
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in meditative seclusion (*pratisaṃlayanā*), there are ten benefits.

What are these ten? First, their minds are not turbid; second, they abide in heedfulness (*apramāda*); third, all Buddhas cherish and mind them; fourth, they believe in the practice of perfect enlightenment; fifth, they have no doubt regarding the Buddha’s wisdom; sixth, they recognize kindness; seventh, they do not slander the True Dharma; eighth, they are well able to maintain restraint and prohibitions; ninth, they reach the stage of self-mastery (*dāntabhūmi*); and tenth, they realize the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
"Young man!
These are the ten benefits for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who dwells in meditative seclusion.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
With a mind free from turbidity and confusion, far removed from all heedlessness,
abiding in heedful conduct within the sphere of meditative seclusion,
he acts as a lamp of mindfulness for the world and increases his faith and joy.
The Buddha’s wisdom is inconceivable, and his skillful means are free from doubt;
Able to recognize the kindness of all Buddhas, one does not slander the True Dharma;
Abiding securely in virtuous discipline, one reaches the stage of subduing.
Having attained unimpeded eloquence, he delights in dwelling alone in the forest;
having renounced honor and gain, he abides in the sphere of meditative seclusion.
His mind is neither turbid nor distracted, and he has never been heedless.
The wise are always cautious; this is the benefit of tranquility.
Always mindful with fearlessness, they have faith in the Buddha’s conduct and harbor no doubt regarding the Buddha’s wisdom; this is the benefit of tranquility.
Constantly mindful of the Tathāgata’s kindness, not slandering the True Dharma,
and abiding in the skillful means of ethical discipline— this is the benefit of tranquility.
Having reached the stage of self-mastery, they swiftly realize unimpeded eloquence.
Expounding hundreds of thousands of sutras, Always remaining free from stagnation;
Swiftly gathering the Buddha’s bodhi, Protecting and upholding all Buddha-dharmas;
Subduing all heterodox arguments, Extensively cultivating the Buddha’s bodhi.
When a bodhisattva passes away from here, they will be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss;
Amitābha will preach the Dharma for them, and they shall attain the patience of non-arising. "O Youth!
There are ten kinds of benefits for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who delights in secluded dwellings. What are these ten? First, reducing worldly affairs;

second, remaining far removed from the clamor of crowds; third, being free from conflict and contention; fourth, dwelling in a place free from affliction; fifth, not increasing outflows (*āsrava*); sixth, not giving rise to strife or litigation; seventh, abiding peacefully in silence; eighth, conforming to the continuous liberation (*vimukti*); ninth, swiftly realizing liberation; and tenth, attaining samādhi through the application of effort.
"O youth!
These are the ten kinds of benefits for a bodhisattva who delights in secluded places.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
Accomplishing few affairs and remaining far removed from the clamor of crowds,
one achieves freedom from conflict and the benefit of solitary, quiet seclusion;
with a mind free from anger and affliction, one does not increase the outflows (*āsrava*).
Always harmonious and free from contention, this is the benefit of dwelling in seclusion;
with a mind settled in tranquil extinction, always delighting in the practice of detachment,
one accords with unburdened wisdom and swiftly realizes the path of liberation.
Dwelling in the forest, one practices meditative concentration;
having abandoned the faults of worldly clamor, one no longer gives rise to conflict. By delighting in seclusion, one gains this benefit:
always weary of and detached from the conditioned, one has no longing for the world.
The various outflows do not increase; such is the benefit of dwelling in the forest.
Quarrels and disputes do not arise; the mind always delights in tranquility.
Well-restraining body, speech, and mind; such is the benefit of dwelling in emptiness.
"Conforming to liberation, one swiftly reaches the state free from hindrances and burdens;
always dwelling in the joy of tranquility—this is the benefit of staying in seclusion.
Young man!"
There are ten kinds of benefits for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who delights in dhūta practices and constantly practices begging for food. What are these ten?
First, they destroy the banner of pride.
Second, not seeking intimacy;
third, not acting for the sake of fame;
fourth, abiding in the noble lineages.
Fifth, he is without flattery, without deception, does not manifest artificial signs, and is not overbearing;
sixth, he does not exalt himself;
seventh, he does not disparage others.
Eighth, to sever and eliminate craving and aversion;
ninth, when entering the homes of others, to practice the gift of Dharma rather than for the sake of food and drink;
tenth, to abide in the dhūta practices so that whatever Dharma one teaches is received with faith by others.
"O youth!
These are called the ten kinds of benefits for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who delights in dhūta practices and engages in begging for alms.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
That person is free from the conceit of "I" and does not seek to rely on kinsmen or friends;
their mind is equanimous toward gain and loss because they abide in the dhūta practices;
they do not violate the noble lineages, and they are without flattery or deceit.
Not exalting oneself, nor disparaging others;
having abandoned the minds of attachment and aversion, one teaches the Dharma without expectation.
If people receive and believe what is taught, this is the benefit of alms-seeking.
Seeking neither intimacy nor fame, dwelling securely within the noble lineages,
gentle, upright, and free from flattery or pride— this is the benefit of delighting in the dhūta practices;
not praising oneself or disparaging others, and feeling no joy upon receiving praise.
Hearing disparagement without resentment or affliction—this is the benefit of delighting in *dhūta* practices.
Giving the Dharma as a gift without seeking food, and not for the sake of honor or respect—what one says is trusted and accepted by others;
this is the benefit of delighting in *dhūta* practices.

"O youth! When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in such merits and benefits, they attain the treasury of the Buddhas, the treasury of the Dharma, and that treasury of wisdom while dwelling in seclusion; they attain the treasury of wisdom of the past, future, and present."
“Young man,
how does one attain the Buddha-treasury?
Young man, [it is thus:]”
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who delight in the practice of seclusion and dwell in empty, quiet places attain the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
What are these five? First, the divine eye;
second, the divine ear; third, the ability to know the minds of others; fourth, skillful knowledge of past lives; and fifth, the sphere of supernormal powers.
With the divine eye-element, purified and surpassing that of humans, this bodhisattva sees immeasurable and innumerable Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, in the eastern direction;
likewise, it is the same in the south, west, and north;
and in the four intermediate directions, as well as above and below, they see immeasurable and innumerable Buddhas, constantly beholding them without ever being parted.
"Young man!
This is called a bodhisattva attaining the vision of the Buddha-treasury.
Young man!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain the treasury of the Dharma?

Young man, whatever Dharma the Buddha, the Tathāgata, has taught, that bodhisattva hears it all with the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans; thus, this bodhisattva constantly hears the Dharma and never departs from it.
"Young man!
This is how a bodhisattva attains the treasury of the Dharma.
Young man!"
"How does a bodhisattva attain the treasury of wisdom?

Young man, it is because by means of this wisdom they are able to uphold all dharmas; with great compassion as their foremost priority toward all sentient beings, they preach the Dharma with a mind free from delusion, knowing the meaning of those dharmas."
"O youth! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the treasury of wisdom. O youth!"
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attain the treasury of wisdom regarding the past, future, and present?

Young man, this bodhisattva knows, as it truly is, that the mental activities of all sentient beings arise solely from the sequential arising of one's own mental activities; they contemplate the phenomena of their own mind with undisturbed thought and cultivate skillful means in accordance with the movements of their own mind.
It is the same with others; whether one sees forms or hears sounds, he knows with perfect accuracy whether there is attachment or non-attachment in the mind.
Young man!
This is called the Bodhisattva’s attainment of the treasury of knowledge of the past, future, and present.

“O youth! I have now briefly explained that a bodhisattva mahāsattva abiding in such virtues attains all buddha-dharmas; this is not the domain of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, much less that of any heterodox outsiders.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"I recall immeasurable kalpas in the past, When there was a Buddha, a Tathāgata of great renown,
Named King of the Multitude of Majestic Virtues, Who was venerated by all humans and devas."
Ten billion bhikṣus possessed supernormal powers, Having reached the shore of mastery in eloquence, Abiding in dhūta practices with minds subdued; That Buddha was endowed with such a multitude.
There were sixty-seven million cities, each two thousand li in width and length;
at that time, the world of Jambudvīpa was composed of the most excellent seven treasures.
That city was exceptionally wonderful, most marvelous and beautiful, adorned with a hundred excellent gardens and noble mansions.
Its groves and forests were like dense clouds, always filled with various kinds of flowers and fruits;
there grew diverse species of trees, such as the *āmra*, the *jambu*, and the plantain.
In Kāñcanī, Campā, and Pāṭalī, and at the Nyagrodha where flocks of birds gather—
there, among the kalaviṅkas, śukas, peacocks, and others, the king of geese, Śarabha, is filled with great joy.
The voices of various kinds of exotic birds gather as they sport within the hundred gardens;
like the sound of the supreme Śuka king Tittira, the Nala, the Bhrṅgarāja, and the swan,
their bodies adorned with various colors of plumage, they dwell amidst the lotuses and emit wondrous sounds.
All those of various species born from eggs, emitting harmonious and elegant sounds that bring joy to people,
roam through the gardens and groves for their own amusement, calling out to one another in mutual delight.
Mundapāśī and sugandhika flowers, pārijāta and kurabaka trees,
and sahakāra trees spread out like clouds; utpala, puṇḍarīka, and kumuda—
various and wondrous flowers of every kind in the water— adorn that pond with exquisite beauty.
Adorned with various blended perfumes and flowers, that grove was at that time most delightful.
At that time, there was a king in Jambudvīpa named Dṛḍhaśrī, who was the lord of men;
that king possessed five hundred sons, who were gentle, handsome, and skilled in the arts.
That land is abundant and exceedingly peaceful; free from all faults, it is ever victorious and joyful.
The ground is strewn everywhere with various fragrant flowers, no different from the palaces of the gods.
At that time, the Muni, the Dharma King, proclaimed this tranquil meditative absorption, saying:
"All realms of existence are like dreams; there is neither birth nor passing away. Sentient beings and persons cannot be found, for all phenomena are entirely illusory."
Like space, lightning, or a magical illusion, And like a mirage or the moon reflected in water,
There are no phenomena of birth and death in this world, Nor is there anyone who goes on to another world.
Actions performed in the past are never lost; the black and white retributions within the three realms do not perish.
Among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), there is neither annihilation nor permanence. One does not accumulate karma, nor does one abide in existence;
it is not that one performs an action and another receives its fruit, nor is it that one performs an action and someone else receives it.
There is no one who goes, nor is there anyone who comes; sentient beings are neither existent nor non-existent.
There is no collection of evil views such as the grasping at views, nor is there any sentient being or pure practice.
The phrase of non-arising, quiescence, and signlessness— The merit of the Tathāgata, the realm of the Buddha;
This dhāraṇī and the talent of the ten powers— This is the supreme sphere of action of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
A mass of merit consisting of pure, white dharmas; the power of wisdom, virtue, and dhāraṇī is most supreme.
The manifestations of supernormal powers are boundless in their momentum; from this, the six superknowledges and eloquence arise.
In its own nature, it has never diminished; practicing non-practice is not practicing according to dharmas.
Within this dharma-realm there is nowhere to go; such practice and non-practice is the true practice of dharma.
Entering the self-nature beyond the nature of sound, One dwells nowhere within the self-nature of the realms of existence;
Practicing the self-nature that is non-abiding and non-reliant, One reaches the Buddha’s realm—dust-free and quiescent.
Concentration, superior practice, and supreme concentration—these have no abiding in their own nature;
they always accord with that which possesses self-nature, being subtle, difficult to see, and immovable.
He dwells eternally in peace, unmoving; dwelling in non-dwelling, he dwells in the dharmatā.
It cannot be said that he dwells in a self-nature; this practice is immovable, abiding in the Dharma.
To teach by means of sound is not the path of sound; the essence of sound is the path, which is the path of Dharma.
There is no separate collection of sounds existing anywhere; such a nature and practice is the practice of Dharma.
The sounds of the practices taught do not give rise to practice; the true meaning of the nature of those dharmas is practice itself.
