Though one speaks of the practices of sentient beings by means of sounds, both the sounds and the practices of sentient beings are non-existent.
Within it, no words can enter; the vastness of wisdom and its meaning are likewise so.
This is the path praised by the Buddha for cultivation—the subtle practice of the luminous principle of the Dharma.
The vast treasury of wisdom, free from all dust and defilement— If there are those who can abide in the peerless state,
They shall constantly pour down the rain of the supreme and wondrous gift of Dharma, Which is the path of the ultimate truth of the foremost emptiness.
Far removed from dust, this is the foremost pure phrase; Nirvana is supreme tranquility, free from defilement.
Without conceptualization, grasping, or proliferation— This is the phrase of nirvana spoken by the Buddha.
It does not abide in the beginning, the middle, or the end; it is neither existent nor non-existent, nor is it a spatial location.
Having thus known the nature of its own activity, this peerless Dharma was taught by the Buddha.
At that time, King Dṛḍhaśrī heard the Two-legged World-Honored One preach this samādhi;
accompanied by a multitude of eight billion nayutas, he approached the Buddha’s dwelling with joy, faith, and reverence.
At that time, the king prostrated to the Hero among Men;
with great faith and reverence for the Buddha, he withdrew to stand to one side, gazing up at him with a respectful heart and joining his palms.
The Buddha, knowing that king’s pure conduct, his mastery over the faculties and consciousness,
and his arrival at the further shore, the World-Honored One, in accordance with the king’s mental inclinations and desires, expounded for him this supreme samādhi.
When this king heard the teaching on the ultimate truth, he gave rise to vast joy and noble faith;
relinquishing all four continents and departing from the pleasures of the five desires, he went forth into homelessness.
Once that king had gone forth on account of this, he became resolutely and deeply devoted to the Buddha;
at that time, all the people of Jambudvīpa likewise abandoned desire and went forth.
The bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs delight in practicing meditative concentration; the Tathāgata’s assembly is vast and immeasurable.
Non-glutinous rice emerges spontaneously from the earth, and all the devas come to serve them.
Dharma robes of the kāṣāya color grow from the trees—stainless, pure, and most lovely.
Cutting, sewing, and mending according to the prescribed measurements—this was due to the power and majesty of that Buddha’s merit. O youth!
You should observe that king, who abandoned his home and left the world behind, casting aside all under heaven; he viewed the three realms as a mechanical puppet, seeking the vast joy of bodhi.
In the future age, during the final period of the Dharma, those who cannot abandon their poor and lowly homes and who suffer the afflictions of shackles,
fetters, and stocks will not give rise to faith in this sublime Dharma.

Though bound in shackles and punished with canes and staffs, Subjected to hundreds of thousands kinds of abuse and humiliation, And though the king’s power pressed him hard, he was able to endure it all;
Even in extreme poverty and hardship, he did not abandon his home.
Lacking wealth and short-lived, they toil in vain without merit;
ignorant and unlearned in various arts and skills, such people always dwell in the realm of the common vulgar.
Coercive, unrighteous, stubborn, violent, and evil, they greedily cherish their own riches while seizing the property of others.
They mock and ridicule virtuous people, yet claim to have already resolved upon Bodhicitta;
they covet the wives of others and seize their assets, being stingy, jealous, deceitful, and full of dissipation.
Having abandoned the heart of compassion, they head toward the evil realms, yet they likewise claim for themselves:
"When I become a Buddha,
seeing others in suffering and distress will give rise to joy in me; [I shall see those who] break the precepts, are violent and cruel, harbor evil intentions,
fail to mindful of gratitude, and destroy others."
"Venerable One!
Teach me the practice of the Dharma.
Yet when hearing others speak of that bodhisattva conduct, I instead give rise to anger toward those people."
If you see even a slight fault in the Dharma Master, you increase it by speaking of hundreds of thousands of kinds.
Child! You have now heard what I say:
Do not associate with such people if you wish to realize the path to enlightenment; do not even visit them in your dreams.
Though one might expound upon the immeasurable virtues of the dhūta practices throughout boundless eons, if one does not abide in such virtues, one will ultimately never attain supreme enlightenment.
With a pure mind, one always speaks well; with pure precepts and a gentle heart, one’s speech is exquisite.
Always maintaining a pure mind toward all elders and superiors, one will before long attain this samādhi.
Not giving rise to foulness through pride, one’s mind remains pure and constantly perfected.
Having abandoned arrogance, indulgence, and anger, one can attain such a supreme samādhi;
constantly mindful of the Buddhas’ mass of merit— their golden-hued skin and immeasurable virtues,
their bodies naturally adorned with all the marks— like the still autumn night when the myriad stars are arrayed.
With victory banners, pennants, and canopies, Scented ointments, powdered incense, and flower garlands—
By making these supreme offerings to the peerless image, One will soon attain this samādhi.
With sandalwood, aloeswood, and powdered incense, And countless varieties of lamps with superior ghee oil,
By making offerings to Buddha-stūpas and shrines as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one will soon attain this samādhi; with the exquisite sounds of lutes,
harps, and drums, flutes, pipes, cymbals, and the chanting of praises—
hundreds of thousands of millions of such beautiful tones— one shall make offerings to the Most Victorious Honored One who is free from evil.
One who fashions immeasurable images of the Buddha, Skillfully adorned with various jewels,
Exquisite, upright, and most supreme— Before long, such a person shall attain this samādhi;
One who always dwells in forests and thickets, delighting in tranquility, Abandoning villages and leaving behind attachment to the mind.
Delighting in solitude and non-duality like a sword, Before long you shall attain this samādhi.
I am the Dharma King and you are my son; Following and training in my practice of samādhi, In the past I attained that great renown, And my name was called King Sthira.
In the past, I made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, Constantly vowing to uphold the pure precepts;
I gave rise to reverence toward those possessed of the Ten Powers, For the sake of seeking such a supreme samādhi.
In former times, I abandoned my wife and children, And gave away my head, hands, feet, eyes, and ears.
Never did he give rise to such inferior thoughts, for the sake of seeking the supreme,
tranquil samādhi; with elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry in immeasurable varieties, and all manner of precious jewels and dwellings,
he gave them all away, his mind never once feeling regret, for the sake of seeking such a supreme concentration.
Servants, wealth, and grain exceeding a hundredfold, Various garments and food and drink,
Filling the needs of all who come seeking— All for the sake of seeking such a supreme concentration;
Māṇi-jewels, pearls, excellent gold and silver, Lapis lazuli, diamonds, cowries, and jade.
I am able to relinquish everything in its entirety, for the sake of seeking such a supreme concentration;
I renounce precious jewels and ornaments for the body— necklaces, armlets, lion-bands, celestial crowns,
and jeweled nets exceeding a hundred kinds— for the sake of seeking such a supreme concentration.
Exquisite, supreme, and numbering many billions, I gave them away with joy at that time—
karpāsa, pattra, and tagara— seeking such a sublime samādhi;
formerly seeing those who were impoverished, imprisoned, and suffering from the toil of excessive labor and the failure to obtain what they sought.
I was able to give extensively to them there, seeking such a supreme samādhi;
elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, white houses, gardens, carriages, and precious ornaments—
I gave these to hundreds of thousands of poor beggars, seeking such a supreme samādhi.
He gave away hundreds of millions of *nayutas* of groves and gardens, adorned with various jewels;
at the time of giving, he felt joy and gave rise to compassion for the sake of seeking such a supreme samādhi.
He relinquished royal capitals, cities, towns, and villages, as well as all kinds of lands.
Having given, one can give rise to supreme joy; for the sake of seeking such a sublime treasury,
I have given away every heap of jewels like Mount Sumeru, and likewise fine garments to adorn the body,
all bestowed upon the poor and beggars, for the sake of seeking such a sublime samādhi.
To enrich the immeasurable poor, to provide protection for those who come to me for refuge,
and to cause suffering beings to attain happiness— for the sake of seeking such a supreme samādhi as this.
Formerly, when I was the wealthiest upon this great earth, Seeing that all the worlds were in extreme suffering and distress,
I renounced my royal throne and all my possessions, Vowing with a heart of compassion to bestow happiness upon them all.

O youth! My past deeds were rare; what was accomplished throughout immeasurable eons is difficult to perform. What is set forth in speech can never be exhausted; even if I were to speak for a hundred million eons, it would still be hard to reach the end.
If those whom I have taught are deluded and unable to believe in the Buddha's conduct,
they will undergo immeasurable sufferings for the sake of seeking this samādhi.
I now exhort you, young man: place deep faith in my words.

The Sugata never speaks what is untrue; the Buddha, supreme in truthful speech and great compassion, has endured hundreds of thousands of other hardships in the past, until his body was utterly withered.
How can one attain this samādhi?
If one liberates hundreds of thousands of beings from suffering and realizes this concentration in a single kṣaṇa, one will immediately obtain the path of true wisdom.
At that time, I beheld Buddhas numbering in the nayutas, more than the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions;
I attained supreme supernormal powers at will, able to travel to hundreds of thousands of Buddha-fields.
I went to that Most Victorious Honored One to inquire, engaging in hundreds of thousands of kinds of elegant debates;
at that time, the Buddha proclaimed to me answers corresponding exactly to the questions and challenges I had posed.
I am fully able to receive and retain them all, not forgetting even a single word or phrase;
having heard this true Dharma, I shall extensively set forth hundreds of kinds of difficult questions and expound the dust-free,
tranquil verses, establishing immeasurable multitudes upon the path of wisdom.
Abiding in this supreme samādhi, I have studied this Dharma for immeasurable kalpas;
in former days, I likewise established countless sentient beings upon the unsurpassed, most excellent path.
If a person has never seen a Buddha from the beginning, And has never heard this supreme Dharma,
They will ultimately be unable to give rise to faith and joy In the true samādhi of the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
Only those with wisdom who can understand it Attain the profound and true merit.
Hearing the ultimate truth without alarm or fear, Having heard it, they give rise to a heart of supreme joy.
Those who can uphold my Bodhi Are the true children of the Tathāgata;
As rare as the udumbara flower, I have practiced asceticism for many eons for their sake.
That person will not fear falling into the evil realms, And shall always remain far removed from the eight difficulties;
They shall behold immeasurable nayutas of Buddhas, And will also be able to believe in this supreme samādhi.
Just as that Maitreya is peerless and without equal, having attained pure wisdom regarding all sentient beings, this Samādhi Sūtra rests in his hands;
I grant him a prediction of enlightenment just like that of Maitreya.
This person accomplishes mindfulness and wisdom; through hearing and retention, they excel in the ultimate path.
Possessing eloquence, delighting in tranquility, and free from sorrow or affliction—this is because this concentration rests within their hands.
Such a person constantly receives the offerings of devas and is further revered by the multitude.
They are constantly protected and guarded by spirits and deities, because they uphold this samādhi;
they are not harmed by fire or poison, and no swords or staves can injure them;
they do not drift or drown when entering great waters—all this is due to upholding this samādhi.
This person constantly dwells within mountain forests, attended and served by various devas;
immeasurable yakṣas come to make offerings because they uphold such a samādhi.
Their wisdom is as vast as the great ocean, and they proclaim the Buddha’s merits without obstruction.
They eloquently expound the true virtues of all Buddhas, because they maintain such a supreme samādhi;
what these people hear is inexhaustible, like the boundlessness of space.
Holding the torch of wisdom to dispel the darkness, it is because these people maintain this samādhi.
With speech that is supple, exquisite, and appropriate to the meaning, he expounds it amidst the assembly, beloved by the wise;
his teaching flows like a spring or a river, never ceasing, because he maintains this samādhi.
Like a king of physicians dispensing excellent medicine, he also acts as a refuge for all sentient beings.
They are able to act as a light for the world, because they uphold such a samādhi;
Such persons are not moved by a mind of craving and desire, but delight in cessation and attain the bliss of dhyāna;
they speak words of tranquility that are sublime and beautiful, because they uphold such a samādhi.
This person’s mind is free from signs and unstained; they thoroughly discern all signs.
Their mind is ever tranquil as they walk in meditation, for they uphold such a samādhi.
They attain the stainless, defilement-free eye, by which they can see immeasurable Tathāgatas.
One attains the vast and boundless eye of a Great Man, by virtue of upholding this samādhi;
The beautiful voice of a peacock becomes tranquil, and the heart-pleasing song of the kalaviṅka bird emerges;
All musical instruments blend together to produce wondrous sounds, by virtue of upholding this samādhi.
They achieve the sound of thunder that resounds afar, With the exquisite tones of geese, bells, and drums;
They harmonize with a hundred kinds of supreme music, Because they maintain such a samādhi.
Throughout immeasurable and countless asaṃkhyeya kalpas, They achieve such harmonious and elegant sounds.
The speech they utter is like nectar, for they maintain this supreme samādhi;
They do not crave delicacies or food and drink, nor do they give rise to attachment toward robes or alms bowls;
Having few desires, being content, and well-disciplined and gentle, all is due to maintaining such a samādhi.
One does not exalt oneself regarding one's own person, nor does one disparage others;
with a mind always supple, one delights in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), by virtue of upholding such a samādhi.
One constantly observes one's own conduct and perceives no faults or deficiencies in others.
They maintain a harmonious countenance with all and never engage in dispute, because they uphold this samādhi;
With a compassionate heart that moistens others and pure wisdom, they are free from evil, upright, and without guile, because they uphold this samādhi;
Their minds are ever supple and they delight in liberation, because they uphold this samādhi.
The mind always delights in practicing the giving of alms;
the knot of stinginess cannot defile it, nor is it captured by sense objects, because one maintains this samādhi.
One’s appearance is upright and extraordinary, bringing joy to others; the skin of one’s body is the color of pure gold.
Adorned with the thirty-two marks, it is because they maintain this samādhi;
their physical form and meritorious qualities are entirely exquisite, and many people love, revere, and constantly protect them;
men, women, the old, and the young never tire of gazing upon them, because they maintain this samādhi.
The hosts of devas, nāgas, spirits, and yakṣas all rejoice in such a person;
they go from house to house and offer praise because he maintains this samādhi.
Brahmā, Śakra, Maheśvara, and all others come to make offerings to him.
Their minds never give rise to pride, because they uphold this samādhi;
they leave behind all perilous paths, for they have no fear of obstacles or evil realms,
and they are liberated from all terrifying matters, by virtue of upholding this samādhi.
They are able to hear the Buddha’s subtle and wondrous Dharma, Free from all doubts and uncertainties;
They follow and enter into the profound Dharma, Because they uphold such a samādhi.
If they hear the subtle teachings of the noble ones, They are able to understand them all and attain the ultimate.
Due to the power of past causes and conditions, and by virtue of upholding this samādhi, the Tathāgata has spoken these words:
"One who skillfully gains offerings without the mind becoming elated attains dhāraṇī through these causes and conditions; this is because of having attained this samādhi."
When this person is on the verge of passing away, the compassionate, wise,
and valiant Amitābha Buddha manifests before them; because they have maintained such samādhi,
they behold the One of Ten Powers who accords with their aspirations, as well as the various śrāvakas standing before him.
One will certainly be born in that Land of Peace and Bliss, by virtue of upholding such a samādhi.
Even if all classes of sentient beings were to simultaneously attain Buddhahood and reach their ultimate limit,
and if one person were to make offerings to them all for kalpas exceeding the sands of the Ganges, [the merit would not equal that of this samādhi].
If, in a future age during the final period, there is a person free from deceit who hears of this samādhi and is able to give rise to sympathetic joy toward it,
their merit will surpass the former by more than any calculable fraction.
"O youth!

You should know that the path of quiescence is the samādhi of the emptiness of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-śūnyatā). Those who write it down, recite it, and uphold it are called 'upholders of the treasury of the Dharma.'"

"O youth! For this reason, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to know the speech and sounds of all sentient beings, as well as the differences among the faculties of all sentient beings—how they vary from one time to another—and wishes to teach the Dharma accordingly, O youth!"
That person should receive, uphold, recite, and extensively explain this samādhi to others.
Furthermore, for the sake of gathering in all sentient beings, they should cultivate the practice corresponding to skillful means.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If a person has once seen immeasurable Buddhas And has also once inquired about this samādhi,
This person of supreme wisdom maintains this concentration, Abiding in the foremost goodness, unshakable."

One attains the sublime and wondrous joys of humans and devas, Constantly receiving the superior offerings of others, And further attaining the bliss of meditative concentration and nirvāṇa; This is because of maintaining concentration through non-negligence.
Upon hearing others praise them, they feel no joy; Even when reviled or insulted, they harbor no resentment.
Unshaken by the eight worldly concerns, like a mountain, because he delights in seeking liberation and maintains meditative concentration;
his mouth never utters meaningless speech, for he is free from anger, pride, and contention,
and through patience and self-mastery, his mind is joyful, because he maintains concentration through heedfulness.
Their speech is gentle, discerning, and truthful; they display a relaxed countenance and greet others with a pleasant smile.
Seeing all sentient beings, they always maintain a smile, for they uphold this supreme and pure samādhi.
Their minds are ever-tamed so as not to afflict others; they skillfully restrain the five faculties and maintain the purity of their precepts.
Abiding in truth, speaking little, and being beneficial and lovely, this is because they uphold the pure and supreme samādhi;
always relinquishing through vast giving with no stingy heart, causing hungry and thirsty beings to be fully satisfied,
they do not delight in eating for themselves but rejoice in giving to others, for these people of virtuous karma uphold upright concentration.
Loved by many hundreds of thousands of devas, Revered by yakṣas, asuras, and nāgas,
He dwells alone in the forest, constantly guarded, For he courageously maintains this supreme samādhi;
Delighting in tranquility and free from noise, Nāgas and asuras always attend upon him.
No one is able to cause them fear, for they maintain meditative concentration through heedfulness;
their voice is like the sound of Brahmā, like the delightful calls of a flock of geese,
and like five hundred exquisite melodies— their fame resounds throughout all the worlds.
All the atoms contained within the great earth— His virtues exceed the number of those atoms.
A treasury of merit that benefits all sentient beings, Arises from cultivating such tranquil concentration.
“O Youth! A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives rise to this aspiration:
‘How may I come to know the intrinsic nature of all phenomena?’”

"O youth! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should receive, uphold, recite, and read this samādhi, explain it extensively for others, and practice it in accordance with skillful means, for the sake of gathering in all sentient beings."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The wise have neither anger nor craving, Nor do they give rise to delusion;
Their afflictions are entirely attenuated, Because they know the supreme Dharma of tranquility."
The Buddha’s precepts are without flaw or transgression; he does not indulge in the charms of women.
With a steadfast mind, he seeks this samādhi; knowing the Dharma, he is free from defilement.
Possessing wisdom and supernormal powers, he visits many lands to behold the Buddhas.
Having attained total retention and reached the further shore through the knowledge of tranquil concentration,
one swiftly becomes the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings. To pacify afflictions,
one skillfully extracts the poisonous arrows of evil and proclaims the stainless words of tranquility.
If one acts as a skilled physician, well-knowing the origins of disease,
and masters this definitive wisdom, they shall liberate sentient beings from harm.
Having attained mastery through the study of principles, they are unattached and worthy of offerings.
He dwells among the multitude without expectation, for he understands and knows the pure Dharma.

This Lion among Men practices patience; though beaten or reviled, he feels no anger, nor is he distressed even by being butchered or dismembered, for he is able to know that the aggregates (skandhas) are empty.
The power of patience is like Mount Sumeru, entirely devoid of any conceptualization of patience;
even the Buddha does not exist, for one knows that all things are eternally empty.
One thoroughly understands the immeasurable perceptions of the three realms and fully comprehends the three periods of time.
They are able to manifest immeasurable principles, for they train in the Dharma with fearlessness.
They do not form conceptualizations regarding phenomena; they grasp neither at love nor hatred.
Knowing that all dharmas are eternally empty and quiescent, they attain supreme nirvana.
If one speaks of this supreme concentration, one will before long behold enlightenment;
having thoroughly mastered the noble realm, one bestows gifts that yield great rewards.
One may speak of billions of sūtras, expounding them without any obstruction.
Their eloquence is uninterrupted, for they know the vastness of the Dharma.
Even throughout inconceivable eons, their concentration and wisdom remain like clouds;
they preach the Dharma without end, for they know this tranquil meditative absorption.
With inconceivable eloquence, they will surely attain the Way;
They shall preach billions of boundless sutras, Knowing the names and characteristics of all phenomena everywhere.
The Buddha preaches the unsurpassed Dharma; Hearing and upholding it, they cause it to be filled [within them].
Within this, there is no doubt; one knows that all phenomena are non-existent.
Always practicing kind speech and giving, they joyfully and skillfully renounce wealth to rescue the poor.
Providing for their livelihoods with complete sufficiency, it is because they feel compassion for the world.
He shall become a king of Jambudvīpa, Compassionate toward the multitude and free from anger;
The people will give rise to loving respect Because he understands the dharma of emptiness.
He renounces his handsome wife and children, As well as his royal throne and his very body.
They are resolutely free from stinginess and regret, because they know emptiness and stillness;
even if someone were to cut off their limbs, they would feel no anger at all, whether dreaming or awake,
for they have made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas by upholding the Dharma of emptiness.
Making offerings to the Muni, they never grow weary throughout the three periods of time;
their great faith is unshakable because they understand the dharma of emptiness.
They skillfully uphold the treasury of the Buddha-dharma and abide in the supreme dhāraṇī.
Before long, one shall attain Buddhahood, because of upholding this supreme sutra.
In every lifetime, one shall not be deaf or blind; throughout vast eons, all faculties shall be complete.
One shall always remain far removed from the eight difficulties, for they fix their minds upon preaching this sutra.
By performing merit, one leaves the evil realms;
adorned with the marks of physical perfection, with a pure mind one dwells in supernormal powers, and thus the Buddha appears before one.
Through various bodies of transformation and response, he delivers sentient beings in all lands.
If one is able to see him, the resolve for bodhi will be firm.
One whose wisdom and mindfulness are free from sorrow gives rise to the power of diligence;
reaching the ultimate within the supreme Dharma, this is because they uphold this sūtra in the final age.
From his body emanate a thousand billion rays of light, Which eclipse both the sun and the moon.
If one cultivates the samādhi of emptiness, Before long, one will become supreme among men.
For a thousand billion *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I have sought the realm of tranquility.
Without abandoning diligent effort, one receives the prediction of enlightenment from Dīpaṃkara.
The wise should practice this sutra, which proclaims the supreme teachings of all Buddhas;
those who are deluded by external paths will lose their way and be boiled in hell at the end of their lives.
The suffering endured is most extreme, lasting for *nayuta* eons before it ends;
once the retribution for sins has been exhausted through many eons, one obtains the cause for the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*).
In this terrifying age of the final dharma, one draws near to the unsurpassed path.
Upholding my treasury of the Dharma, they are prophesied as those who shall uphold this sutra.
*Candrapradīpa-samādhi-sūtra*, Scroll Six;
*Candrapradīpa-samādhi-sūtra*, Scroll Seven.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Gao Qi Dynasty:
"O Youth! If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva wishes to practice, they should always delight in cultivating the fundamental karma of the supernormal powers."
What is the great fundamental karma of the supernormal powers of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva?

It is said to comprise all wholesome dharmas, yet without grasping at the aggregate of morality, without attachment to the aggregate of concentration, without engaging in conceptual proliferation regarding the aggregate of wisdom, and without grasping or attachment to the aggregates of liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
"O youth! This is the fundamental practice of the great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.

If they achieve this fundamental practice of supernormal powers and attain great supernormal power, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gains mastery over all manifestations and is thus able to preach the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings."
"In order to encompass the Mahāyāna, this Bodhisattva should constantly practice and study these fundamental activities of great supernormal powers.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The fundamental and supreme activity of supernormal powers Manifests as being without karmic retribution;"
Cultivating various practices with hope for their fruits, one does not eliminate the grasping at a self-conception.
That which is called "supernormal power" is the inconceivable wisdom of the Buddha;
if one dwells in grasping and attachment, that person possesses no true wisdom.
The inconceivable dharmas are manifested through sounds;
yet if one clings to those sounds, one does not penetrate the teaching of skillful means.
Not understanding the instruction of skillful means, one knows nothing of the discourse of skillful means.
To speak of what is not the Dharma as the Dharma—how could one truly awaken to the Dharma?
Within the three thousandfold world-system, when I preached various sūtras at that time, their meanings were of a single essence yet possessed manifold flavors; all of these are ultimately ineffable.
All the Buddhas of the ten directions Proclaim the immeasurable Dharma;
If one contemplates the meaning of a single phrase with discernment, Then all will be understood.
All phenomena are without self; If a person studies this meaning, [they shall realize it].
At that time, by practicing even a single phrase, one will find it not difficult to awaken to the Buddha-dharma.
All dharmas are the Buddha-dharma; if a person studies this dharma and understands it according to the Dharma, they will then accord with the dharma of emptiness.
All speech is the Buddha’s speech; all phenomena of sound do not exist.
Even if one searches throughout the ten directions, the Buddha’s speech cannot be apprehended.
The Buddha’s speech is the most supreme; the Buddha’s speech is unsurpassed.
Subtle phenomena are entirely non-existent; this is the supreme speech.
That Dharma is most unsurpassed, manifesting without interruption;
not even so much as a speck of dust can be apprehended—this is what all Buddhas have taught.
All phenomena are unattainable; there is no phenomenon to be realized.
Knowing phenomena in this way, one can understand the Buddha’s bodhi.
If one awakens to this dharma, one then turns the wheel of Dharma.
When turning the wheel of Dharma, he then pours forth the supreme nectar.
The Bodhisattva is able to understand and realize the unsurpassed Buddha-enlightenment;
having attained the status of an incomparable Honored One, he causes others to awaken to the Buddha’s wisdom.
Non-cultivation, wishlessness, signlessness, and emptiness—
these four gates are taught by the Buddha as liberation.
The faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and so forth...
All these are empty in their essential nature; Kauṇḍinya was the first to see this.
If one can know the essential nature of these phenomena as they truly are, then disputes will cease, for one has thoroughly realized the characteristics of phenomena.
This refers to the sphere of valor: the Bodhisattvas, who are protectors, are entirely free from doubt, for they have realized that the essence of phenomena is empty.
Because they are able to penetrate the nature of all phenomena, they are named Buddhas.
By means of the immeasurable Dharma-realm, he awakens those who are ready to be saved.
He attains the deeds of all Buddhas, all of which are produced through the body of precepts;
the words of the Buddha and the sound of the precepts are both identical in their mark of equality.
Having explained all sounds— namely the low, middle, and high pitches—
which are all equal and of a single characteristic, the Buddha is able to demonstrate the teachings of the Dharma.
The Buddha-dharma has no abiding place, nor does it reside in any direction;
it is neither born nor extinguished, and for this reason it is called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*).
It is neither new nor old, neither dispersed nor conjoined.
Neither blue nor yellow, neither white nor black;
Ineffable and ungraspable, yet made clear through words.
This is not a realm of sound, but the skillful wisdom-attainment of all Buddhas.
Those are the untainted dharmas; they are said to have no basis.
They do not exist within the ten directions; these are the dharmas taught by the Buddha.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one should contemplate the marks and features of the Buddha’s body.
Even though they behold the Buddha’s body, by the power of the Buddha,
there is ultimately not a single sentient being who realizes nirvana; yet,
when this Dharma is preached, immeasurable multitudes attain liberation.
Just as the sun and moon reflect their images in a hundred rivers,
such that all behold their forms, so too are the characteristics of all phenomena.
If one knows the nature of all phenomena to be like these reflections, [one realizes the truth].
One can never perceive the True Buddha By means of the physical body.
All phenomena are formless; Their characteristics cannot be found upon seeking.
Such formless phenomena Are precisely the Buddha’s Dharma-body.
If a person sees the Dharma-body, this is called seeing the Teacher;
the Dharma-body is itself perfect enlightenment—thus it is called seeing the Buddha.
That which cannot be attained is shown as attained; that which cannot be attained is spoken of as attained.
If one seeks to become a śramaṇa, one should know this path.
I have already explained the true practice; knowing the inclinations of sentient beings, if one enters the secret teaching, one will then be free from attachment.

If one claims that what is to be realized has already been attained, yet there is nothing actually accomplished therein, such a person does not obtain the fruit of the Path and is therefore called a non-śramaṇa.
This Dharma is exceedingly profound and subtle; those who have not yet mastered it make such assertions.
That teaching is exceedingly profound and abstruse, difficult to proclaim or demonstrate.
The five aggregates are all non-existent; they all arise from delusion.
There is no one who can give rise to them, nor are there the dharmas of the five aggregates.
The nature and characteristics of the five aggregates are the very characteristics of all phenomena;
the Buddha has taught that such characteristics are unattainable.
Just as space contains no substance, so too are all phenomena.
The past, the future, and the present— One contemplates these three periods as they truly are.
Verbal expression is like space; Within space there is nothing to grasp.
Such is the nature of phenomena: Without grasping, it is like space.
To expound such a Dharma, yet there has never been anything spoken;
to have no perception of dharmas—this is indeed inconceivable.
This Dharma lacks intrinsic nature, for the essence of dharmas cannot be apprehended.
One who realizes the Bodhi of the Buddhas dwells in the realm of cessation;
if one can know thus, one will have no attachment to dharmas.
If one has no attachment to dharmas, that person understands the notion of dharmas.
At all times, the bodhisattva abandons all conceptualizations;
if a person abandons conceptualization, they will have no attachment to the Buddha-dharma.
Since its limit is ungraspable, it is called the "limit of reality" (bhūtakoṭi).
One who thoroughly understands the limit (koṭi) will remain unattached for billions of eons.
Through false conceptualization regarding the original limit (pūrvakoṭi), the deluded revolve in saṃsāra;
though one searches throughout the ten directions, the original limit cannot be found.
Because all phenomena are empty, the bodhisattva has no attachments;
they undertake practice for the sake of awakening, yet that practice cannot be apprehended.
It is like a bird flying through the sky: its tracks cannot be found.
Such is the nature of perfect enlightenment, which the Bodhisattva is able to understand and realize.
It is like a person skilled in illusion who creates various objects through magic;
though they manifest all manner of forms and appearances, in reality, these cannot be found.
If one grasps at gain and loss, one has nothing at all to obtain;
that wisdom is like an illusion, yet it is not identical to the illusion itself.
Within this realm of empty phenomena, the foolish engage in false conceptualization.
Acting within conceptual discrimination, those people go to evil realms.
Beings undergo birth and the transition of old age;
they transmigrate without end, sinking into the midst of birth and death, their suffering and affliction being immeasurable.
The world gives rise to suffering and affliction through foolish and deluded conceptualization;
as long as that conceptualization is not severed, one drifts for a long time in birth and death.
Initially finding pleasure and its association, one becomes habituated to and attached to the fruits of desire.
Grasping has not yet been relinquished, for they abide in karma and afflictions.
As long as the karma of sentient beings is not exhausted, they are swept away by the torrent of desire;
they undergo birth again and again, and repeatedly pass into death and extinction.
Afflicted by ignorance and the provocations of Māra, they commit various evil deeds;
taking birth in every place, they consequently experience the retribution of death.
Ordinary people, shrouded in the darkness of folly, thus undergo the cycle of birth and death.
Poverty is compounded by suffering, and one further proceeds toward evil destinies.
With swords, whips, staves, and the like, they inflict harm upon one another;
by committing such evil deeds, they increase all manner of afflictions and distress.
"My children and my wealth"—thus do ordinary people engage in false discrimination;
through such false discrimination, they further increase their outflows.
As they increase these births and deaths, they are indeed called ordinary people.
Wandering through various realms of existence, they are therefore called ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Having abandoned the Buddha’s Dharma, they increase all unwholesome qualities;
thus they do not attain liberation, for they remain bound within the net of Māra.
Because of lustful desire, the fool pursues the defilement of female beauty;
he returns to defiled places and falls into the various evil realms.
The Buddha does not praise the taint of desire, nor does he approve of being near female beauty.
Among all these snares of fear, the snare of women is the most terrifying;
the Bodhisattva always keeps far from it, as if from a venomous serpent.
He never associates with female forms, knowing them to be not the path of the Buddha.
Practicing the path to enlightenment as the Buddha himself originally practiced;
having completed the training in the Buddha-way, one swiftly accomplishes the unsurpassed path.
Attaining that which is most unsurpassed, one becomes a shrine and a stūpa for the world.
With wisdom beyond reproach, he became the God among Gods;
he established others in the eight precepts, so that their bodies of morality remained free from defilement.
To immeasurable billions of beings, he exhorted and instructed them to cultivate bodhi.
Bringing benefit to the multitude, he gives rise to compassion for all.
That one of steadfast wisdom beats the drum of the Dharma,
shaking the palace of Māra and his retinue.
Countless billions of māras were exhorted to cultivate bodhi;
he subdued all rival disputants and triumphed over all non-Buddhists,
causing the great earth, the vast oceans, and the myriad mountains to tremble.
Manifesting as many bodies of various and diverse kinds,
great wisdom can display hundreds of thousands of divine transformations;
it causes immeasurable lands, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, to tremble.
Having subdued those hosts of Māras, he immediately awakened to the unsurpassed path.
He further manifested a wondrous tree, adorned with various kinds of jewels;
its flowers and fruits were exceptionally lush and flourishing, so fragrant and lovely that they were most delightful.
Some are transformed into terraces and pavilions, multi-storied towers and palace chambers;
these manifestations are bold and vigorous. The flower ponds are exceedingly brilliant and pure, filled with water of eight virtues—cool, clear, and free from any impurity.
If there are sentient beings who drink, they shall extinguish the three kinds of thirst.
If one drinks this water, they will all attain the stage of non-retrogression;
they shall be able to realize unsurpassed wisdom and become a guide for the world.
The unsurpassed path of tranquility—this is what the practitioner should know;
those who do not reach this path are called outsiders.
If one associates with them and accepts their teachings for practice, [one follows the way of the non-Buddhists].
Falling into great places of evil, in the Avīci hell from which it is difficult to be rescued,
they undergo immense and extreme suffering that cannot be fully described.
Only I can know this, as well as the Great Victorious Bodhisattvas.
Profound and difficult to perceive, it is not the domain of foolish ordinary beings;
those who dwell in grasping and attachment will give rise to doubt regarding this Dharma.
It manifests as supreme adornments, in immeasurable varieties that are lovely to behold.
All are able to go to the supreme buddha-fields;
in all those buddha-lands, every variety of color appears,
for the great supernormal powers of the bodhisattvas can manifest everything.
Possessing great power and great valor, clad in firm and supreme armor,
grasping the great vajra-pestle, he shatters the dharmas of emptiness.
From his own body, he emits countless great rays of light.
In number like the sands of the Ganges, they extinguish the darkness of the world.
They are not stained by female beauty, nor do they follow after it;
one should abandon this perception, for the perception of women is most deceptive.
The Buddha-fields are never empty, for they are the abode of the courageous;
even Māra Pāpīyas and his like cannot cause them disturbance.
Those who dwell in wrong views shall not encounter the Buddhas.
Restrained by anger and dwelling in stinginess and greed,
he is Māra Pāpīyas; he creates obstacles for those seeking rebirth in heaven and liberation,
and for this reason, he falls into the evil realms.
Observing all perceptions, one dwells in the perception of detachment;
such a person is able to know the unsurpassed wisdom of the Buddhas.
They are able to see the past, the future, and the present.
He expounds such meanings, yet therein there is nothing spoken.
These are but provisional names and conventional expressions;
the Bodhisattva understands them thus, benefiting sentient beings in ways immeasurable and inconceivable.
"Perception" (saṃjñā) has the meaning of measuring and knowing;
because it manifests the grasping subject, its characteristic is that there is nothing to be grasped, which then reveals the meaning of quiescence (nirvāṇa).
That which is not quiescent is perception; that which is quiescent is wisdom (jñāna).
If one knows the intrinsic nature of perception, one is then free from all perceptions.
If there were any perception to be discarded, that would mean perception still exists;
such a person engages in the conceptual proliferation of perception and is not free from it.
If a person forms this thought:
"By whom was this perception created?
By whom can this perception be realized?"
Who can extinguish this perception?
As for the dharma that gives rise to perception, not even the Buddhas can find it;
it exists right here, yet is without self and free from grasping.
If the mind does not arise, by what means could conceptualization be produced?
If the mind attains liberation, then there is no basis for its arising.
If one realizes liberation, the mind is inconceivable.
Because the mind is inconceivable, one accomplishes the inconceivable.
I originally made this thought:
"Once I am firmly established in the ground of the mind, I shall relinquish all mental activity and vow to accomplish the inconceivable."
The fruit of pure and white dharmas is the vision of the unconditioned;
in a single thought-moment, one can fully comprehend the thoughts of all sentient beings.
Sentient beings are themselves the mind, and the mind is itself the Tathāgata.
The inconceivable Buddhas have fully revealed this mind.
If a person should think: "How can one attain the mind of equanimity?"
Contemplating the mindless, one is able to leave behind all minds.
If, at the time of death, the mind follows after perceptions,
that person gives rise to a conceptualizing mind, preventing the mind from attaining liberation.
When a fool dwells upon the perception of a woman, he gives rise to lustful desire;
if he can eliminate that perception, he will be free from lustful desire.
If one contemplates the unsurpassed Dharma, this contemplation is the greatest of all contemplations.
By contemplating all phenomena, one attains the mind of reality.
Recollection is inexhaustible; throughout the long night, it constantly takes objects as its focus.
Amidst various false and divergent conceptions, the mind of contemplation can never be exhausted.
That which is called the "dharma of the exhaustion of the mind" is fundamentally without wisdom within that exhaustion;
wisdom is not the ground of exhaustion, because dharmas are inexhaustible.
Through the path of provisional names and language, one speaks while transcending words.
This Dharma is without differentiation, and wisdom is inexhaustible.
Neither arising nor ceasing, it is signless and formless;
throughout billions of eons, it manifests the signless Dharma.
Observing all that exists, one dwells in non-existence;
never having seen any difference, nor seeing any non-difference.
Through conventional designations and verbal expressions, one reveals what is neither existent nor non-existent.
Yet regarding all those Buddhas, existence and non-existence are not seen.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are revealed as non-existent;
if one can understand this dharma, one will then be able to see that which is non-existent.
There is always nothing to be realized, for ultimately nothing exists;
if there were anything to be realized, it would be called the world.
If one should form such a thought:
"If I am to become a Buddha in the world"—
to harbor such thoughts of self-existence, one will never awaken to Bodhi.
The fearless Bodhisattva seeks nothing within the dharmas.
Spontaneously free from afflictions—this is called bodhi.
People say these words:
"I am proceeding toward bodhi."
Because they do not know this path, they remain far from the Buddha’s bodhi.
He teaches the Dharma through sound:
"All conditioned phenomena are empty; the essence and intrinsic nature of sound are subtle and invisible."
Manifesting great supernormal powers, he proclaims this sūtra to benefit all bodhisattvas, as clarified by all Buddhas.
He cuts off those various antidotes, namely the afflictions and the like.
Abiding in great supernormal powers, he has skillfully cultivated the four bases of power.
Having attained ethical discipline, he reaches the ultimate in emptiness;
dwelling securely in supernormal powers, his psychic faculties are inconceivable.
Abiding securely in the wisdom of wishlessness, cultivating wisdom until it is perfectly pure,
seeking wisdom without weariness— immeasurable and inconceivable.
Within the samādhis of supernormal powers, they proceed spontaneously and effortlessly.
This retribution is eternally empty and non-existent; all things are forever in a state of quiescent extinction.
This retribution is the power of the divine feet, by which one travels to visit billions of worlds, beholding Buddhas—the lamps illuminating the world—as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
That person attains mastery over arising and ceasing through the power of the mind;
having attained mastery of the mind, their body becomes purified.
Among all the disciples of the Buddha, if one cultivates the power of supernormal knowledges (ṛddhi),...
Compared to this power of retribution, the powers of all the hosts of devas do not equal even a sixteenth part; none can see his body,
except for the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and those who have attained the same.
His body shall be free from all ailments, nor shall there be white hair, wrinkles, or the frailty and decay of old age;
at the time of death, he shall have no bitter suffering.
He shall be free from doubt and hesitation, as well as from all forms of delusion.
Day and night, he constantly expounds ten billion sūtras;
All afflictions, along with their habitual tendencies, are entirely severed;
Toward all sentient beings, he always gives rise to a mind of equanimity.
Within hundreds of thousands of samādhis, they attain mastery free from defilement;
cultivating great wisdom, they expound it for the sake of others.
Regarding the male and female faculties and so forth, they are entirely free from all conceptualizations.
Abiding in the state of non-perception, he is able to proclaim the true certainty.
With pure wisdom, he expounds the Dharma as it truly is;
this accords with the conforming Dharma, the realm of concentration and insight.
Those who cultivate the various meditative concentrations are not hindered by anything;
always speaking words of truth, their teaching of the Dharma is never without benefit.
Having well obtained this human body, they remain far removed from all calamities.
They are able to repay the kindness of all Buddhas;
because they always delight in this sutra, for immeasurable kalpas they have abandoned the world.
If, regarding this wondrous scripture, one should even uphold a single verse, [the merit is beyond measure].
Having already seen various Buddhas and repeatedly made offerings to them,
because of their love for this sutra, they shall swiftly awaken to the Bodhi of the Buddhas;
they will see those Buddhas constantly residing on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
He bestowed this prediction upon that person:
"You shall behold the Buddha Maitreya.
When you behold the Buddha Maitreya, even during the final age,"
Those who uphold this sutra attain a heart of supreme love and joy.
Abiding securely within the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), they accomplish the inconceivable;
regarding that inconceivable limit, they harbor no doubts whatsoever.
That person has no doubt, nor even the slightest confusion;
being certain in the Buddha’s words, awakening will not be difficult to attain.
In this age of fear during the final era, it is difficult to practice.
If one hears this sutra, one immediately attains inexhaustible eloquence.
Those who cherish and delight in this sutra— the unsurpassed treasury of the Buddha's Dharma—
have already made offerings to the Buddhas and all their śrāvakas.
Whoever recites this sutra is one who upholds the treasury of the Dharma;
among all forms of offering, the offering of the Dharma is supreme.
If one can uphold this sutra, the unsurpassed enlightenment of the Buddha will be inconceivable.
It is said:
"The Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom—this wisdom is not difficult to attain.
If, in the world of former Buddhas, one has once upheld this sutra,"
Then, in the final age, one shall encounter this sutra once again;
traveling to the various Buddha-fields, one will be able to roar with a great lion’s roar— the inconceivable roar of the Buddha.
In the presence of those billions of Buddhas,
the Lion of the Śākyas, employing immeasurable eloquence, expounded the Dharma with utter fearlessness.
The descendant of the Ikṣvāku lineage, endowed with merit, bestowed upon that person the prediction of enlightenment.
And in the final dharma-age, they shall be able to protect the Buddha’s bodhi.
Endowed with all wondrous forms, adorned naturally with the marks and signs,
they will swiftly travel by their supernormal powers and behold immeasurable Buddhas.
By their supernormal power they manifest flowers, exquisite and most fragrant;
with silver, crystal, and various kinds of lapis lazuli,
as well as all manner of precious treasures, these all emerge from the palms of their hands.
For the sake of seeking Bodhi, they make offerings to all Buddhas;
with immeasurable offerings of music and songs of praise,
these emerge from the pores of their own bodies, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
When billions of sentient beings hear this sound,
they shall immediately attain non-retrogression in the unsurpassed wisdom of the Buddha.
Praised by the Buddhas, their names shall be heard everywhere.
His name is proclaimed in all directions, and one may hear and see it for oneself.
Those who hear his name shall extinguish all conceptual thoughts;
once those thoughts are extinguished, they shall behold immeasurable Buddhas.
With such wisdom, practicing the conduct of enlightenment for the benefit of all sentient beings, one seeks the virtues of bodhi.
Those who practice with wisdom obtain such benefits as these.
Furthermore, they shall obtain other benefits by being able to uphold this sutra.
If there are women who hear and uphold this sutra,
they shall immediately transform their female bodies and be able to preach the Dharma of ambrosia.
She shall never again receive such a female body,
endowed with all exquisite forms and adorned with the perfection of the marks.
If one were to display its merits within this supreme sūtra, [it would be immeasurable].
Having fully obtained these wondrous fruits, they swiftly realize bodhi;
in every single birth, they constantly achieve fearlessness.
If a person, regarding this sūtra—the realm of the bodhisattvas— [should practice it...]
The Inexhaustible Supreme Samādhi, the mother of all bodhisattvas,
by which one swiftly realizes awakening—
those who wish to draw near to the Buddha and likewise draw near to the Buddha’s awakening should uphold this sūtra.
Before long, through this sutra, they shall attain supreme and wondrous nirvana.
These courageous ones on this stage, the bodhisattvas who dwell therein,
behold the lamps of the world’s illumination, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

He became a powerful Cakravartin King; beholding the Buddha’s ten powers and his mind in tranquil concentration, he praised him with immeasurable hundreds of verses and attained the sublime samādhi of the Stainless Stage.
He made peerless offerings to the Buddha, who possesses a great name as the supreme among men;
casting aside his royal throne like spittle, he cultivated the most excellent and sublime holy life.
Having gone forth into the supreme Dharma of the Buddha, he attained this tranquil, stainless meditative concentration.
Having attained supreme, virtuous, and exquisite speech, they expound many billions of sūtras without interruption—the subtle dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Tranquil, sublime, stainless, and free from outflows, their nature is empty and still, transcending all verbal expression;
yet upon emerging from meditative absorption, they are able to teach for the sake of many people.
Profound wisdom is ever immeasurable; vast wisdom possesses boundless meaning.
Having attained this profound samādhi, one can act as a light for the world.
Constantly practicing the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), one remains eternally bright and clean, free from all pungent odors and vulgar impurities.
They cause immeasurable sentient beings to dwell in peace, Enabling them to attain tranquil concentration and be free from all defilements.
They constantly possess sharp, swift, and eloquent discernment, With vast learning like the ocean and immeasurable wisdom;
Their speech is excellent and they master all phenomena, Because they uphold this supreme sūtra of tranquil concentration.
Having thoroughly understood all karmas and crafts, and being proficient in the treatises on causes and medical prescriptions,
they have reached the shore of universal valor and strength by maintaining this stainless,
tranquil samādhi; they are skilled in all verses and treatises, as well as in jests, and have mastered singing and dancing to perfection.
They constantly act as teachers of the world, because they uphold this stainless, tranquil concentration;
They always possess supreme and wondrous retinues, and constantly receive all manner of sublime offerings,
because they are able to cultivate the excellent and wondrous practices of bodhi by upholding this stainless, tranquil concentration.
The poison arrows of grief and affliction press upon the heart; for those possessed of wisdom, such ailments do not exist.
They are forever free from disease and always at peace, because they maintain this stainless, tranquil concentration.
All the various illnesses that exist in the world—every physical ailment as well as mental distress—are absent in them.
That person shall never suffer such afflictions, for they maintain this stainless, tranquil concentration;
Whether it be pain of body or pain of heart, or if there be toothache or headache,
the wise one shall never experience such suffering and distress, for they maintain this stainless, tranquil concentration.
The mind has immeasurable other pains and afflictions, Arising from its own thoughts that burn the body;
Yet he has no arising of any afflictions at all, Because he maintains this stainless, tranquil meditative concentration.
Just as space is unstained, His self-nature is stainless and eternally pure.
The purity of that person's mind is likewise so, because they maintain this stainless, tranquil concentration;
Just as the radiance of the sun and moon, whose light is pervasive and ever-pure,
so too is that mind clear and void, because they maintain this stainless, tranquil concentration.
Just as a person holding various pigments Wishes to paint the void but cannot do so,
So too is that person’s mind pure like space, Because they maintain this stainless, tranquil concentration;
Just as the wind moves through the ten directions, Traveling everywhere without attachment.
The flow of their mind is like the wind; unstained by the world, they have attained liberation.
The movement of the wind is swift and cannot be seen; it cannot be bound by nets or snares.
The intent of such a person is profound and difficult to know, for they maintain this stainless, tranquil meditative concentration.
The light and shadow on a wall cannot be grasped; The reflection in water is difficult to seize.
When one attains samādhi within the body, No one can know the mind of that person.
The speech of all sentient beings Throughout the worlds of the ten directions may yet be counted, But the mind of one in samādhi cannot be known.
When one has attained this samādhi within the body, no one is able to know the mind of that person;
having attained such a state of tranquil extinction, their mind is stainless and free from attachment.
Among the sentient beings of the three realms, none can equal them, except for the Buddhas, the Honored Ones of the three realms.
Free from craving and desire, untainted by passion, One does not, with a deluded mind, become attached to women.
When one attains such a supreme meditative concentration, One obtains sublime tranquility, free from all defilement;
Having no affection for men or women, One is unstained by wives, concubines, or kinsmen.
When one attains the supreme meditative concentration of tranquility, The practice of sublime stillness remains untainted.
Having no regard for wealth or goods, One does not hope for celestial rewards nor cling to riches;
With a mind pure and free from conceptualization, One gains supreme benefit through the attainment of this concentration.
The wise do not practice the holy life for the sake of rebirth in heaven;
they practice generosity without seeking reward, practicing the holy life as a cause for Bodhi, because they have attained the stainless, tranquil meditative concentration.
They do not seek royal power when practicing the conduct of precepts; many people practice the holy life for such reasons.
Seeking enlightenment for the benefit of sentient beings, he is solely intent on accomplishing this samādhi.
Having abandoned all desires, his body is not afflicted; he never again yearns for sexual matters.
He has severed lust and pride, because he has attained such tranquil concentration.
He is never afflicted by anger; the defiled mind of wrathful affliction never arises.
Always removing rage with a mind of loving-kindness, he has attained such supreme, tranquil concentration.
His mind is never obscured by delusion; this is because wisdom has severed ignorance.
One attains immeasurable and unobstructed wisdom; by attaining this samādhi, one gains such benefits.
Through the contemplation of impurity, one eliminates lustful desire; through a mind of loving-kindness, one eliminates anger without remainder;
through wisdom, one cuts asunder the net of ignorance. By attaining this wondrous samādhi, one illuminates the world.
Free from sleep and indolence, detached from the arising of afflictions and the [four] elements,
having attained eternal liberation free from defilement— one gains these benefits by attaining this samādhi.
Not oppressed by stinginess or greed, their minds always delight in bestowing gifts upon others;
they relinquish everything and grant happiness to all, for such people are able to maintain this samādhi.
Endowed with majestic power beyond compare, Always possessing great physical strength,
Peerless throughout all the worlds— This is because the Bodhisattva maintains this supreme samādhi.
Furthermore, they may become a Wheel-Turning King, Possessing the seven treasures and traveling through the air;
At that time, all shall come to offer their allegiance— Such is the retribution obtained by those of wisdom.
Born into the most excellent, virtuous, and noble families, with all necessities of life and retinues fully provided;
possessing elephants, horses, carriages, and palanquins, and abounding in gold, silver, and every kind of jewel;
always being born into aristocratic and wealthy households—thus one is successively reborn in superior places.
Deeply believing in and delighting in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, they will be born there and honored by all.
Within Jambudvīpa, they will cause every household lacking faith to give rise to right faith;
they will enable them to establish the bodhicitta, and furthermore, cause them to attain the fruits of the Path.
Having attained unsurpassed bodhi, he turns the unsurpassed, wondrous wheel of Dharma;
if anyone understands the Dharma he preaches, they shall all attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
The Bodhisattva always delights in compassionate love and nurturing, Able to sustain and bring all sentient beings to maturity;
Constantly providing immeasurable and supreme benefit, He opens the eyes of sentient beings and dispels the darkness.
If the Buddha instructs a single bodhisattva, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of sentient beings all plant roots of goodness therein;
having heard it, they immediately resolve their minds upon Bodhi.
At that time, the buddha-field will not be empty, for the wise ones uphold the Buddha-dharma;
O Son of the Buddha!
Wherever a bodhisattva dwells, they bring vast benefit to immeasurable sentient beings.
Guarding the precepts with peerless meditative concentration and pure conduct, purifying samādhi throughout immeasurable kalpas,
and remaining ever-certain in dhyāna and liberation— such a bodhisattva is called a son of the Buddha.
They constantly cultivate the supreme bases of psychic power, And are able to travel to immeasurable Buddha-fields;
There, in the presence of the Tathāgatas, they hear the True Dharma, And having heard it, they remember it all exactly as it was taught.
If a Bodhisattva dwells in dhāraṇī, they can expound immeasurable sūtras;
furthermore, they know all sentient beings of the past, and likewise those of the future and the present.
He clearly awakens to the births and deaths of all sentient beings, and likewise thoroughly understands the future;
there is no one who goes from here to there, for even a slight portion [of such a transition] cannot be found upon investigation.
Since karma does not travel to that place, it is difficult to find even when sought;
yet the Bodhisattva of great renown is able to understand it.
One whose most excellent mind is pure dwells in emptiness and stillness.
By means of the unsurpassed Mahāyāna, they transport the multitudes of beings.
They do not engage in discursive thought or recollection, nor do they harbor the notion of a "sentient being.
Those of great renown are able to awaken to the dharma of non-arising.
Although he has something to say, he does not grasp at the notion of sentient beings;
realizing that their realm is empty, he abides in steadfast wisdom.
He clearly expounds this samādhi, the dwelling place of the Buddha-dharma.
Without giving rise to thoughts of men and women,
he contemplates all women while seated at the site of enlightenment;
having sat at the site of enlightenment, he utterly destroys the armies of Māra.
Seeing no Māra at all, he subdues the hosts of Māras;
seeing no Māra-maidens come to where he is,
when sitting at the site of enlightenment, he eliminates all conceptualizations.
Because all perceptions have been severed, the entire great earth trembles;
Mount Sumeru and the vast oceans, as well as the ten directions, are likewise moved.
Within those worlds of the ten directions, he fully knows all those sentient beings.
By the supernatural power of the Bodhisattva, the great earth is shaken;
when it quakes in six ways, he realizes the path to enlightenment.
All conditioned phenomena, as well as unconditioned phenomena—
He has fully realized all these phenomena;
there is only the sound of the teaching of the Dharma, yet no one is able to know it.
This is the path of all phenomena; he who knows this path is called the Knower of the World.
Through causes and conditions phenomena arise; through causes and conditions phenomena cease.
The essential nature of causes and conditions—this one understands thoroughly as it truly is.
If one studies all phenomena and can bring the dharma of emptiness to its ultimate consummation, [one attains liberation].
He immediately knows the path of all dharmas, exhausting all phenomena to their end.
As for the path of dharma he practices, even a bodhisattva cannot find it;
those who know this path realize the inconceivable perfect awakening.
If one knows all paths, one can attain the ultimate goal;
far removed from evil realms, one is able to know the characteristics of all phenomena.
Having sat at the site of enlightenment, one lets out the great lion’s roar.
Throughout boundless billions of worlds, his voice completely fills them all.
He can further shake those lands; the World Hero of great renown, who skillfully delivers sentient beings, is called the Noble Tamer of Men.
Having already realized supreme enlightenment, he rose from beneath the Bodhi tree;
having delivered those among the immeasurable billions who were ready to be saved,
he was then able to manifest transformations, conjuring forth infinite Buddhas.
Traveling through various worlds, they benefit all sentient beings.
The Buddhas are able to establish immeasurable billions of beings;
these manifested Tathāgatas preach the most supreme Dharma for them.
This is the true Mahāyāna, Named the wisdom of the Tathāgata;
It can arouse faith in sentient beings And act as the cause for attaining Buddhahood.
This is the true Mahāyāna, The most wondrous vehicle of the Tathāgata.
One should show reverence to the Tathāgata, And show even greater reverence to the Bodhisattvas.
Showing profound reverence for the Buddha, And likewise for the Dharma and the Saṅgha,
One who desires to realize supreme enlightenment Should not allow the mind to become inferior.
By reverently serving the Bodhisattvas and honoring those who are courageous,
one will swiftly ascend to perfect enlightenment and before long become a Tathāgata.
Throughout the thousandfold world-systems, the Bodhisattva shall go to visit them all.
Beholding the Honored Muni, the Bodhisattva was free from fear.
With powders of various supreme jewels, he scattered them everywhere over the Great Hero,
mingled with māndārava flowers, because he joyfully sought awakening.
Adorning this realm to seek the merits of a Buddha,
they cover it with nets of jewels extending throughout the ten directions;
they hang banners of supreme excellence and erect billions of precious victory banners and canopies.
Adorned with immeasurable varieties, they illuminate and beautify the world.
They transform into sublime terraces and pavilions, as well as wondrous palaces;
their corridors and galleries are all exquisite and elegant, interspersed with a myriad of precious gems.
The windows and palatial chambers are all shaped like half-moons;
together with various incense jars and the like, they are all adorned with exquisite jewels.
All manner of fragrant substances emerge from the wondrous cloud-platforms.
Within the thousandfold world-systems, the pervasive fragrance is most delightful.
From those clouds of universal incense, a rain of fragrant flowers falls;
whoever smells it shall become a Great Teacher who attains Buddhahood.
He has removed the thorns of craving, likewise eliminated the affliction of hatred,
and shattered the net of delusion; having distanced himself from all darkness,
he has attained supreme supernormal powers, as well as the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment.
Those who dwell in the various dhyānas and liberations should receive the offerings of the faithful.
One should arrange billions of couches and seats, spread them with myriad exquisite garments,
cover them with jeweled nets, and adorn them with flower garlands.
Fearless bodhisattvas, heroic mahāsattvas,
sit there with bodies adorned with the primary marks and endowed with all the secondary characteristics.
With groves of exquisite jewels, they adorn this realm.
They transform into various flower ponds, filled with water of eight virtues;
those who drink that water will be far removed from all afflictions,
quickly able to leave behind thirst and craving, and become a shrine (caitya) for the world.
Furthermore, there are other worlds, where great beings have all come together to praise the Buddha’s virtues:
"The Guide, the Lion of the Śākyas."
If there are those who hear this sound, they will be able to become teachers of the world’s path.
They shall attain the inconceivable, which this sutra is able to reveal:
a lotus flower of exquisite golden hue, with billions of densely packed petals.
The most honored and wondrously enlightened Jewel dwells upon this lotus pedestal;
its stem and leaves are of lapis lazuli, its filaments are of pure gold,
and amidst the maṇi-jewels of its treasury of virtue, it transforms into billions of flowers.
The various exquisite fragrances that emanate from it cause all who smell them to rejoice;
they eliminate every ailment and bring complete satisfaction to the six sense faculties.
Greed, hatred, and delusion are all extinguished at once.
Having eliminated all afflictions, one will certainly attain Buddhahood.
These flowers emit wondrous sounds, praising the virtues of the Buddha;
they do the same for the Dharma and the Saṅgha, their voices filling the worlds of the ten directions.
The gate of emptiness, signlessness, And the dharma of wishlessness—
When the multitudes of nayutas have heard them, They all attain the stage of non-retrogression.
All the sounds that are produced Pervade billions of worlds.
Having heard this, immeasurable multitudes gave rise to the bodhicitta.
Among the various exquisite sounds produced by swans, peacocks, parrots,
mandarin ducks, and the like, the Buddha’s voice is supreme.
With trees of supreme and wondrous jewels, he manifests within this land;
most preeminent in their majestic beauty, with strings of pearls hanging down,
all the various adornments throughout every Buddha-field [are displayed].
The most supreme among them manifests in this realm;
Exquisite garments and jeweled necklaces, And trees hung with all manner of musical sounds;
Wondrous flowers that gladden the heart, Constantly draped and spread everywhere.
These various wondrous adornments, by which sentient beings attain peace and happiness,
are sustained by Śākyamuni through the power of his holy spiritual might.
Thus have I briefly explained the virtues of the Lion of the Śākyas.
The Bodhisattvas of great renown have no doubt regarding this wisdom.
If one can have faith in this, their conduct will be inconceivable;
their wisdom will increase like rivers flowing toward the sea.
If one wished to measure the great ocean, no one would be able to know its number;
likewise, when I speak of the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas, all of it is inconceivable.
These inconceivable Bodhisattvas dwell securely within such a limit.
He utters exquisite speech, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
throughout immeasurable kalpas, the bodhisattva remains ever free from grasping.
If one cuts off the grasping for signs, one draws near to enlightenment.
Even if the Dharma were to perish entirely, one would never violate the pure precepts;
being without deficiency in practice, such a person is the foremost among the assembly of Bodhisattvas.
It is solely because of craving and desire that the precepts become tainted and deficient.
Having severed the signs of desire, one attains the concentration of non-negligence.
Constantly practicing the samādhi of quiescence, one does not cling to the flavor of concentration.
Being without attachment and without negligence, one is not defiled by the world.
Transcending the mundane world, one is able to go to the various Buddha-lands,
namely the Land of Peace and Bliss, where one beholds Amitābha Buddha. Furthermore,
one sees the various bodhisattvas, fully adorned with the marks of perfection.
Having reached the shore of supernormal powers, they have perfected the gate of dhāraṇī.
Traveling through billions of worlds, they prostrate their heads at the feet of the Buddhas and are further able to illuminate immeasurable Buddha-fields.
Dispelling all afflictions and destroying all defilements,
severing every fetter and bond, one becomes a successor to the Buddha in a single lifetime.
Bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, one shall never again fall into the evil realms.
The sentient beings of that land have severed all evil paths.
Amitābha, the Savior, cultivated and purified his Buddha-world through the practice of non-negligence for inconceivable eons.
Do not harbor doubts; through the sovereign power of that Buddha, you shall be able to give rise to supreme faith and swiftly attain rebirth in that land.
When women hear this praise of the realm, they too shall be able to give rise to supreme faith.
Having attained a male body, one may travel to billions of Buddha-fields;
though one were to offer all manner of requisites to every Buddha across those nayutas of billions of fields,
it would not equal even a single fraction of loving-kindness.
Constantly cultivating precepts and meditative concentration, The immeasurable dhyānas and liberations,
And practicing the three gates of liberation, One swiftly becomes supreme among humans.
In the evil age of the final dharma, If a bodhisattva maintains the precepts,
To make offerings to the Buddha’s body of constant compassion is the most supreme of offerings.
Such a person makes offerings to all Buddhas— the most supreme Honored Ones of the past, present, and future.
In this degenerate age, those who uphold the precepts are seen by the Buddhas of the ten directions.
When the Dharma is in its final stage, Bodhisattvas protect and maintain the Buddha’s prohibitory precepts; these virtuous sons are able to safeguard the Dharma.
When women hear praise of that jewel-adorned land, If they give rise to a mind of superior faith and joy,
They shall immediately obtain a male body of wisdom and sagacity, Able to travel and roam through billions of Buddha-fields.

Within nayutas of billions of buddha-fields, all the various implements for making offerings to the Buddhas used to honor them do not equal even a small fraction of a single moment of a compassionate heart;
nor do the observance of the precepts and samādhis, together with the practice of the various dhyānas and the four immeasurables, [equal it].
They also cultivate the three gates of liberation, swiftly attaining the Unsurpassed One in the world.
Making offerings to the Buddhas, whose bodies are ever-compassionate—such an offering to the Buddhas is peerless in the world.
If there is a bodhisattva who does not forsake the precepts, in that final age of a degenerate world,
this person is able to make offerings to all Buddhas— those of the past, those of the present,
and the Most Victorious Honored Ones of the future.
If there are those who uphold the prohibitive precepts in an evil age, the Buddhas of the ten directions behold such persons.
If a Bodhisattva, in a future evil age, maintains pure prohibitions, they are praised by the Buddhas: "This one is my son, able to protect the Dharma."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the youth Candraprabha:

"In the past, immeasurable, countless, inconceivable, vast, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Śabdaguṇa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
"O youth!

After that Tathāgata Śabdaguṇa had established immeasurable and inconceivable numbers of sentient beings in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and caused all devas and humans to cultivate the Buddha-work, he subsequently entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*."
“O youth! At that time there was a king named Guṇadatta.

After the parinirvāṇa of that Buddha, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, that king, in order to make offerings to the Tathāgata Śabdaguṇa, erected eighty-four koṭī-nayuta stūpas. Before each stūpa he lit hundreds of thousands of nayutas of lamps, and with all kinds of music, incense, flowers, jeweled garlands, ointments, powdered incense, as well as all kinds of robes, jeweled canopies, banners, and pennants—all for the purpose of making offerings to the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas—he placed them at the sites of the stūpas.”

At that time, King Virtuous Sound, having made offerings at the stūpa of the Tathāgata’s relics, assembled a full eighty hundred thousand million billion nayutas of great bodhisattvas.
