He provided them with all manner of musical instruments and articles of pleasure; these bodhisattvas were all great Dharma-preachers, skillfully able to expound the Dharma and attain immeasurable eloquence, and were well able to manifest the true merits of immeasurable dharmas.
"O youth!

At that time, there was a bhikṣu in the assembly named Kṣemaśrī, who sat in that gathering. He was in his early twenties, with a radiant countenance and black hair; he abided in the noble and wondrous conduct of a celibate youth and had never experienced the pleasures of sensual desire, being at the beginning of his summer retreat after having first received full ordination."

“O Youth! At that time, King Virtuous Sound invited the assembly of great bodhisattvas because he wished to fulfill the six pāramitās, the bodhisattva-piṭaka, the great dhāraṇīs, skillful means, mastery, and unimpededness; therefore, during that night, he invited the assembly of great bodhisattvas to be before the Buddha for a Dharma assembly.”

At that time, hundreds of thousands of nayutas of lamps were all blazing brightly; the halls and chambers were swept and sprinkled, various flowers were scattered, and diverse exquisite garments were spread out.

Then, King Śrīghoṣa, together with his harem of queens and concubines, his court ladies, the ministers, the people of the cities and towns, and his kinsmen and retinue, went forth carrying various musical instruments, as well as ointments, powdered incense, flower garlands, robes, precious parasols, banners, and streamers, to make offerings to the Buddha’s stūpa.
Having completed these offerings, he and eighty thousand palace attendants ascended the high pavilion in order to hear the Dharma.
At that time, immeasurable devas and humans gathered together for the sake of hearing the Dharma.
Then, the bhikṣu Kṣemadatta saw hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of lamps blazing and illuminating everywhere; observing the great assembly, he immediately thought:
"I too practice the Mahāyāna, seeking with joy the samādhi of the equality of the essential nature of all dharmas and the absence of conceptual proliferation."
"If I now wish to attain this samādhi, I ought to make offerings to these Buddha shrines and stūpas.

I shall now perform such offerings that devas, humans, asuras, and others will conceive thoughts of wonder, leaping for joy and attaining the light of the Dharma; that my offerings will outshine all the offerings of that king; and that King Devasvara, along with his palace women and retinue, will all rejoice upon seeing my offerings."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Kṣemadatta, seeing the great assembly gathered before the stūpa to hear the Dharma, immediately wrapped his right arm with cloth and smeared it with oil during that very night; for the sake of making an offering to the Buddha, he set it ablaze.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Kṣemadatta, dwelling in superior faith and seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, burned his right arm; yet his mind remained unaltered and his countenance did not change.

“O youth! At that time, when the bhikṣu Kṣemaśreṣṭha set his arm ablaze, the earth shook violently. The radiance [of the fire] eclipsed immeasurable hundreds of thousands of burning lamps so that they were entirely without light, while the light from this arm shone everywhere throughout the ten directions.”

At that time, the Bodhisattva Kṣemadatta was filled with joy; regarding the samādhi of the equality of the essential nature of all phenomena and the absence of conceptual proliferation, he composed a song of praise using harmonious, elegant, and exquisite eloquence, with correct speech, phonemes, and phrases, so that the entire great assembly might hear it everywhere.

At that time, twelve thousand devaputras of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven felt great joy in their hearts and presented various kinds of offerings; they had all come to this assembly for the sake of the Dharma.

At that time, King Virtuous Sound (Guṇaruta), together with his retinue in the inner palace—consorts, queens, and court ladies—beheld the bhikṣu Aniruddha (Anvayagupta) setting ablaze his right arm, its brilliant red flames illuminating all directions.
Having seen this, he thought to himself:
"This bhikṣu must have attained supernormal powers (ṛddhi), for he has manifested such a rare transformation, showing no stinginess even toward his own life."

“At that time, King Śrīghoṣa, seeing the unprecedented spiritual transformations of the bhikṣu Kṣemadatta, felt a heart of love and joy. Empowered by the熏資 (perfuming and support) of his pure faith and his own roots of goodness, he leaped from a palace eight hundred cubits high along with his queens and eighty thousand court ladies—desiring to see this bodhisattva bhikṣu. Through the power of his reverent roots of goodness, he obtained a manifest karmic reward: he was immediately protected and sustained by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, and mahoragas, so that he did not fall.”

By the power of the protection of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, and mahoragas, King Śrīghoṣa, along with his queen, consorts, and maidservants, sustained no injury to body or mind despite falling from the high palace; they were neither exhausted nor terrified.

"At that time, King Virtuous Sound (Guṇarāja) clasped his arms with both hands and wailed aloud; the entire assembly did likewise, for they saw the bhikṣu Peaceful Virtue (Anvayaśrī) with his upper arms like a garland of *campaka* flowers, and his arms slender and long like the trunk of an elephant king.
All who beheld him marveled in wonder; there was none who did not cry out in lamentation, weeping with tears falling like rain."
At that time, the bhikṣu Kṣemadatta, seeing that the great king and the entire multitude were all weeping and filled with distress, asked the king:
"Great King!..."
"For what reason do you wail so piteously with falling tears, and why does this great assembly likewise weep so bitterly?
At that time, King Deon replied in verse:
"O An-yin-te (Anvaya) of Great Wisdom!..."
O Distinguished Dharma Master of keen wisdom!
I weep with compassion because I see you thus burning your own body.
Your countenance is exceedingly handsome and wondrous, like a mass of blazing fire.
Seeing you thus mutilate your own body, my grief and affliction increase all the more.
When you burned your right arm, its radiance illuminated the worlds of the ten directions,
eclipsing all other lamps so that even the stars and moon no longer appeared.
The great earth shook in its entirety, yet your mind remained unshaken;
my heart gave rise to reverence, knowing you are no ordinary person.
Within that palace of a thousand cubits, together with eighty thousand palace ladies,
I cast my own body down, yet my body suffered no harm at all.
Excellent,
O you of pure wisdom!
Excellent!
O Unsurpassed Mind!
Excellent!
Vīryavān! Excellent!
You have accomplished great faith!
When you burned your body and arms, your mind remained unmoved;
you gave rise to a heart of joy while simultaneously preaching the sublime Dharma.
You were like the full moon, and again like the sun in a clear sky.
Like Sumeru, the king of mountains, so too is his exquisite beauty.
I have made such a vow and fulfilled great diligence;
therefore, I sacrifice this beloved body to benefit all sentient beings.
Weeping out of love for the Dharma, you who delight in the vast and stainless—
because you have sacrificed your own body, I am filled with the utmost grief.
You, who are honored by gods and men, possess boundless and supreme eloquence.
Kṣemadatta replied to the king, speaking these verses:
"One is not called deficient in limb merely because one lacks a body or hands;
if one does not uphold the precepts, that is what is called being deficient in limb."
With this foul and impure body, I have already made an offering to the Tathāgata,
the inconceivable field of merit, the stūpa for all the world.
If one were to fill the three thousandfold world system with the sands of the seven treasures, [the merit would not equal that of making such an offering].
To the Buddha, the World-Honored One, one gives for the sake of Bodhi;
though such offerings are made, there are other offerings even more excellent than these.
If one can realize the emptiness of all phenomena, one is then able to relinquish both body and life.
I now speak words of truth:
O Great King, pray listen attentively, as do all those gathered here; let everyone hear my words.
If it is certain that I shall truly attain supreme enlightenment, [then may my limbs become golden].
"This is truly so and not false; it causes the earth to shake in six ways.
When these words were spoken, the great earth trembled, and seeing this rare occurrence, the devas rejoiced greatly.
When humans and devas were filled with joy, they gave rise to the bodhicitta;
an immeasurable and inconceivable multitude all turned toward supreme wisdom.
The bhikṣu Kṣemadatta brought benefit to all beings.
I establish billions of sentient beings, placing them in unsurpassed wisdom. By this word of true Dharma—
"The nature of all things, when analyzed,
is found to be without reality"— if these words are indeed truthful and not false, let my arm be restored as it was before.
If these phenomena were truly real, even the name "peaceful" would not exist;
though sought throughout the ten directions, they cannot be found because they are empty.
All phenomena are like echoes; sound emerges from within them.
Sound cannot be found when sought; thus one knows all phenomena.
Those who have attained ultimate and thorough realization have no fear regarding emptiness.
Such people speak what is true; the fire of marks cannot burn them.
All sentient beings in the world— gods, humans, yakṣas, and nāgas—
through the power of omniscience, are all caused to awaken to tranquil concentration.
Whatever worldly hardships there may be for humans and devas,
his irreversible majesty can swiftly destroy them all.
As he spoke these words, his body and arm returned to their original state.
The bhikṣu Kṣemadatta was endowed with a body of perfect marks and adornments.
Countless billions of devas, dwelling in the pure space of the sky,
with hearts of faith, scattered māndārava flowers over that bhikṣu’s body.
These are all flowers surpassing those of humans, filling the entire Jambudvīpa.
With billions of nayutas of celestial maidens performing music and singing hymns,
the bhikṣu Anuruddha utters the great lion’s roar.
The Honored Muni Tathāgata causes billions of other buddha-fields,
each within their own lands, to proclaim the name of that pure Great Being, the bhikṣu Kṣemadatta.
Monks and nuns, laymen and laywomen of pure faith,
devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, and the rest—
having heard this teaching on determinate karma, they shall attain peace and be freed from defilement.
Those who seek the Way with faith are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The bhikṣu Anvayaśas, wise and having attained mastery,
for the sake of the Buddha’s wisdom, lit his arm without any distress.
That person, within a thousand lands, transforms his body like the sands of the Ganges;
the light from his arms shines everywhere, like the fire at the end of an eon.
He rains down various powdered incenses, filling all lands completely.
Reaching down to the great earth, all the heavens gathered together.
With every kind of offering, they adorned this buddha-field;
the ground was covered with pearls as an offering to An-yin-de (Śāntaśrī).
All manner of precious flowers adorn this land;
the dragons rain down exquisite pearls as an offering to An-yin-de (Śāntaguṇa).
Furthermore, with every kind of jewel, they embellish and decorate this land.
The dragon rained down precious ornaments as an offering to Aninyagupta.
The most supreme Lion of the Śākyas, dwelling on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa,
let out a lion’s roar before all the bhikṣus.
I am the one named Kṣemadatta; The one of virtuous renown is Maitreya.
Throughout those thousands of billions of kalpas, We together cultivated the practices for awakening.
At that time, seeing the upholder of the precepts, Kṣemadatta possessed such wisdom.
Countless women were all transformed into men;
all Buddhas bestowed upon them predictions of enlightenment, leaving no room for doubt.
They shall swiftly achieve fulfillment and realize the self-arisen wisdom of the world.
Having heard this sutra, one should proclaim its definitive merits;
without giving rise to attachment toward oneself, one should train in such a Dharma.
*Candrapradīpa-samādhi-sūtra*, Fascicle Seven.
The Moon Lamp Samādhi Sūtra, Volume Eight.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas during the Northern Qi Dynasty.
"O Youth! Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, desiring to seek and attain this samādhi..."
Therefore, one should cultivate roots of goodness by practicing the gift of Dharma or the gift of material wealth, dedicating these acts of giving through the four kinds of dedication.
What are the four?

First, the Buddhas of the past attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* through skillful means; may I also attain such skillful means, and dedicate these roots of goodness toward enlightenment—this is called the first dedication.

Second, having heard such skillful means taught by a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), one upholds, recites, and trains in them; thinking, "By these skillful means may I attain unsurpassed bodhi," and vowing to always encounter them throughout the long night, one dedicates these roots of goodness—this is called the second dedication.
Third, may the wealth and resources I obtain be enjoyed in common with all sentient beings; dedicating through these roots of goodness is called the third dedication.

Fourth, may I obtain wealth and the Dharma in all my future births, and may I gather, protect, and benefit all sentient beings; may I always attain such a body as this—dedicating these roots of goodness in this way is called the fourth dedication.
"O youth!
By means of these four kinds of dedication, one should dedicate all roots of goodness.
Furthermore, youth!"
Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas seek this samādhi, whether they are laypeople or renunciants, they serve those who uphold the precepts with a mind free from deceit and crookedness.

If there are those who can uphold this samādhi—whether they be monastics or laypeople—and if such persons encounter the suffering of illness and are on the verge of death, if one can remove that patient's affliction by giving them the flesh and blood from one's own body, and if there is one who has achieved superior faith, a bodhisattva should provide such gifts with an unshakable mind and a pure mind.

“O Youth! In the past, beyond incalculable, even more than incalculable, immeasurable, boundless, ineffable, unfathomable, vast, and inconceivable kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Acintyapraṇidhānaviśeṣasamudgatarāja, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.”

"On that very day, that Buddha, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. He manifested immeasurable and boundless emanation Buddhas to preach the Dharma, skillfully subduing countless sentient beings and establishing them on the path of the untainted Arhatship;
he likewise established immeasurable sentient beings in Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, causing them to attain the stage of non-retrogression."

On this very day, the Tathāgata Acintyapraṇidhānaviśeṣasamudgatarāja reached the end of his lifespan and entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*; his True Dharma remained in the world for eighty-four thousand *koṭi-nayuta* hundreds of thousands of years.

“O Youth! After the True Dharma of the Buddha Acintyapraṇidhānaviśeṣasamudgatarāja has vanished, during the final age, there will be immeasurable bhikṣus who cling to views; those bhikṣus will have no affection for, no joy in, and will not give rise to faith in sūtras such as these, but will instead slander and revile them.”
If there are those who can uphold such sutras as these, they may be oppressed and distressed in body by evil associates, or reviled and slandered in speech, even unto the taking of their lives.
For the sake of greed for gain and honor, those evil bhikṣus will kill twenty thousand bhikṣus who uphold these sutras.

“O Youth! At that time, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a king named Jñānabala, who upheld the True Dharma, protected the True Dharma, had fulfilled his original vows, and had previously planted many roots of goodness under former Buddhas.”

“O youth! In the past, within this Jambudvīpa, there was a Dharma-preacher named Satyamati who upheld such sūtras of samādhi. He entered royal palaces as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra); because he possessed great compassion, he was able to provide rescue, benefit, and sympathy.”

That king took delight in seeing this bhikṣu and never grew weary of it; he listened to his teachings and discourses, visited him to serve him, attended upon him with offerings, and questioned him on difficult points. Having heard his explanations, he was able to retain them and skillfully provide answers.

At that time, that bhikṣu was well-versed in the meaning of how the detailed and the concise mutually encompass one another; he was fully endowed with dignified deportment and all modes of conduct; he was proficiently able to penetrate the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense bases (āyatanas);

he well understood the coming together and parting of all sentient beings, as well as their reuniting after having parted; he also knew the deportment, conduct, inclinations, dispositions, and habitual tendencies of sentient beings; he well understood the faculties (indriyas), powers (balas), and diligence of sentient beings; he well understood the distinctions in their wisdom, dispositions, and habitual tendencies; he well understood what is associated with and dissociated from the Truths (satya);
his responses in speech were definitive in meaning and possessed profound, wondrous eloquence; and he was also well able to know how to discipline sentient beings.

Smiling as they speak first, those who see them find joy; far removed from frowning, their minds are vast and expansive. Abiding thus in the four immeasurable minds in conjunction with great compassion, they cannot be defeated by any opposing doctrines.

“O Youth! At that time, King Jñānabala had a daughter named Jñānamati, sixteen years of age, whose countenance was upright and whose form was exquisite; her features were full and nothing was lacking, and she took the bhikṣu Tattvārtha as her teacher and guide.”
"At that time, the elements of that bhikṣu were out of balance, and a malignant black ulcer developed on his right thigh that was difficult to treat; all the physicians abandoned him and departed."

At that time, King Jñānabala, seeing that the bhikṣu was gravely ill and suffering, feared he would die; weeping aloud and shedding tears, he was joined by his consorts and queens, eighty thousand court ladies, as well as the people of the kingdom, cities, and towns, the crown prince, the various officials, the army, the generals, the gatekeepers and sentries, the servants and attendants, and the rest of the great assembly—all of whom saw this bhikṣu and wept together.

"O Youth! At that time, King Jñānabala had a kinsman who had previously passed away and been reborn in the heavens. This being appeared in the king’s dream, urging him on and speaking these words: 'This bhikṣu is ill;

he must be washed with the fresh blood of a maiden who has not yet reached puberty, and this blood must also be used to anoint his sores. Furthermore, one must take her flesh and boil it into a broth, seasoned with various flavors, and give it to him to eat along with rice; only then will he recover.'"
"If this medicine is not obtained, it will certainly be difficult to rise.

At that time, King Jñānabala, having seen such a dream, awoke at dawn; he immediately rose from his bed and entered the inner palace, where he assembled all the palace attendants and related the dream in detail:
"I have seen these things."
"Who can provide medicine for this sick bhikṣu, so that my good friend, who teaches the path of virtue, may be cured?
"O Youth! At that time, none among all the women of the inner and outer palaces, nor the court ladies, were capable of doing so."
"O youth!

At that time, having heard these words from his father the king, Jñānamati understood that the sick bhikṣu required such medicine. Having heard this, he was filled with joy; his body and mind leaped with delight, and he reflected thus:
'According to what my father says, I shall now give fresh blood, flesh, and so forth from this body of mine, which has never yet engaged in sexual union, to that venerable one.'"

I am the youngest among those in the palace, and I have conceived a profound sense of reverence for this Dharma Master Ācārya. With body, speech, and mind purified, I seek untainted wisdom; thus, I offer my own flesh and blood to the unattached Dharma Master, taking my own flesh and seasoning it with various flavors.
"I ought to prepare medicine for this sick bhikṣu so that my Great Teacher’s suffering may be eliminated and he may recover.

At that time, Jñānamati—dwelling with a profound mind in the Dharma—took a sharp knife and cut the flesh from her own thigh. As the wound bled, she took the fresh meat, seasoned it with various flavors, and prepared a stew. She collected the blood from her body in a golden bowl, then followed the King's command to summon the sick bhikṣu into the palace. She had him sit upon a mat before his father, the King; she first washed his wound with the blood and then applied it as an ointment. Furthermore, she prepared a fine meal by seasoning the meat with various other superior flavors and offered it to the Dharma Master in order to obtain merit.
At that time, that bhikṣu did not know, perceive, or suspect that there was a transgression, and he immediately ate it.
When this sick bhikṣu ate this food, his suffering and affliction were immediately removed.

At that time, having been freed from the suffering of illness and possessing a body at peace and full of joy, the Dharma Master preached the supreme and wondrous Dharma for King Jñānabala—specifically for the sake of seeking this samādhi—and caused the thirteen thousand court ladies within the palace to resolve their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, King Jñānabala immediately spoke these verses, questioning his daughter:
“From where did you obtain this fresh, excellent human flesh and blood?
How can you prepare such a fine meal for the sick, so that this bhikṣu may find peace and comfort?”
Who was sent, to what place, and who was slain, that you obtained such excellent flesh?
How did you combine it with various exotic flavors, and how did you obtain pure blood to wash and anoint it?
When the Dharma Master partakes of this food, he also uses fresh blood to wash and anoint his sores;
it can eliminate such great and evil afflictions, causing that Venerable One to attain joy and bliss.
In the presence of my kinsman, the deity, I heard these words in a dream:
"If you can obtain such medicine as this, only then can that bhikṣu’s illness be cured."
One must take fresh blood from a human body to wash and anoint the foul, malignant sores of the Dharma Master;
having seasoned human flesh until it is fragrant, one offers it as food for him.
If a bhikṣu employs only this remedy, the illness will surely be eliminated at once;
since only this medicine is capable of providing healing, O King, do not rely on other methods, but prepare it with haste.
Having awakened from sleep and arisen from my bed, I immediately entered the inner palace and spoke these words;
when all the palace attendants heard this speech, they all remained silent, unable to respond.
At that time, I again addressed the palace attendants, saying:
"Take fresh flesh and blood from my own body, mix them with various other delicious flavors, and offer this medicinal food to him;
furthermore, wash and anoint [the wound] with pure blood."
The Dharma-preacher bhikṣu has a malignant black ulcer; Only by this method can it be healed.
If one does not employ such a medicine To treat the bhikṣu’s malignant ulcer, The Dharma-preacher will surely pass away, Precisely because of the lack of this method.
At that time, when the palace ladies heard these words, they were all silent and spoke no further;
none among them was able to offer such a gift of flesh and blood as medicine.
Even throughout all the people of the triple world, there was not a single one capable of giving their own body’s flesh.
The palace was informed in every detail, yet not a single person could speak a word in response.
My heart holds this bhikṣu in deep reverence;
all people cherish their own bodies, and because they are so attached to their own flesh, they cannot bring themselves to sacrifice their own flesh and blood.
"Excellent!
Tell me where it can be obtained.
Having heard this at that time, my heart was filled with joy; hearing my father’s respectful and sublime words, my mind became courageous and undaunted.
The maiden Jñānamati replied to her father:
"I pray that you, with a pure mind, will deign to listen.
I have no attachment to my own self, nor do I harbor any clinging to the notion of 'I'."
Able to sacrifice my own body with valorous resolve, for the sake of seeking unsurpassed bodhi.
I pray only that the King, my father, will grant me further audience: though I searched everywhere for human flesh, I could find none;
therefore, I have cut the flesh from my own thigh and seasoned it with various flavors to offer to the Dharma Master.
Not killing others nor eating the flesh of the dead, I have cut my own body to bring about vast benefit;
since the bhikṣu has thus been freed from suffering and affliction, I too shall obtain immeasurable merit.
The king then asked:
"When you cut your own body, were you not greatly oppressed by suffering?
Quickly prepare medicine to apply to your wound, lest your body undergo great agony."
Hearing his father, the king, speak with compassion, he said:
"I only pray that Your Majesty will grant me further audience; having heard this, I shall contemplate deeply the practice of the True Dharma. Such is the inconceivability of karmic fruition."
Having heard the words of the deva from my father, I disregarded my own body and life;
with a heart of faith and reverence, I offered them as a gift, and thus I gave up my own fresh flesh and blood.
By using my own body to bring benefit, I have been able to eliminate the monk’s malignant disease;
having now performed immeasurable merit, I have exchanged this non-enduring body for an enduring one.
The girl spoke again in this way:
"I pray only that the King, my father, will listen further; having heard the true Dharma, I wish for you to accept and uphold it, and contemplate those inconceivable fruits of karma."
In the past, unwholesome karma was created; through delusion, sentient beings fall into the evil realms.
Though their flesh and bones waste away, they join together once more; therefore, the retribution of karma is inconceivable.
At first there is only a skeleton of bones; in the blink of an eye, the flesh of the body joins together once more.
How much more so for those who perform virtuous deeds—how could they not obtain whatever their hearts desire?
Though his own flesh was cut, he felt no pain at first; though the wound bled, he felt no suffering.
Even when all parts of his body were being severed, because he was mindful of the Dharma, there was no place of injury.
I have deep love and joy for the True Dharma; therefore, I cut my own flesh to offer it as a gift.
All conditioned phenomena are like illusions; the wound on my body has healed and is restored just as it was before.
Just as the udumbara flower appears only once in the course of immeasurable kalpas, so too is the bhikṣu who is a Dharma-preacher: he is seen but rarely within Jambudvīpa.
Just as a mass of Jambu-river gold radiates light, such that no one who gazes upon it ever tires;
so too is the true intention of this Dharma Master, whom gods and humans behold without weariness.
Just as drinking cool, clear water can remove the affliction of parching thirst when it is hot, so too is the bhikṣu who is a Dharma teacher:
he can eliminate all the cravings of sentient beings.
I have severed my own thigh flesh to offer to the Dharma Master, And bestowed upon him the fresh, pure blood of my own body;
To eliminate the suffering of the four elements of that Dharma Master, I have performed what the Buddha has praised.
The noble one has accomplished the qualities of yoga and maintains such a supreme, true concentration;
I have made offerings to that bhikṣu, and by this merit and goodness, may I attain Buddhahood.
Just as fragrant incense is most delightful, Its seasonal scent surpasses that of sandalwood;
Its wondrous fragrance permeates everywhere without exception, So too it is with those who maintain precepts and meditative concentration.
Just as Mount Sumeru is most majestic, Shining throughout the ten directions and exceedingly lovely,
The radiance illuminates the earth and the void; so too is the Dharma-master who upholds the precepts.

If a person, pure and with deep faith and joy, erects a most excellent and wondrous jeweled stupa, and other people come to honor and support it, the supreme merit of the original builder increases all the more.
The Dharma teacher who speaks is likewise so; with a pure mind, I have brought him peace and security.
Having sacrificed my own fresh flesh and blood, I have now constructed a stūpa of the True Dharma.
If there is a stūpa or temple on the verge of collapsing, a wise person supports it so that it does not fall;
furthermore, if another person comes to make offerings to the stūpa, they enable the one who supported it to obtain supreme merit.
So too is it with the Dharma-stūpa of a bhikṣu: I have used excellent medicine to eliminate his afflictions.
This one can expound the supreme and wondrous Dharma, establishing sentient beings in the Unsurpassed Way.
If the Dharma-preaching Bhikṣu should pass away, how shall this Dharma be heard?
O Father King, you should know that with the death of the bhikṣu, this samādhi has been lost.
The Dharma Master was like a pure and wondrous lamp, healing the darkness of the afflictions of sentient beings;
abiding in the vast samādhi, he rescued all living beings from the evil realms.
The conduct of a bhikṣu is unfathomable; he constantly dwells in the great mind.
Having thoroughly mastered the definitive meaning of the teachings, he cannot be defeated by any evil or heterodox doctrines.
Throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas, I shall never again receive a female body;
having honored the Dharma-master according to the supreme method of reverence taught by the Buddha, I have paid my respects.
If one were to fill Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges with precious objects and offer them to the Tathāgata,
yet another person, possessing a pure mind, were to give even a foot or a finger— this merit would be far superior to that.
After such a woman has passed away, she shall behold ten billion Buddhas;
having gone forth under all those Buddhas, she will receive and uphold this supreme samādhi.
In the presence of all those Buddhas, the Honored Ones among two-legged beings, and at the final moment of their parinirvāṇa—
such as these they always leave the household life, these sons of the Buddha, pure and free from defilement.
Furthermore, in the presence of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, I cultivated the holy life within that Buddha’s teaching;
at that time, I transformed my female body and became a great Dharma teacher who expounded the supreme Dharma.
The King of Wisdom Power is Maitreya, who constantly and valiantly protects and upholds the Dharma;
the Dharma Master is none other than Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
Able to relinquish his own flesh and body without regard for parsimony, he made offerings to the Sovereign of Merit.
Constantly remaining far removed from a crooked mind, for the sake of seeking such a samādhi;
seeing that bhikṣu oppressed by the suffering of illness,
all those who then wept shall all attain the stage of non-retrogression and ultimately be forever separated from all evil realms.
That person shall no longer be oppressed by manifold afflictions, nor shall they be separated from the Dharma or suffer the pains of illness;
their five faculties will be complete and without deficiency, and their minds shall be free from the thorns of sorrow.
All their features will be dignified and exquisitely sublime, and the majesty of their merit and spiritual power will always blaze forth.
Adorned with a hundred blessings and the thirty-two marks, all resulting from having made offerings to the sick;
they shall all go forth into homelessness within my Dharma, and in the future age of the final dharma,
if they can uphold my treasury of the True Dharma, they shall behold billions of Buddhas.
Those who receive, uphold, and revere my Dharma thereby sustain the seed of Bodhi;
being able to extensively benefit all sentient beings, they shall behold the Buddha Akṣobhya.
Hearing that I practice the supreme conduct for enlightenment, they immediately attain that which is beloved by the noble ones;
all the adornments of my past lives and the supreme offerings presented to all Tathāgatas.
A bhikṣu who is learned and upholds the precepts—having seen him, serve him with a pure mind;
furthermore, one should be able to distance oneself from all anger and pride, for this is always the cause of the most supreme and great merit.
Having swiftly abandoned all anger and pride, make offerings to my son, the protector of the Dharma.
For immeasurable billions of kalpas they will remain free from darkness, never falling into the suffering of the evil realms.
A contentious mind inevitably leads to rebirth in the miserable destinies;
even if one observes the precepts, possesses great learning, makes offerings to the Buddhas, practices extensive generosity, or dwells in forest meditation, none of these can save them.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!
"I have a few questions to ask the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; I pray that the Buddha will grant me leave to ask, and that he will explain them for me as I inquire.
At that time, the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Return to your seat. The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha grants you leave to ask whatever you wish; I shall explain it for you so that your heart may find joy."
At that time, the Elder Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Indeed, we shall receive your instruction, Sugata!”
"So be it; we shall receive the teaching, Blessed One!
Having received permission, Ānanda then cleared his throat and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!

By what causes and conditions do other individual bodhisattvas, while practicing the bodhisattva path, encounter the severing of their hands, feet, ears, and noses, or the gouging out of both eyes and the cutting away of their limbs, yet endure all such various sufferings and do not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Having asked this question, the Buddha said: “Ānanda!

If you were to know that I have undergone all these sufferings for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, you would not even be able to bring yourself to speak of it, let alone be able to pose such a question.”
"Ānanda!
Suppose there were a person whose body, from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, was ablaze with a fierce fire. Then another person were to go to that place and say:
'Good man, come here; while this body is burning and unextinguished, unite it with the five desires and enjoy songs, dances, and amusements as you wish.'"
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda, what do you think?”
"Would this person, without extinguishing the blazing fire of his body, be able to enjoy at will the pleasures of the five desires— song, dance, play, and laughter?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha,
"No, World-Honored One."
"World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!"
This person has not yet extinguished the fire within their body, and thus might still experience the pleasures of the five desires, such as song, dance, and joyful play;

the Tathāgata is not so, for when he formerly practiced the bodhisattva path, upon seeing sentient beings suffering in the three evil realms or those in various states of poverty and misery, he never experienced any joy or pleasure.

“Ānanda! When bodhisattvas of the past were practicing the bodhisattva path, they accomplished the precept that is unbroken, the precept that is unperforated, the precept that is unblemished, the precept that is unmixed, the precept that is unattached, the precept that is immovable, the precept that is unturbid, the precept that is indestructible, the precept that is not shallow, the precept that does not manifest signs, the precept that is non-contradictory, the upright precept, the precept according to one’s vow, and the precept that gathers in sentient beings.”

Ānanda! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who thus accomplishes these precepts and practices the bodhisattva path will never encounter the cutting off of hands, the amputation of feet, the slicing of ears, the excision of the nose, the decapitation, or the gouging out of eyes; nor shall they suffer various other pains regarding their bodily parts, and they will swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

“Ānanda! In the distant past, incalculable upon incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago—vast, immeasurable, inconceivable, incomparable, unfathomable, and without limit—there was a Buddha named Ratnapadmacandraviśuddhodbhavaraāja, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.”

Ānanda! At that time, the lifespan of the Buddha Ratnapadmacandraviśuddhyabhyudgatarāja was ninety-nine billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of kalpas; throughout all the days, months, and seasons, he established nine billion hundred thousand sentient beings in the Buddha-dharma so that they would not regress.

“Ānanda! After that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnapadmacandraviśuddhodbhavarāja has entered parinirvāṇa, and after the True Dharma has vanished during the period of the Semblance Dharma, there will be immeasurable sentient beings who loathe this sūtra, immeasurable sentient beings who distance themselves from it, immeasurable sentient beings who oppose it, and immeasurable sentient beings who abandon it.”

During times of great terror, times of great calamity, times of drought, times of excessive rain, times of unseasonable rain, times of famine, times of false views, times when seeking the speech of external paths, times of fierce beasts and yakṣas, times of thunder, lightning, and thunderbolts, and times when the Bodhi of the Buddha was being destroyed—seven thousand bodhisattvas departed from the cities, royal capitals, and villages among the populace and went to dwell within the Forest of Samantabhadra, staying there together with the Dharma Master Sumanacandra.
At that time, that bhikṣu expounded the Dharma-gate of dhāraṇīs for that assembly: "Ānanda!

Once, while the Dharma Master Puṣpacandra was sitting alone in a quiet place, he saw with his divine eye—purified and surpassing that of humans—many billions of bodhisattvas who had planted various roots of goodness, passing away from other Buddha-worlds and being reborn here."
"If they should hear this dharani dharma-gate, they will immediately attain non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
if they do not hear this dharani dharma-gate, they will then fall away and lose anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Thereupon, after forming this thought, the Dharma Master Sumanacandra arose from samādhi and went to where that assembly of great bodhisattvas was.
Having arrived at that assembly, he spoke these words:
"Sons of good family!
"I now wish to go to cities, towns, and villages to expound the essential Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
At that time, the assembly of great bodhisattvas said to the Dharma Master Sumanacandra:
"We, the entire assembly of bodhisattvas, do not delight in your leaving this forest to head toward those royal cities, towns, and villages."
Why is this? Because there will be immeasurable bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who, during the period of the Semblance Dharma, take pleasure in taking human life out of their great pride.
At that time, the Dharma Master Supuṣpacandra addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"If I were to cherish and protect my own body and life, I would be unable to protect the teachings of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present."
At that time, the Dharma Master spoke these verses:
"By never dwelling in the notion of a self, One is able to protect and uphold the Tathāgata’s Dharma—
The vast and supreme Bodhi of all Buddhas— And manifest it within this evil age."
If one is free from all grasping at the notion of a self, And likewise free from the notions of a sentient being and a life-span,
One who can swiftly detach from forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles Protects the Buddha-dharma.
If one were to make offerings to ten billion nayutas of Buddhas, providing pure-hearted gifts of fine delicacies,
as well as lamps, garlands, banners, and canopies, for as many as hundreds of millions of kalpas as there are sands in the Ganges;
yet if, during the final age when the True Dharma declines and such Buddha-dharma is about to perish—
One who can protect the Dharma for even a single day and night possesses merit far superior to that [of the former].

I am the Holy Lion among Men; if one fails to provide protection when the True Dharma is about to perish, they cannot be said to have made an offering to the Buddha, nor can they be called one who respects the Teacher.
May you all abide in peace and happiness for your own benefit; may you skillfully protect yourselves.
Do not be negligent regarding the true Dharma and Vinaya, but should always dwell securely in the practice of loving-kindness.
Upholding the true precepts without admixture, pure, radiant, and free from defilement,
one thereby makes offerings to all Buddhas— past and present Tathāgatas alike.
Bestowing the supreme jewel of the Dharma, constantly practicing patience, Cultivating meditative concentration in secluded places to achieve sublime gentleness,
Free from all strife, performing wondrous causes, He travels to cities and towns to rescue sentient beings.
As the Great Wise and Supreme Sage was about to descend, some wept with grief while others prostrated themselves, saying:
"Please behold these forest trees, so lovely with their fragrance; O Wise One, do not depart, but save us!"
In the past, the Teacher, endowed with the ten powers, With senses stilled and well-disciplined in gentleness,
Went to that secluded place within the mountain forest To pursue unsurpassed, supreme enlightenment; Furthermore,
he skillfully practiced the causes of enlightenment, Cultivating and accumulating both merit and wisdom.
Dwelling in the forest, you follow and train in accordance with them; O Great Sage of majestic power, pray do not descend.
The marks and signs of your body are exceptionally subtle and wondrous; your hair is deep blue-black and most lovely.
Your skin is radiant and beautiful like gold, its brilliant splendor illuminating the great earth.
The tuft of hair between his brows is most lovely, Resembling the brilliant white luster of a conch shell;
Do not let others give rise to envy or jealousy, Lest the lord of the land or a great minister take his life.
"Ānanda! At that time, the Dharma Master Supuṣpacandra addressed those bodhisattvas in verse, saying:
'All the Tathāgatas of the past, Those who have attained all-knowledge and exhausted all outflows, ...'"
May all beings bring benefit to the three realms of existence and realize the unsurpassed, supreme enlightenment.
Seeking that enlightenment, they cultivate sublime causes, accumulating merit and wisdom;
practicing and training therein, they constantly engage in cultivation for the sake of rescuing and liberating sentient beings.
All circumambulated the wise seer to the right; they bowed their heads to his feet in reverence.
Yearning and gazing up at him, they all sighed and lamented; they wailed aloud with piercing cries of grief.
Some fell down from high places, fainting like great trees toppled over.
He does not turn back because of their words; for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, the Sage of Merit takes up his robe and bowl and desires to depart.
Like a valiant and fierce lion king, he pays no heed to gain or loss, for he dwells securely in the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
"May I not remain in the mountain forests, causing the various roots of goodness in sentient beings to diminish.
Thus he proceeded to the excellent cities and towns, desiring to benefit sentient beings.
“Ānanda! At that time, the Dharma Master Supuṣpacandra immediately traveled through cities and villages to teach the Dharma as was appropriate for all sentient beings.

During the early morning, this bhikṣu caused nine hundred million sentient beings to abide in non-retrogression regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Thereafter, he traveled by stages until he reached the city of Ratnarāja, where he sat beneath a *pippala* tree.”

At that time, that bhikṣu sat through the night until dawn; he entered the city and caused three billion six hundred million sentient beings to attain the stage of non-retrogression within the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, a bhikṣu did not eat for one day;
having finished his fast, he departed from the royal city and went to the site of the Buddha’s nail-relic stūpa, where he stood upright in reverent devotion for one day and one night.

Then, at dawn on the second day, that bhikṣu, still having not yet eaten, returned once more to the city of Ratnarāja and caused two billion three hundred million sentient beings to dwell securely in the Buddha-dharma and attain non-retrogression.

Having fasted on the second day as well, he again departed from the royal city and went to the site of the Buddha’s nail-relic stūpa, where he stood upright day and night until the end of the night and the arrival of dawn.
On the third day, still not having eaten as before, he returned to the royal city and established nine hundred million beings within the Buddha-dharma, causing them to abide in non-retrogression.

Having fasted for three days, he again departed from the royal city and went to the site of the Buddha’s nail-relic stupa, where he stood upright day and night until the end of the night and the arrival of dawn.
On the fourth day, still having not eaten, he returned once more to that Royal City of Jewels, establishing nine million sentient beings in the Buddha-dharma so that they would never regress.
On the fourth day, having fasted and departed the city, he went to the site of the Buddha’s nail-relic stupa and stood there day and night until the end of the night and the arrival of dawn.

On the fifth day, still without having eaten, he returned to the royal capital and established all those within the great king’s palace, as well as the people of the cities and villages, within the Buddha-dharma so that they would not regress.
Having fasted for five days, he again departed from the royal city and stood day and night before the stūpa of the Buddha’s fingernails until the night had ended and dawn arrived.
On the sixth day, still not having eaten, he caused the king’s thousand sons to abide in non-retrogression toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Having fasted for six days, he returned once more to that city of King of Jewels, went to the site of the Buddha’s nail-relic stūpa, and stood there in reverent attendance throughout that day and night until the end of the night and the arrival of dawn.
When the seventh day arrived, he still had not eaten and went to the gate of the royal city.
At that time, there was a king named Śūrabala (Valiant Power).

The king emerged from the inner palace and ascended a golden chariot, which had railings of white silver and an axle made of exquisite sandalwood; its wheels were of *vaiḍūrya* (lapis lazuli), and it was adorned with spread canopies and precious banners. Precious trees were arranged in rows, and various silk nets covered the top of the chariot, with layers of fine silks hanging down. Eight hundred young maidens held precious ropes to pull the jeweled chariot; these women were beautiful and possessed every exquisite feature.
The fool delights in this, not the wise man.

There were eighty-four thousand noble Kṣatriya clansmen standing as his guard behind him; furthermore, there were eighty-four thousand noble Brāhmaṇa clansmen and eighty-four thousand noble Gṛhapati clansmen, all serving as his retinue. There were also five hundred celestial maidens ascending a palanquin adorned with various jewels, proceeding before the king.
"At that same time, she saw this bhikṣu attain non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
six million eight hundred thousand palace attendants all saw this bhikṣu and likewise attained non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

At that time, the multitude all removed their necklaces and jeweled sandals, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and with palms joined, paid homage with reverence to the bhikṣu while standing before him.

At that time, the woman—sustained by the seeds of roots of goodness planted in her past lives—immediately descended from her precious carriage, bared her right shoulder, adjusted her robes, knelt with her right knee on the ground, and having joined her palms in reverent salutation to the bhikṣu, spoke these verses:
“Today his majestic radiance shines everywhere throughout this city of the King of Jewels;
because this bhikṣu has entered the city, all the people stand gazing up at him.”
Having severed all faults of craving and desire, And being likewise free from anger,
delusion, jealousy, false imaginings, and all fetters of bondage, He is able to extinguish them all completely.
At that time, King Śūradatta was out on a journey, unobserved by anyone;
neither his sons nor any of his other kinsmen followed him as his retinue.
The bhikṣu stands amidst that great assembly of kings, Exquisite and peerless in his majesty,
Like the full moon on the fifteenth day, Surrounded by all the stars.
His body is like an image of refined gold, further adorned by the craftsmanship of an artisan;
like the king of trees with its wondrous flowers in full bloom, so too is the monk’s dignified majesty.
Furthermore, like Śakra of great majesty, the thousand-eyed Lord of Devas, as he ascends and traverses the sky.
Like the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven atop Mount Sumeru, so too is the bhikṣu when entering the city;
like the Brahmā King dwelling among the Brahmā host, or like the Lord of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven,
or as the Suyāma Heaven of the desire realm is most majestic, so is the bhikṣu when entering the city— wondrous indeed.
Just as the sun shines resplendently in the void, its thousandfold rays of flame dispelling the darkness and illuminating all the ten directions,
so too is the wondrous entry of the bhikṣu into the city.
Having practiced giving extensively throughout immeasurable eons, Always guarding the precepts without defilement or confusion,
Cultivating patience beyond compare in this world, Your body is thus adorned with sublime marks;
Able to arouse the diligence praised by the sages, With a courageous and superior mind you cultivate the four dhyānas.
Having arisen with wisdom, he cuts through the web of afflictions; therefore, the bhikṣu illuminates the world.
The Buddha, the peerless hero, supreme among men, has already showered the rain of the sublime Dharma in the past;
so too shall it be in the future and the present. Such a one is a true son of that Dharma King.
"May this bhikṣu remain forever unchanging; may his radiant color illuminate all worlds.
Upon seeing your majestic virtue and hearing your voice, the king’s own majesty is so utterly eclipsed that it is no longer seen."
"You have personally realized the Dharma within your own body; having received and practiced the Buddha's teachings, you wander through the world.
We vow to cast off this female body and likewise attain the state of such a bhikṣu."
All of them joined their palms together and spoke these verses, scattering their ornaments from their bodies:
exquisite golden garlands, pearl necklaces, earrings, and golden neck-chains.
"His power is like that of a Wheel-Turning King surveying the great earth; as he travels through the four continents, he regards all beings as his own children.
Toward kings, kṣatriyas, and those of the four castes alike, he maintains an impartial mind, free from both hatred and affection."
The bhikṣu, having mastered the dhāraṇīs, discriminates the faculties, powers, and the path of awakening;
like the full moon amidst the host of stars, he is also like the solar disc radiating brilliant light.
I take refuge in the One of Ten Powers, the Tamer;
though one were to praise him for a hundred eons, or speak for immeasurable billions of many eons, one could not exhaust the virtue of even a single hair on his body.
To the one who turns the wheel of Dharma with wisdom, whose subtle and stainless teachings are difficult to perceive—
to the Physician-King, the Peerless Son, who is honored by śramaṇas, Māras, Brahmās, and brahmins, I pay homage.
When the women had finished speaking these verses, they were all filled with joy; they scattered pearls and gold upon the ground and spread exquisite robes.
They offered their crest-jewels and necklaces, worth ten billion, to that bhikṣu for the sake of awakening.
At that time, King Vikramaśakti had this thought:
"The hearts of these palace women have all become altered; they are in rebellion against me.
How do I know this?"
He completely removed his armlets and pearl necklaces, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and joined his palms in salutation to this bhikṣu.

At that time, King Śūrabala, seeing that the countenance of Sumanacandra was upright and handsome, looked at his own appearance and realized it did not compare to that of the bhikṣu; he was immediately struck with alarm and fear, dreading the loss of his royal throne, and became exceedingly enraged.
At that time, as the bhikṣu stood upon the royal road, dust blew into his eyes, causing him to blink and move his eyelids.
King Śūrasena then thought to himself:
"This bhikṣu has a defiled mind and is fixated on my palace women; he is blinking his eyes to signal a rendezvous."
"Who is there capable of killing this bhikṣu?
At that time, King Vikramaśakti was followed by his thousand sons as attendants, and he then commanded his sons, saying:
"You must now take the life of this bhikṣu."
The king’s thousand sons refused the royal command for the sake of the bhikṣu.
The king thought to himself:
“If even my sons do not obey my commands, I am now alone and without companions; who else could possibly kill this bhikṣu?”
At that time, King Śūrabala had a caṇḍāla named Nandin, whom he constantly employed for executions; he was cruel, violent, and devoid of any sense of pity.
When the king saw Nandin, he leaped for joy and said:
"He will surely be able to kill this bhikṣu for me."
Immediately, he issued an order to summon him.
At that time, Nandika went to the king's presence,
and the king said to him:
"Can you now kill this bhikṣu?
If you can kill him, I shall grant you a generous reward.
"Indeed, Great King! [he replied.]
"I shall obey your command.
Following whatever Your Majesty dispatches me to do, I am able to kill him; this very day, I shall take his life.
The King then addressed Nandi:

"You should know that now is precisely the right time; you ought to take a sharp blade and sever that bhikṣu’s hands, feet, ears, and nose, for he looked upon my palace attendants with a defiled mind. You must use iron hooks to gouge out his eyes."
At that time, Nandi immediately received the king’s command; grasping a sharp blade in his hand, he cut off the bhikṣu’s hands, feet, ears, and nose, and gouged out both his eyes.
"After the king had killed the bhikṣu, he immediately went to the park;
at that time, the multitude wailed with grief and distress and returned once more to the precious royal city.
Then, for seven days, King Yuǎngjiàn remained in the garden without any joy in his heart, finding no pleasure in play nor any delight in amusement."

After seven days had passed, he departed from the garden and returned to the city; on the royal highway, he saw this bhikṣu who had been dead for seven days and discarded on the road, yet his physical appearance had not changed during those seven days.
At that time, King Śūra made this reflection:
"The bhikṣu has been dead for seven days, yet his physical appearance remains unchanged; he will certainly attain non-retrogression in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, of this there is no doubt.
As for me, having committed evil karma, I shall surely fall into hell and suffer before long."
While he was reflecting thus, eighty-four thousand devas in the air simultaneously raised their voices with one accord:
"It is so, Great King!
Just as you have reflected and just as you have spoken, this bhikṣu is truly non-retrogressive from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Upon hearing these words, King Śūradatta was struck with alarm and trepidation; his hair stood on end and a sense of regret arose within him.
At that time, having become sorrowful, distressed, and filled with remorse, the king spoke these verses:
“I have renounced my royal throne and my city, Gold, silver, pearls, and mani-jewels.”
"I, a fool of ignorance and evil karma, shall take up a sharp blade and slay myself.
Formerly, the Dharma Master Supuṣpacandra was adorned with the thirty-two marks;
entering the royal city, his light shone everywhere, like the full moon, the king among stars."
Deluded and distracted by sensual desires, surrounded by my court ladies, I went out from the city;
mounted upon a precious chariot followed by kṣatriyas, I arrived here with my beautiful, lovely eyes.
When the women saw the bhikṣu, they were all filled with joy; with hearts full of delight, they scattered golden garlands.
All the women joined their palms together and spoke verses in song to praise that bhikṣu.
At that time, while I was out enjoying a pleasure excursion, surrounded by Kṣatriyas and riding in a precious chariot,
I encountered a person of upright form and wondrous eyes— a son of the Tathāgata possessed of great majestic power.
At that time, I saw him give rise to evil thoughts;
out of jealousy and anger, he conceived a harmful intent because he saw a bhikṣu entering the royal city, and the many women gazed upon him with joy.
The radiance shines universally throughout the four quarters, like the moon emerging from the mouth of Rāhu;
all the people raise a great cry of acclaim, and the ladies-in-waiting behold it with universal joy.
In the past, I spoke harsh and evil words, commanding all my thousand sons:
"Quickly kill this bhikṣu and cut him into pieces; he is my greatest enemy."
All the youths observed the precepts and felt compassion and affection for this Dharma-master;
they all refused to obey my commands, and at that time, my heart was filled with extreme grief and distress.
Seeing this bhikṣu upholding the pure precepts, his wisdom corresponding to that of a compassionate father,
I then, with a mind of anger, dispatched someone to kill him, without considering Avīci hell or my subsequent remorse.
At that time, seeing Nandika standing on the royal road, causing harm and inflicting suffering upon others,
I gave this evil command to those men:
"Cut down this bhikṣu like a garland of flowers."
The Samantabhadra Grove is exceedingly sublime and wondrous; Myriad immortals gather there in fragrant abundance.
Yet now that the Great Assembly has lost its Dharma Master, They are like an only child who has lost its mother.
"O Bhikṣu, you should rise and go to the Śiṃśapā Grove to bring extensive benefit to the multitude of people;
now that you have entered this royal city, that assembly will soon arrive and weep with great sorrow."
Exquisite flowers and banners are arrayed on the right; the left wing is likewise majestic and beautiful.
With various fine garments spread upon the road, O Bhikṣu, arise quickly and preach the sublime Dharma!
It has been a long time since you entered the royal city; those crowds will surely be filled with great sorrow.
Before that Buddha-dharma has come to an end, they shall not allow your life-force to be severed.
Suppose there were a person of great majestic power, Whose widespread fame pervades all directions,
Who possesses the strength to turn the great earth, And who completely outshines the three-thousandfold world system;
One who is liberated from the arrows of suffering and free from affliction, Having attained the Dharma associated with noble joy.
If even seeing or hearing of him gives rise to such distress, how much more so for those in the world who are not deluded?
Dharma Master Huayue was like the King of Mountains, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man;
yet he was suddenly torn apart into different fragments, like a garland of flowers vied for by a multitude of women.
I have committed an exceedingly grave unwholesome karma; I shall fall into that Avīci hell where no rescue is possible.
I am utterly estranged from all Buddhas because I have mutilated a bhikṣu.
Neither my sons nor my kinsmen can save me;
neither the ministers, the nobles, nor the servants—since I have committed grave and evil karma, none of these people can provide salvation.
All Buddhas of the past and future, And those currently present throughout the ten directions—
Leaders endowed with the ten powers, free from afflictions, Whose minds are like adamant— I take refuge in you.
Seeing that bhikṣu divided from his kin, all the devas wept and cried out in lamentation;
they went to inform the assembly of bodhisattvas:
"The bhikṣu Puṣpacandra has been killed by the king."
The Dharma Master of keen intelligence and wisdom, Possessing great majesty and virtue with a name renowned afar,
A Bodhisattva dwelling securely in dhāraṇī, Is now being slain within the royal city;
Having practiced giving extensively for immeasurable kalpas, He guarded the precepts immovably, free from defilement or impurity.
One who was able to practice incomparable patience, yet is now being killed in the royal city;
one who for immeasurable kalpas has always been diligent, cultivating the four dhyānas with a superior and exalted mind,
and giving rise to wisdom capable of severing afflictions, yet is now being killed in the royal city.
Having renounced all attachment to the body and disregarded even his own life, he emerged from that Forest of Samantabhadra;
now, in the royal city, he is being put to death.
The great assembly from that forest entered the royal city, wailing aloud with piteous cries and weeping;
seeing the body of this bhikṣu cut into several pieces, they all fainted and fell prostrate upon the ground.
Then those bhikṣus addressed the king, saying:
"O Great King!
What fault does this Dharma Master have?
He maintains the precepts without flaw and possesses great renown; he is able to know the boundless events of past lives."
Having attained ultimate mastery in those dhāraṇīs, they skillfully understand that the world is entirely empty and quiescent;
for the sake of all sentient beings, they manifest the signless and relinquish all conceptualizations of vows.
He proclaims a subtle and lovely voice; his faculties are tranquil and well-tamed.
Having thoroughly understood the events of past lives, he transcends all worlds.
One shall attain the Buddha’s spontaneous wisdom, which is most rare in this world;
with pure eyes seeing clearly without the obscuration of darkness—this is what is called the illumination of a compassionate heart.
Craving and lustful desire are most base and defiling; they give rise to suffering and distress, causing one to lose the celestial realms.
Those who indulge in desire abandon extensive learning and are called those whose wisdom has diminished.
Being blinded by attachment to sensual craving, they are then able to bring harm upon their own parents.
It can likewise harm those who uphold the precepts; therefore, one should abandon desire.

Great King, if you indulge in sensual craving, you will lose your majestic power and supreme sovereignty, and proceed toward the most wretched hells, being born in places of extreme suffering and great terror.
Having committed such a grave evil deed as the murder of a wise and eminent Dharma Master,
those who aspire to seek Bodhi should distance themselves from such wickedness.
Supreme and wondrous forms, sounds, scents, tastes, and textures— With a courageous mind, they are able to renounce them all;
Body and mind are both empty, like an illusion, And so it is with the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue.
Having cultivated giving and ethical discipline beyond compare, and likewise patience and diligence,
you have reached the further shore of meditative concentration and wisdom, and are thus able to benefit all sentient beings.
All the devas and humans in the world who are able to contemplate the Tathāgata with a mind of loving-kindness,
their eyes can dispel the great darkness and awaken to the most supreme and sublime Bodhi.
With joyful faith, he renounced his palatial towers, elephants, horses, chariots, and couches;
all types of litters, cattle, sheep, and the like; his entire realm, cities, and various villages;
he abandoned his royal throne, along with gold, silver, pearls, crystal, and coral.
He was able to give away his head, eyes, wife, and children, seeking for the sake of unsurpassed bodhi.
With incomparable joy he made offerings: exquisite flowers, unguents, and powdered incense;
various banners, supreme victory standards, and canopies; and the beautiful sounds of singing and manifold musical instruments.
Having abandoned all aspirations for existence within the various realms of being, and having realized that the three worlds are entirely empty,
you are thus adorned with the marks of the Ten Powers, your radiance shining universally throughout the ten directions.
Without attachment to the realms of form or desire, and likewise regarding the formless realm as well—
those who abide in the bodhisattva’s dhāraṇī cast off the three realms like a snake sheds its skin;
they have no notion of a self or a sentient being, nor do they have notions of male or female.
He cultivates the holy life without defilement or impurity, for the Bodhisattva dwells securely in dhāraṇī;
Perceptions of existence and non-existence are entirely absent, and the same is true for perceptions of peace and unrest;
There are neither perceptions of non-number nor perceptions of number, because he dwells in the Bodhisattva’s dhāraṇī.
Neither existence nor the perception of existence exists at all;
there is no perception of a life-principle, no perception of a sentient being, no perception of a village, and no perception of a city, because the Bodhisattva dwells securely in dhāraṇī;
there is neither the perception of non-attachment nor the perception of attachment, neither the perception of non-hatred nor the perception of hatred.
Neither the notion of non-delusion nor the notion of delusion, for they abide in the bodhisattva’s dhāraṇī;
Regarding the faculties, the powers, the meditative concentrations, and the factors of enlightenment, they are entirely unattached,
And are able to relinquish the three realms of existence, because the bodhisattva dwells securely in the dhāraṇī.
Untainted by greed or hatred, and free from delusion, confusion, or a crooked mind,
one who beholds the Buddha’s ten powers and makes offerings does not, as a wise person, long for rebirth in the heavenly realms.
Having heard the profound and wondrous Dharma from another, one gives rise to no doubts whatsoever;
just as a vessel filled with pure oil, so too is the principle of the exhausted and the inexhaustible.
Precisely because of greedy attachment, craving arises; this is what is called the great affliction.
Furthermore, because of hatred and resentment, aversion is stirred up; this is what is called the terror of evil enmity.
The wise person distances themselves from these two extremes; this is said to be the ability to proceed toward supreme bodhi.
Having become a bull-king among men endowed with the ten powers, he transcends all worlds.
Having completely relinquished all internal and external matters, he dwells securely within the reality-limit of the dharma-nature.
He upholds the prohibitive precepts with perfect purity—without breach, without flaw, and without defilement.
He is without interruption or admixture in pure precepts, nor does he rely on the rituals of *karma*;
the wise person abandons these two extremes and is able to awaken to the unsurpassed Great Bodhi.
*The Scripture on the Moon-Lamp Samādhi*, Scroll Eight;
*The Scripture on the Moon-Lamp Samādhi*, Scroll Nine.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Northern Qi Dynasty.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"When I was practicing the path in the past, I was a king named Bravery-Acquired.
At that time there was a city named Jewel-Treasure; That king left the city and went to a grove."
Riding in a precious chariot, he encountered a bhikṣu, Elegant, extraordinary, and most exquisite,
adorned with the thirty-two marks, Whose radiance shone universally throughout the ten directions.
The one named Good Flower Moon is renowned throughout all realms; dwelling securely in compassion, he is able to benefit others.
For the sake of saving sentient beings, he enters the city, his majestic power and merit being most sublime and dignified.
At that time, my appearance was not as good as his; consequently, I gave rise to a mind of intense envy and jealousy.
Bound and fettered by the ravages of lustful desire, I feared that the bhikṣu would usurp the royal throne.
In the past, he possessed a retinue of a thousand sons who followed behind him in precious chariots;
adorned with various jeweled crowns, they moved like the sons of the gods in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
Among those sons, five hundred sons all wore exquisite mani-jewel sandals;
they adorned themselves with jeweled crowns and necklaces, while golden nets completely covered their chariots.
The court ladies and retinue numbered eighty thousand; all were exquisite and magnificently adorned.
Ascending their precious carriages, they beheld the bhikṣu, whose upright majesty was like Mount Sumeru.
Seeing him, they all regarded him as their father; each gave rise to the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta).
From him, they received the pure Brahma-conduct and, having removed their exquisite necklaces, scattered them over the bhikṣu.
I immediately gave rise to supreme jealousy, and instantly produced a mind of anger and defilement;
deluded by my wealth and power, I commanded my son, saying:
"Kill the bhikṣu standing before me."
Having heard their father’s command, the sons were deeply filled with grief and distress, and said to him:
"We pray that Your Majesty will not speak such words; we can never bring ourselves to kill this man."
Even if one were to cut my body into pieces for as many billions of kalpas as there are sands in the Ganges,
one could never kill this Dharma-preacher, because it was from him that the mind of enlightenment was first conceived.
Having brought forth this mind before that Honored One, we pray: "May I attain Buddhahood, the supreme among men;
may those who proceed toward Bodhi commit no evil; may we all be sons of the Buddha."
When the king heard these words from his sons, he immediately commanded his servant, saying:
"Quickly summon the executioner to kill the bhikṣu who stands before my palace attendants."
Soon the executioner was brought forth, named Nandika, most cruel and fierce;
holding a sharp blade in his hand, he hacked this bhikṣu into eight pieces.
Though the bhikṣu was beheaded, his body was without blood;
from the site of the incision flowed a thousand kinds of light, and there also appeared the auspicious wheel of merit, shining brightly within the flesh.
Having committed such exceedingly grave and evil karma, I then went to the gardens for amusement;
yet I found no joy in any song or dance, for I was thinking only of the Dharma Master Huayue.
At that time, he quickly departed from that garden and returned to enter the city of Jewels;
thereupon, mounting his carriage, he went to the place where the bhikṣu had been dismembered.
Immediately, a terrible sound was heard in the air, as immeasurable nayutas of devas wailed and cried out:
"This evil king has committed grave karma; upon death, he shall fall into Avīci and undergo extreme suffering."
When the king heard those voices of the devas, his heart was filled with grief and he was seized by great terror:
"I have committed immeasurable and grave transgressions because of my killing of the bhikṣu Supuṣpa."
The Tathāgata is endowed with immeasurable wisdom; he is that most excellent true son of the Buddha, whose faculties are tamed and whose mind is stilled.
Yet for the sake of sensual desire, I killed him.
If there be one who can uphold the Dharma of the Tathāgata when the treasury of the True Dharma is being destroyed, [I shall protect them].
One who is able to kindle the lamp of wisdom in the world— I killed that person for the sake of desire;
one who acts as a great physician for all the worlds,
healing the afflictions of sentient beings and causing the nectar of immortality to flow down once more— I killed him for the sake of craving and lust.
He upholds the supreme Dharma-treasury of the Teacher, serving as a lamp for sentient beings in the darkness;
he who holds the Dharma-king of dhāraṇīs—him I killed out of desire.
He expounds for the world the supreme and wondrous Dharma, which is profoundly deep, subtle, and difficult to perceive.
He clearly taught the path leading to the site of enlightenment; yet out of craving, I killed that man.
His wisdom was pure and free from defilement; he was serene, tranquil, and ever-abiding in meditative concentration.
Blinded by craving, I nevertheless killed him; one must abandon desire, for it is the cause of suffering.
All Buddhas of the past and future, And those currently present, the Honored Ones among men,
Whose merit is as immeasurable as the great ocean— I join my palms and take refuge in them all.
This one shall die and go to the evil Avīci hell; there, no savior can be found.
Since the karma for an undesirable fruit was created by oneself, it is precisely due to having slain a supreme Dharma-master.
Alas! With an evil mind one creates the karma of suffering. Alas!
The throne is born of pride;
here there is ultimately no solidity. One must abandon everything and depart alone.
Having been free from desire and passion from the start, one cultivates pure deeds; with compassion and kind speech, such is a true son of the Buddha.
Alone you are the Kinsman of the World, free from all faults; where has my virtuous Puṣpacandra gone?
Alas! O Noble One, endowed with the wealth of patience!
Alas! You who possess a wondrous form and are endowed with virtue;
you who are a mass of merit free from flattery and frivolous discourse—where are you going now, leaving me behind?
Only now do I understand the words of the Great Sage: that the world is ruined by desire, which is the cause of physical and mental torment and the path to evil realms;
having realized this, I have abandoned the pursuit of desire.
This one has died and gone to the evil hells, where no one can provide rescue;
having committed such extremely grave evil karma, it was precisely because of harming that bhikṣu.
Having renounced fear, fatigue, and the station of kingship, you upheld the prohibitions and cultivated the holy life;
for you, who are now a sovereign master, I now joyfully and with a pure mind construct this great stūpa,
as an offering to the one free from affliction and endowed with wisdom, the treasury of wisdom, the one possessed of shame and modesty.
"Do not let me fall into the three evil realms, nor suffer ill repute or slander.
My queen, palace ladies, and all my kinsmen; my most eminent ministers and servants;
the kṣatriyas, elders, and all the officials—O King, weeping at that time, he spoke to them:"
"Quickly prepare for me all kinds of excellent and wondrous fragrant woods, renowned garments,
superior robes, and clarified butter, so that they may be used to cremate this bhikṣu’s body."
Now, quickly gather here all kinds of supreme and wondrous fragrant fuel—
timely sandalwood and liquid aloeswood, *sūrpaka* and camphor—
and wrap the body of that Venerable One entirely with hundreds of thousands of garments smeared with ghee and oil.
With a mind of supreme faith and reverence, I made offerings with various ritual implements.
Having heard the command of that Great King, the Chief Minister and the citizens of the city used various fragrant oils,
incense wood, and diverse, exquisite powders of many kinds of incense.
They wash him with various powdered perfumes, then smear his body with a variety of fragrant unguents;
wrapping his body in garments soaked in ghee and oil, they place him upon this pyre of fragrant wood.
In ancient times, the sublime body of the Honored Muni left behind three *shu* and six *dou* of relics;
that king constructed a most excellent stūpa for them, making various offerings and constantly prostrating.
With ointments, powdered incense, perfumes, garlands, and a hundred kinds of hymns, and with hanging exquisite bells, banners, and canopies,
the queen, the concubines, the palace ladies, along with their sons and grandsons, departed from this city and proceeded toward that place.
The King made offerings three times each day, and only then did he return from the site of the stūpa;
with exquisite flower garlands he made his offerings, adorning it with precious banners, pennants, and canopies.
Precisely because of delusion, they committed many sins;
at that stupa, they repented them all, continuing this repentance for ninety-five billion years without ever growing weary.

Embraced by wisdom, they attain supreme purity; Firmly upholding the precepts without flaw or omission, They constantly observe the eightfold fast day, both night and day, Purely guarding them without ever transgressing.
Enshrouded and obscured by craving and desire, the king himself committed unwholesome deeds;
when his body perished and his life ended, he fell into hell, dwelling within the extreme suffering of Avīci.
From ancient times until now, they have not encountered ninety-five billion Tathāgatas;
throughout those ninety-five billion kalpas, they were constantly born blind.
For sixty-two billion nayuta kalpas, although they obtained the faculty of sight, it was lost once again.
Furthermore, throughout one hundred million nayutas of births, even if they were to regain their sight, it would be lost again;
