likewise, they would constantly have their hands, feet, ears, noses, lips, and tongues severed.
This would occur for hundreds of millions of nayuta kalpas among human beings, and the same would be true for all other places of rebirth.
That king committed immeasurable evils and constantly suffered throughout all the worlds;
if there are those who wish to attain peace and happiness, they should reflect on this and refrain from committing even the slightest unwholesome deed.
Although that king repented for his past transgressions, he could not escape the consequences of what he had done;
having created such evil karma as this, after death he shall fall into the Avīci Hell,
where his body, head, and four limbs will be severed, and his ears cut off and his nose slit away.
His two eyes were plucked out beyond counting, for the sake of desire throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas.
Having fully exhausted the evil karma he extensively created, he later gouged out his own body to give to others—
namely, by severing his head, as well as his hands and feet— and renounced his kingdom and his son for the sake of Bodhi.
Beloved wives, vast wealth, palace attendants, maidservants, elephants, horses, chariots, boats,
and various exquisite jewels— I have given these as offerings for the sake of the Way throughout immeasurable billions of lifetimes.
I myself am that King Vikrama;
those thousand sons of his were the Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa;
and Padmottara Buddha was Puṣpacandra.
Kuai-kuei was none other than the Buddha King of Stillness;
the palace ladies, queens, and consorts, as well as the city dwellers, kinsmen, friends, and servants,
along with the eminent Kṣatriyas and the lord of the city— all such people as these were my retinue.
If there are those who uphold the prohibitive precepts therein and make offerings with a heart of faith and reverence,
they shall all attain parinirvāṇa, and by virtue of their wholesome intent, realize bodhi.
"O youth!

In the past, throughout immeasurable eons, I beheld the Buddha Vimalaprabhāsa-viraja and cultivated the supreme practices for awakening; even in those former times, I underwent such suffering as this."
If there is a bodhisattva who dwells in dhāraṇī, skillfully cultivating the practice of loving-kindness with unshakable stability,
they shall never fall into any evil realms, but will instead make offerings to the stainless Buddhas free from affliction.
If you wish to become a Buddha, a King of Dharma, adorned with the thirty-two marks,
you should protect the precepts without defilement or agitation, and dwell in dhāraṇī while preaching the Dharma without interruption.
"Therefore, young man,
if a bodhisattva should think:
'How may I now attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment in peace and happiness?'"
"Those bodhisattvas should abide in the accumulation of pure ethical discipline (śīlaskandha) and regard all other bodhisattvas as their teachers.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If there are bodhisattvas who abide in the accumulation of precepts, And practice for enlightenment with a mind intent on benefiting others,"
That person shall swiftly go to the land of Sukhāvatī, where they will attain supreme patience and become a Dharma King.
Thus, with a mind peaceful and unshakable, they constantly perform deeds that are lovely;
thereafter, they shall behold many Buddha-suns and swiftly attain Bodhi, free from the net of doubt.

Having heard this most supreme teaching of mine, and seeing the bhikṣus who maintain pure precepts, one should serve them with a mind free from guile; thereafter, before long, one will attain this samādhi.
If there were as many hidden treasures as the sands of the Ganges, all filled with the seven precious gems,
and those treasuries were thus exceedingly vast, like immeasurable lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
If there were a bodhisattva who delights in giving, constantly and without interruption day and night,
practicing courageous generosity without ceasing for immeasurable kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
yet if another were to hear this samādhi, they would thereby uphold the entire treasury of the Munis.
This constitutes an immeasurable mass of merit, far exceeding the inconceivable merit of the former gift.
Such merit is vast and boundless, capable of extinguishing the sufferings of the world;
it is the most supreme accumulation of virtue, its breadth and measure surpassing that of the merit derived from giving.
The foremost treasury that accords with bodhi, which the wise Bodhisattvas are able to uphold—
if there be one who maintains this samādhi, they are called a supreme Bodhisattva endowed with great wealth.
This constitutes the ocean of extensive learning in the Buddha-dharma; the merit of such a person is difficult to reach its limit.
Regarding this supreme, wondrous, and inconceivable Dharma, one is then said to be a Bodhisattva who truly upholds it.
If there is one who can speak of the samādhi of tranquil extinction, that person’s bodhi will increase;
except for the Teacher of the World, the Tamer of Men, who is fully endowed with great compassion and spontaneous wisdom,
they shall be able to obtain immeasurable merits, and their accomplishment of merit will grow ever more sublime.
Within this trichiliocosm, there is none who can be compared to them;
no other person’s merit is equal to theirs. It is the same for the wisdom praised by the wise.
If anyone hears this samādhi and is able to receive, uphold, read, and recite it, [their merit shall likewise be immeasurable].
Those who seek the supreme enlightenment of all Buddhas are equal to such people as these.
Their birth of vast learning is like the ocean; the merit of those people is immeasurable.
By upholding and reciting this samādhi, such a person gathers such merit.
"O Youth! If merit were material form, no world could contain it.
Therefore, O Youth!"
If a bodhisattva wishes to make offerings to all Buddhas—those pure ones of the past, present, and future—they should receive and uphold this samādhi.
This is the supreme enlightenment of all Buddhas;
O youth, you should believe my words! What the Tathāgata has spoken is without deviation; the speech of us Buddhas is not in vain.
In the past, throughout inconceivable hundreds of eons, for this very purpose I exhausted my body;
I constantly cultivated the most sublime practices of bodhi, seeking such a supreme samādhi as this.
Therefore, you should receive this treasury of Dharma, from which ten billion sūtras emerge;
this mass of merit is vast and inconceivable, for by it one attains the wisdom of all Buddhas.
This is the foremost of all sūtras; it gives birth to immeasurable wholesome deeds.
One who constantly and fearlessly preaches this sūtra will find that the limits of those dharmas cannot be apprehended.
One might be able to know the number of atoms If the three thousandfold world-system were crushed to powder;
But though one constantly preached hundreds of thousands of inconceivable sūtras, No one would be able to measure them.
The inhalations and exhalations of all sentient beings within this buddha-field may still be known;
yet no one can know the limits of the sūtras constantly expounded by the Bodhisattva.
If there were Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and within them all the sentient beings of the six realms of existence,
one might be able to measure the number of their thoughts, but no one could know the sutras they have preached.
Even across immeasurable billions of world-systems, the sands of the great oceans, rivers, and ponds in those realms—
The number of grains of sand in these rivers may be calculated and known, yet none can know the Dharma he has preached;
If a single hair-tip were split into a hundred parts, and with those drops one could count many billions of lands,
Even if all the masses of water that exist were counted, his various sounds and voices could not be known.
Throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas in the past,
The number of atoms in the bodies of all sentient beings may still be calculated, But one cannot know the sūtras they have preached;
The voices of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions May likewise be counted and known.
His preaching continues without interruption, yet one cannot fully comprehend those sūtras.
Having thoroughly mastered words, phrases, and meanings, he is further able to expound all dharmas;
with vast, swift, and sharp wisdom, he understands the true nature of phenomena as well as how to engage in questions and answers.
With wisdom that penetrates the profound and vast meaning, one should always know that the mind is inconceivable;
knowing fully the intrinsic nature of sounds, one’s speech is thus unimpeded.
He is named the Unobstructed Great Dharma Master; for the sake of the world he preaches the Dharma without attachment.
Having thoroughly mastered questioning, answering, and explaining, he has fully realized the ultimate truth.
Within a single phrase, there are billions of commentaries and expositions; In inconceivable discourse, there is no obstruction or attachment.
Having studied the meaning of unimpeded phrases, One expounds them among the assembly without any hindrance.
If one constantly abides in this samādhi, One achieves fearlessness and remains unshakable;
Having attained the power of the Dharma and practiced the supreme conduct, One is able to benefit immeasurable billions of sentient beings.
Just as Mount Sumeru stands firm and unmoving, such that no fierce winds can destroy it;
so too is the Dharma-preacher bhikṣu, whom no treatises whatsoever can unsettle.
Within the lands of the three thousandfold great thousandfold world system, all the mountains and such may be shaken by every wind;
yet the bhikṣu dwelling in space cannot be moved.
If one can remain in constant accord with emptiness, this is the definitive dwelling place of the Buddhas;
if a person definitively knows that all phenomena are empty, no opposing arguments can prevail over them.
Unshakable by any other heterodox teachings, No external treatises can destroy them;
There is none who can assail or disparage them, Because they have taught such tranquil concentration.
Those people have exhausted the nature of emptiness And dwell eternally in immeasurable wisdom.
They will have no doubt regarding any phenomenon, for they uphold this most supreme samādhi;
the various powers and the factors of enlightenment will not be difficult to attain, nor will the bases of psychic power, the unimpeded eloquence,
and the superior supernormal faculties— likewise, by upholding, reciting, and studying this sūtra.
To die here and be born there is not difficult; one who can see the most supreme, immeasurable wisdom—the inconceivable billions of nayutas of Buddhas—shall all behold them by upholding this sutra.
In the presence of all these Buddhas, they hear this stainless samādhi;
they achieve the most supreme wisdom of correspondence and reach the further shore of the four kinds of eloquence.
Throughout all the trichiliocosm worlds, from their lower limits up to the Peak of Existence,
may they be entirely filled with lovely light-mani jewels of the devas and the seven precious gems; likewise,
throughout the infinite Buddha-fields of the ten directions, from the great earth up to the Peak of Existence.
The Jambudvīpa is filled with gold, all of which is offered to the Muni.
All the treasures that exist throughout every world, used for giving through immeasurable kalpas—
offering them to the Tathāgata without ceasing, out of deep faith and for the sake of seeking bodhi;
If there is a bhikṣu who delights in emptiness, and with a single thought joins his palms to pay homage to the Buddha,
compared to the mass of merit from the aforementioned extensive giving, the merit of that gift does not equal even a *kalā* (a minute fraction) of it.
If a person obtains vast and abundant wealth and practices giving with a faithful mind for the sake of merit,
seeking the peerless Bodhi of a Buddha— I have already calculated and weighed such a case in this world.
But if a person, having heard even a four-line verse from within this samādhi, accepts and upholds it;
The merit accumulated by such a person— Even a hundredth part of his prior blessings does not equal it.
Though a most excellent Bodhisattva practices giving, He cannot yet swiftly attain the Unsurpassed Way;
But if one hears of this supreme Jewel Samādhi, They will swiftly attain supreme Bodhi.
Even if one were to obtain a treasury of rare jewels, filling immeasurable lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
with all kinds of precious objects completely full, the Bodhisattva would not consider this sufficient wealth;
yet if one cuts off craving and cultivates merit, and is further able to attain this samādhi, [then one is truly enriched].
One may possess all necessities of life, with storehouses overflowing and filled with great wealth;
even if one were to obtain the four continents, the wise would not find joy therein.
But if one attains such a stainless concentration, one rejoices and leaps for joy, benefiting all sentient beings.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya donned his armor and praised the benefits of this samādhi; furthermore, so that future bodhisattvas might receive, uphold, read, and recite it with joy, he empowered them by speaking these verses:
“Those who can uphold the Dharma of the wise ones, Who possess the majestic power to provide protection, And who can likewise receive and uphold The vast, supreme, and wondrous Eye of the Dharma.”
In this degenerate age of evil, when greed and anger abound,
Who is there capable of receiving and upholding this supreme scripture, Which fulfills the true meaning and abandons heedlessness for constant vigilance?
With the various riches of precepts, concentration, patience, and learning, they are adorned by training well in dignified conduct;
they delight in the tree of Dharma-knowledge and liberation, wear the supreme raiment of shame and modesty,
and, upholding great wisdom, find joy in renunciation— these are the mountain kings of the great earth of the Dharma.
Observing that the world has no guide, they proceed toward the Buddha’s bodhi;
having tamed themselves and attained mental tranquility, these people advance toward omniscience.
Those who tame untamed sentient beings are the most supreme sons of the Omniscient One.
Having realized liberation for oneself and led others to it, one is freed from the branches of craving;
toward sentient beings who sleep in the slumber of constant negligence, one is able to awaken them.
In all things they always delight in being well-disciplined, And they ever take joy in the gift of Dharma;
They do not dwell with any envy or jealousy, But love to practice giving without stinginess.
Seeing those destitute and suffering beings, They constantly ensure they have sufficient means of livelihood.
This is the supreme path that fulfills all merit; the wise always cultivate it at all times.
With a joyful heart, they beat those various sublime and wondrous great Dharma-drums;
severing the net of doubt, they realize the subtle Dharma, their wisdom as firm and solid as a vajra.
Abiding amidst the assembly in the place of the supreme noble Dharma, he is able to know the inclinations and desires of sentient beings,
and proclaims the unsurpassed nectar-like Dharma— namely, the most excellent and essential Sūtras.
Each abiding in their own supreme supernormal powers, they are able to bestow the most excellent eye upon the world;
like the sun, they dispel the darkness of ignorance, and like ore, they produce wisdom.
They reveal the truth to eliminate fear, increasing superior wisdom and cultivating meditative concentration.
He teaches the most wondrous and subtle Dharma, which is called the supreme transcendence of cessation (nirvāṇa).
Those who hear and uphold it are honored by the wise; they establish faith and integrity, increasing their merit.
Being able to know the supreme treasury of the world's Dharma, he constantly proclaims beautiful and sublime words.
Skilled in speech and proficient in ritual, they are the reliance of the lamp of the Dharma;
always benefiting sentient beings with a virtuous mind, they practice the supreme and subtle Dharma.
Abiding in the path of Dharma, free from the stains of dust, And possessing moistening benefit and serene faith,
he teaches and transforms all the world with the Dharma. Having become the most supreme Great Dharma King,
capable of being the Unsurpassed Honored One of the Dharma, He dwells in the foremost and highest reverence.
Constantly upholding the sublime and perfect enlightenment, he turns the supreme wheel of Dharma in accordance with reality.
Beholding those various beings who are deluded and self-indulgent— those evil sentient beings whose minds are bewildered as they head toward perilous paths,
standing at the gateway to the miserable realms from which it is difficult to escape— [he acts for their sake].
Arousing a vast, compassionate, and pure mind, Having arisen, he is able to eliminate the suffering of the world;
He expounds the most supreme and subtle path, Which is called that excellent way of the Eightfold Right Path.
Thus, through those dharmas, vast and firm, he constructs the unsurpassed, supreme vessel of Dharma;
able to ferry across the ocean of birth-and-death and afflictions all the worlds in their fear,
he regards the emptiness of the factors of enlightenment as his armor, becoming a courageous and mighty master mariner.
The further shore is free from fear and eternally peaceful; there one establishes sentient beings in that supreme state.
By maintaining various mantras and proper conduct, one is liberated from the oppression of all suffering and reaches the further shore of the wisdom of vidyā-mantras.
The wise are able to know the desires of sentient beings.
Beholding the disease of afflictions with no place of refuge, and seeing how various evils and transgressions distress the world,
he causes them to purge through the medicine of the Dharma, treating them according to the Dharma.
With various supreme teachings he subdues opposing arguments; his speech is sublime and sovereign.
Knowing all sounds and voices, he masters the meaning of the Dharma; courageous, he dwells on the ground of supreme wisdom.
With patience as his strength and wisdom as his weapon, he dons the firm armor of compassion.
The Noble One delights the wise with wisdom, dwelling peacefully within the Dharma without guile.
He is the most supreme among all those in the three realms of existence, having attained mastery over all sentient beings.
Seeing that the multitudes of living beings rely upon the path of Māra and wander, lost on the way to the True and Right, he acts for their sake.
That path is supreme, noble, and stainless;
it can manifest fearlessness, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of beings proceed upon this path to the place free from sorrow.
They act as lamps for the world, providing rescue, refuge, and an island-home;
they bestow fearlessness upon sentient beings in terror and comfort all living creatures.
Seeing them thus afflicted by these hundred sufferings, like those born blind who see nothing, [they provide light].
Yet regarding the most supreme torch of the Great Dharma, he expounds and reveals the true meaning.
By training in crafts to benefit sentient beings, he is able to obtain renown, merit, and happiness.
Abiding in skills that accord with the Dharma, he causes all sentient beings to attain peace and joy.
All have reached the further shore; They are able to act as the most supreme Great Teachers.
Out of compassion for the world, they proceed toward Bodhi, Causing all to dwell securely in the state of fearlessness.
The Muni is ever insatiable regarding wisdom and merit;
having reached the further shore of ethical discipline, patience, and meditative concentration, he dwells securely in the profound and subtle Dharma.
Feeling no weariness toward others, he proclaims the supreme Dharma of tranquility;
just as rain from the heavens falls everywhere upon the great earth, so too does the rain of Dharma fill all things.
If there are sentient beings who go to his presence, seeking to understand the profound Dharma and its names and meanings,
they shall hear the jewel of the Dharma at that place, which is able to eliminate immeasurable and boundless suffering.
Those vast and manifold doubts he swiftly severs with the sword of Dharma;
having reached the shore of ethical discipline, patience, and samādhi, he is able to know the many inclinations and faiths of sentient beings.

The Great Being has attained ultimate wisdom; having thoroughly understood the desires of all living beings, he observes the mental activities of sentient beings and knows with certainty exactly how their minds function.
Those who hear his words of wisdom cause millions of beings to attain the pure eye;
they cross to the further shore of meditative concentration and liberation, and are able to enter and abide securely upon the true path.
Even a hundred billion nayutas of māras cannot fathom his mental conduct;
it is like the tracks of birds in the sky, which no one at all can perceive.
Through the power of wisdom that subdues and pacifies, you abide securely within the supreme, holy Dharma;
with mastery, you crush all demonic forces and awaken to the most excellent, supreme Bodhi.
Constantly attaining the further shore of supernormal powers, they are able to travel swiftly to hundreds of thousands of realms,
where they behold billions of nayutas of Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
With pure eyes free from all obstructions, they behold all the Teachers of the ten directions;
guarding their sense faculties without defilement, they travel with mastery to immeasurable lands.
Even if all sentient beings throughout the ten directions were simultaneously to become Teachers,
and for the duration of many nayutas of eons they were to constantly praise [the Buddha] without interruption—
possessing inexhaustible, unimpeded eloquence— the virtues thus extolled would likewise be infinite.
"Regarding this peerless, stainless samādhi, one who holds it in mind can act in such a way.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing further to reveal the merits and benefits of this samādhi, spoke of the bodhisattva’s past conduct; moreover, in order to manifest and increase the power of the youth Candraprabha, he recounted his own past causes and conditions, speaking in verse:
"O Youth!..."
You should now listen well:
throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, I have practiced and made offerings to hundreds of thousands of Tathāgatas, seeking this supreme, tranquil samādhi.
In inconceivable kalpas past, throughout as many hundreds of lands as there are atoms in the sands of the Ganges—
know that what has been described therein was when there was a Buddha named Viśveśvara.
That Buddha-Tathāgata has a retinue, numbering sixty billion in full;
all have exhausted their outflows and are free from afflictions, being well-established in the eight liberations.
At that time, all the great earths were peaceful, prosperous, and free from turmoil;
all people were entirely at ease and happy, traveling and coming and going with full contentment.
Great wealth and riches abounded everywhere, and they fully enjoyed every celestial pleasure.
Maintaining the precepts and being self-disciplined, one has few afflictions; with a handsome and upright appearance, one delights in the power of patience.
Like the sons of the gods in their celestial palaces, the wise are fully endowed with virtuous conduct and merit.
At that time in that world there was a king, whose fame was vast and who was known as Śubhavimśa;
at that time, that king had many sons, numbering five hundred, all endowed with mindfulness and wisdom.
At that time, the Victorious King, in the presence of the Buddha,
relinquished six million groves adorned with exquisite trees of flowers and fruit, offering them to the Buddha who is endowed with great compassion;
he likewise constructed six million monasteries, complete with walkways and seats.
Kāṣāyas and robes by the hundreds of thousands, Spread out at places for walking meditation and rest;
In such infinite hundreds of thousands of varieties, All that is required by śramaṇas was provided.
At that time, with a heart of faith and reverence, the Victorious King offered everything to the Sugata;
having accomplished all the power of merit, his physical form became upright, majestic, and most lovely.
That king constantly established himself and others in the ten paths of wholesome action;
hundreds of thousands of nayutas of people followed the king as he proceeded to the presence of the Buddha.
Holding exquisite flowers and fragrant ointments, as well as supreme parasols, banners, pennants, and music,
they made offerings to the most excellent Buddha, the World-Honored One, standing with palms joined at their crowns.
The assembly of a thousand bhikṣus remained silent, while humans, devas, asuras, nāgas,
and yakṣas all gazed upon the Buddha with reverence,
saying: "Excellent!"
What Dharma does he naturally proclaim?
The Muni, the World-Honored One, knows their inclinations; he also knows the supreme mind of the eminent king.
The Buddha, being able to fully comprehend their faith and delight, proclaims this samādhi for them.
When the Sugata spoke these words, the great earth and all its mountains shook;
in the space of a thought, a rain of various flowers fell from the sky, and hundreds of thousands of lotuses emerged from the ground.
Having thoroughly understood the words of sublime meaning, the Buddha, knowing his aspiration, gave this prophetic teaching:
"I shall speak of this samādhi of cessation for you, O King;
listen to what was distinguished in the past."
All existence and non-existence arise from false conceptualization;
they are empty like a mirage, like foam, like clouds, and like flickering lightning—all are empty and non-existent. All things are without self and without sentient beings.
Past and future phenomena are likewise empty; they neither go nor stay, being devoid of location.
They are eternally without solidity, having a nature like an illusion, and are all supremely pure like space.
Neither blue, nor yellow, nor red, nor white; names are empty and non-existent, being merely the nature of sound.
That mind is detached from the mind and lacks the nature of mind; it is detached from all sounds and is empty and non-existent.
He expounds the meaning of the phrases yet does not dwell therein;
though he does not speak, the syllables are not empty, and these characters do not go to any other direction, nor do they come from any other place.
Its syllables are inexhaustible; this is the treasury of the exhausted. Whether spoken or unspoken, they are ever inexhaustible;
though the phrases and flavors are constantly proclaimed, they are never exhausted. One who knows thus attains the inexhaustible.
If one knows that these dharmas are inexhaustible, one can always preach the inexhaustible Dharma;
though one may preach a thousand kinds of sūtras, one always knows that all dharmas are free from words and letters.
Hundreds of thousands of Buddhas have already passed away, And they too once preached hundreds of thousands of dharmas;
Yet all dharmas are inexhaustible, For since no dharma can be apprehended, they are inexhaustible.
If a person expounds the Dharma for others, Without clinging to words and letters,
Knowing that the Dharma is fundamentally without self and without sentient beings, They can expound it exhaustlessly.
The wise one proclaims all speech, yet does not allow language to alter that mind;
knowing all sounds and voices to be like echoes from a valley, they thus have no attachment to words.
This Dharma is taught through various sounds and words; yet in the mere instant of thought, these words perish and vanish.
Such is the nature of all these sounds and words, and so too is the nature of all phenomena.
All phenomena are signless and free from signs; they are eternally signless, their signs being empty and quiescent.
Being empty and quiescent, they are without desire, without grasping, and without rejection or acceptance; therefore, this tranquil concentration cannot be apprehended.
Completely transcending both the conditioned and the unconditioned, such a Great Sage is free from conceptual discrimination;
having distanced himself from all paths of evil views, he thoroughly realizes that all realms of existence are ultimately unconditioned.
Ever free from defilement, hatred, and delusion, the essence of the mind is thus eternally quiescent;
by the supreme power of this samādhi, one is therefore able to know that these phenomena are empty.

Just as in empty mountains, rivers, and valleys, One hears sublime and wondrous sounds and voices, So do conditioned phenomena arise through the causes and conditions of saṃsāra; All worlds are empty, just like an illusion.
With the power of wisdom, delighting in the dharmas of merit, Abiding securely in the sages of wisdom and supernormal powers,
He is skillful in the articulation of speech, And is able to expound such a samādhi of quiescence.
What are called *vitarka* and *vicāra* are but false imaginings; one cannot find their limit within the world.
Their original limit has never possessed any marks, yet they serve as the path of causes and conditions for the future.
The performance of karma gives rise to existence, which is produced according to the superior, middling, or inferior [faculties].
This dharma is by its very nature devoid of cognition; one should know that dharmas are empty and selfless.
Black and white karmas do not perish; what one has done oneself, one receives back oneself.
Karma does not travel to the place where its fruit arises, yet karma can act as its cause.
The Buddhas expound the teachings of conventional truth; One should view the conditioned and the unconditioned in this way:
There is no reality, nor self or person; Such is the nature of all worldly phenomena.
All states of existence are utterly illusory, Like magical illusions or the moon reflected in water;
Empty and non-existent like a mass of foam upon the waves, They are eternally quiescent, as revealed through sound.
Relinquishing everything without grasping, maintaining precepts and dignified conduct without reliance,
and not clinging to the power of patience toward any sentient beings— the practitioner who acts thus attains tranquil concentration.
According to the king’s own inclinations and desires, the Tathāgata expounded the Dharma in accordance with his capacity;
having heard the World-Honored One’s teaching, the king and his retinue all received the precepts.
Having heard this samādhi, the Victorious King was filled with joy and exultation, and spoke these words: "Excellent!
You are able to expound this samādhi; therefore, I take refuge in the Buddha, the World-Honored One."

At that time, the assembly consisted of eighty thousand people; having heard this most excellent nature of the Dharma, which expounds the true ultimate truth, they all attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena.
Sentient beings have no birth or extinction; all phenomena are unborn, eternally empty and quiescent.
When the King and his retinue realized this, they each attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas.
At that time, King Supuṣpa abandoned his royal throne And entered the Buddha’s Dharma to become a renunciant;
All five hundred sons of that king Also followed the king and became renunciants.
When the king and his sons went forth, There were immeasurable numbers of other people as well.
For the sake of seeking the Buddha-dharma, they all likewise went forth from home in that Dharma.
The Tathāgata Svayambhū preached the Dharma for them for a full two thousand years;
the king, his son, and their retinue practiced the Dharma throughout those two thousand years.
After such a number of years had passed, that Buddha, the World-Honored One, entered parinirvāṇa;
at that time, all his śrāvakas likewise attained extinction, and thereafter the True Dharma became exceedingly diminished.
That King Supuṣpa had an excellent son named Puṇyaprajña, who possessed right faith;
the king had a Dharma-master as his guide, who upheld this supreme, tranquil samādhi.
Intelligent, wise, and possessed of the power of mindfulness, he is honored by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of people;
attended by ten billion devas, he goes to various places and offers praise.
His speech is supple and not coarse or harsh; he is disciplined, delights in the precepts, and is well-guarded.
His voice is harmonious and elegant, his words are lovely, and he is fully endowed with the power of wisdom and dhāraṇī.
He obtained ten billion superior *kāṣāya* robes; the bhikṣu was named Yaśaḥprabha.
By the power of that person’s merit, he was beyond compare, yet immeasurable bhikṣus gave rise to envy and jealousy.
Fully endowed with merit, physical strength, and beauty, And likewise possessed of wisdom and supernormal powers,
Guarding the pure precepts and the power of meditative concentration— These are what arise from the Dharma-power of a bhikṣu.
The fourfold assembly, both lay and ordained, all yearn for, look up to, and cherish them;
those who have gained faith in the Buddha’s Dharma honor, revere, and make offerings to them with hearts of deep respect.
In the past, the son of King Supuṣpa, known as Puṇyaprajñāśraddhā,
perceiving that the bhikṣu had conceived an evil mind toward his own teacher, protected him.
At that time, there were five hundred thousand troops, all clad in armor and holding swords,
constantly ordered to protect this Dharma Master as he expounded the practice of bodhi and tranquility.
Within the great assembly he preaches this Dharma—namely, emptiness, non-self, and the absence of a life-principle;
those who harbor attachments to a self find no joy in the Dharma Master’s teaching.
The assembly of bhikṣus who did not believe in the dharma of emptiness immediately rose up, holding knives in their hands, and said:
"This man speaks falsely of what is not the Dharma; by killing him, one will surely obtain great merit."
The Dharma Master beholds the sword without fear, because he contemplates the dharma of emptiness;
there is no sentient being to be killed, for emptiness is devoid of self or person, like a stone wall.
The Dharma Master Bhikṣu then joined his palms, And spoke, uttering "Namo Buddha":
"If this teaching of emptiness is truly not false, May this blade be transformed into a māndārava flower."
Because of the aspiration of one who upholds the precepts, As soon as words are spoken, flowers rain down from the void;
The great earth and all its mountains tremble, And blades are instantly transformed into exquisite fragrant flowers.
At that time, those who had taken up the view of holding a blade felt shame and regret;
their hands were rendered unable to move as they were seized by the sword, struck with alarm, dread, and great terror.
Those who have gained faith in the Buddha, and all those who delight in the dharma of emptiness,
raised a great cry of lamentation and wept, scattering all their garments as offerings.
The Dharma Master Bhikṣu, giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness, spoke these words before the great assembly:
"If anyone should give rise to anger toward me, for their sake I shall practice the path to Bodhi."
The faction of those following his Dharma was extremely small, and the Dharma Master was constantly subjected to their insults and oppression;
though he heard all their unpleasant words, his power of patience increased all the more.
At that time, for eighty years, that Dharma Master expounded the Tathāgata’s treasury of the Dharma of emptiness;
by the power of that king, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of wicked bhikṣus were made to retreat and disperse.
At another time, that Dharma Master, having benefited immeasurable hundreds of thousands of beings and reflecting upon his flawless conduct of the precepts,
proceeded to the abode of Puṇya and Prajñā.
Seeing that the Dharma Master was deeply reverent, the King immediately asked that bhikṣu:
"Do not cause my Great Teacher’s mind to be disturbed or displeased."
He then replied: "O King!
Please grant me your hearing: It is through the power of forbearance that all Buddhas arise; if you should direct harsh words toward me, I shall instead give rise to supreme and superior patience."
"Throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas in past lives, I cultivated patience;
I am that very monk named Kīrtidhvaja," so said the Tathāgata Śākyamuni.
"He who was the prince Puṇyaprajñā in the past, the one who protected the Dharma-master Kīrtidhvaja—"
Throughout a thousand lifetimes he was my friend, and I have already prophesied that he shall become the Maitreya;
he who in the past made offerings to the Buddha Īśvara and constructed a most excellent and wondrous stūpa—
this King Supuṣpa who then went forth as a renunciant— shall attain Buddhahood under the name Padmottara.
I, too, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas, have upheld the Tathāgata’s most supreme Dharma;
I have already accumulated the power of patience, O youth!
You should train yourself accordingly.
After I have entered parinirvāṇa and passed away, at a time when the True Dharma is about to perish, there will be bhikṣus who delight in external treatises; they shall then revile my supreme Dharma.

Fickle and frivolous, lacking shame and remorse, greedy for food and drink and failing to guard against transgressions, they will instead become attached to robes and alms bowls; such people will slander my supreme Dharma.
Always delighting in strife and lacking any sense of reciprocity, they will [despise] those of poor and lowly birth.
Having gone forth within my Dharma, they do not delight in emptiness and quiescent extinction;
these deluded sentient beings follow the will of Māra, adhering to it with sovereign ease;
these greedy, self-indulgent, and vulgar fools do not delight in emptiness and quiescent extinction.
Whether laypeople or those who have left the home life, among the fourfold assembly, those who are slanderous, fawning, foolish, and give rise to evil thoughts—
those who follow such an evil faction will, in the final age, revile the Dharma of emptiness.
"O youth!
Having heard my teaching, you should always serve the forest-dwelling monks—those who delight in emptiness and stillness—for such as these uphold the Buddha-Dharma."
In my Buddha-dharma, I admit such a person; they may leave the household life, receive the precepts, and observe the poṣadha.
Having abandoned all faults and defilements, they digest the offerings of the faithful; such a person is able to uphold Bodhi.
Even to the point of relinquishing body and life, one cultivates the dharma of emptiness and delights in tranquility;
with a mind in accord with that dharma of emptiness, one dwells joyfully in the araṇya like a wild deer.
With banners, streamers, parasols, flowers, and incense, one should offer worship at the abodes of all Buddhas;
by making offerings to these peerless and supreme shrines (caityas), one can swiftly attain this samādhi.
They established incomparable and supreme stūpas and temples, adorned with various gold and silver;
they fashioned immeasurable varieties of images, generating a heart of compassion for the sake of awakening.
All articles of offering, pure and exquisite, found among gods and humans—
you should seek them all to make offerings to the Buddha, for the sake of seeking the unsurpassed wisdom of a Buddha.

One should contemplate the Buddhas according to the Dharma: All the Tathāgatas dwelling in the ten directions, Those who abide before one’s eyes, immeasurable and established in the Dharma— All these sons of the Buddha are able to realize and know them.
Their minds are constantly intent on benefiting others and they delight in giving;
they maintain pure ethical discipline and abide in the power of patience, rejoicing in the practice of forbearance and seclusion. They are able to know that all phenomena are empty;
with courageous diligence and without indolence or retreat, they strive to cultivate meditative concentration, ethical discipline, and extensive learning.
Through wisdom one thoroughly realizes eternal purity, and before long becomes a Great Compassionate One.
By means of the contemplation on impurity, one eliminates greedy defilement; through the power of loving-kindness, one can cure hatred;
by means of the dharma of dependent origination, one shatters ignorance, and thus attains the supreme, unsurpassed path.
Contemplate the body as being like a mass of foam on water; all things are empty and devoid of solidity.
Observe that the five aggregates are entirely empty and non-existent, and you will swiftly attain the most supreme wisdom.
Free yourself from grasping at all erroneous views, and do not rely upon the notions of life-span, self, or person.
Thoroughly knowing that all phenomena are empty, one swiftly attains the state of that Muni King.
Without craving for gain and honor, nor feeling sorrow when gain is not obtained,
and with no change in mind whether hearing praise or blame from others— one remains unmoving like Mount Sumeru.
Rise with reverence for the sake of seeking the Dharma; Do not, having heard it, become attached to it.
Abiding in the sphere of action of all Buddhas, One can swiftly travel through a hundred worlds.
Regarding all worlds as entirely equal, Do not give rise to a mind of partiality, such as hatred or love.
Be careful never to seek profit or fame; you shall swiftly become a Teacher of Gods and Humans.
Constantly praise and speak of the Buddha’s virtues, extolling them with words and phrases as they truly are.
When sentient beings hear such praise, they will conceive a deep love and joy for the Buddha’s virtues.
Parents, teachers, elders, and all sentient beings— Revering them all in this way,
and not following the power of Māra, One shall then obtain the thirty-two marks of a great man.
Always remaining far removed from all worldly clamor, dwelling in quiet and secluded forests, one is able to benefit both oneself and others;
thus, seeking liberation, one should swiftly apply oneself to practice.
Always delight in cultivating loving-kindness and compassion, And likewise with sympathetic joy and equanimity;
One who is disciplined and tranquil is worthy of praise, And shall swiftly achieve the benefit of the world.
If there are those who wish to attain the samādhi of tranquility And proceed toward unsurpassed bodhi,
They should carefully avoid associating with evil friends And always remain close to virtuous persons.
Furthermore, do not aspire to the stage of a śrāvaka, nor take delight in their practices;
with courageous resolve, delight in the virtues of the Buddha, and you shall swiftly attain Buddhahood just as I have.
Always speak words that are true and pure; Be careful not to utter falsehoods or harsh speech.
Constantly speak lovely and exquisite words, And you shall attain the most supreme Buddha-enlightenment.
Do not cherish attachment to your own body or life; be careful never to praise yourself or disparage others.
Reflect only upon your own merits, and do not observe the conduct of others.
Constantly contemplate emptiness and liberation; do not yearn for or delight in the various realms of existence.
Abandon all signs without exception, and let the mind always abide peacefully in signlessness.
Always able to remain far removed from the two extremes, Making no discrimination between existence and non-existence,
Observing all sentient beings as merely dependent origination— One who can know this is a Great Teacher.
Having abandoned all conduct of sensual desire, having completely severed and detached from the defiled mind,
and having cut away all the darkness of ignorance, he has become a Lion among Men who has attained nirvana.
Constantly delighting in the contemplation of impermanence, And being detached from suffering, pleasure, and the like within all states of existence,
From defilement, impurity, and non-self— One who practices in this way is a venerable person among men.
The Buddha acts as a lamp for the world, And is able to proclaim this supreme, true Dharma;
He has likewise subdued the power of Māra, Having already attained unsurpassed, supreme Bodhi.
The various merits I have described, as well as the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of faults I have shown—
you should abandon faults and cultivate merit, O youth!
In this way, one will certainly attain Buddhahood.
*Candrapradīpa-samādhi-sūtra*, Scroll Nine;
*Candrapradīpa-samādhi-sūtra*, Scroll Ten.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the High Qi Dynasty:
"O Youth! For this reason, a bodhisattva should fully cultivate and train in the precepts of the body.
How does a bodhisattva fully perfect the precepts of the body?"
If a bodhisattva is fully endowed with bodily precepts and attains unimpeded wisdom regarding all phenomena, this is called the excellent practice of the body.
If one has excellently practiced the body and thereby attains unimpeded wisdom regarding all phenomena, this is termed a bodhisattva being fully endowed with bodily precepts.
"Furthermore, youth!

A bodhisattva who is fully endowed with bodily discipline can obtain the thirty-two marks of a great man, attain the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, and the eighteen unique qualities."
“O youth! This is called the bodhisattva’s fulfillment of bodily discipline.
Furthermore, youth!”
A Bodhisattva who is fully endowed with bodily discipline is able to attain the three gates of liberation.
What are these three?
They are the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness; this is called being fully endowed with bodily discipline.
"Furthermore, youth!
A bodhisattva who is fully endowed with bodily discipline is able to attain the four sublime abodes (*brahmavihāra*).
What are these four?
That is to say, one maintains loving-kindness toward all sentient beings; the same applies to the minds of compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
Young man!
This is called a bodhisattva’s fulfillment of physical discipline.
"Furthermore, youth!
How does a bodhisattva cultivate the good conduct of the body?

It refers to the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path; this is called the bodhisattva’s perfection of bodily precepts."
"Furthermore, young man!

A bodhisattva who is fully endowed with bodily discipline is able to attain the four dhyānas and the four right attainments, is able to abide in great compassion, and attains wholesome vitarka and vicāra as well as tranquilized vitarka and vicāra; this is called a bodhisattva being fully endowed with bodily discipline."
"Furthermore, young man!

If a bodhisattva is fully endowed with the precepts of physical conduct, they remain far removed from the ten unwholesome karmas: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, covetousness, malice, and wrong views."

Deceiving with measures and weights, deceiving with speech, deceiving with clothing, and—due to official authority or influence—seizing, mutilating, destroying, oppressing, binding, being crooked and false, acting in concert with greed: one should distance oneself from all such evil karmas.

Restraining and governing oneself, one should eliminate them all—being without greed and without grasping—just as when the crown of a *tāla* tree is cut off, it will never sprout again in future lives; there shall be no further arising of dharmas.
"Young man, you should know that this dharma constitutes the bodhisattva’s perfection of bodily discipline.
Young man!"

In the distant past, beyond incalculable upon incalculable, vast, immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable kalpas, there was a Buddha named Jñānaprabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, who dwelt in the world for sixty billion years.

At that time, there was a king named Victorious Reflection who, together with his retinue of eighty trillion people, went to the place where the Tathāgata Jñānaprabha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the Tathāgata Jñānaprabha spoke these verses on the restraint of the body:
"Just as space is free from defilement, Its self-nature luminous and ultimately pure;
So too is this discipline of the body— It cannot be expressed by means of sound."
Sound and emptiness cannot be known; these two are of one and the same characteristic.
It is said that space has no marks, and those marks are identical to the precepts of the body.
If one knows that these precepts have but a single characteristic, then one is fully endowed with the discipline of the precepts.
The nature of wisdom is unborn and its objects are quiescent; within true outflowlessness, deluded conceptualization is exhausted.
There is neither attachment nor craving, and no thirsting desire for wealth or form.
If one does not perceive the faults inherent in all states of existence, one will ultimately be unable to know the precepts of this body;
yet if one can know the untainted precepts, then for such a person there will be no further rebirths whatsoever.
One should know that the Dharma of the Arhat is thus, something unknown to any of the non-Buddhists.
With a mind that fears the three realms and has no craving for sensual desires or possessions, they do not long for royal rank or wealth;
such a person is able to fulfill this discipline of the body.
I now explain the meaning of this bodily restraint; this meaning cannot be expressed by words or teachings.
If one can understand this mother of dharmas, that person will always abide in bodily restraint.
The wise cherish and delight in this mother of meanings; because they have faith and joy in these meanings, I speak thus.
Staying far removed from what is non-beneficial and abiding in the true meaning—this is what is always called dwelling in the precept of the body.
What is the meaning taught within the teachings of all Buddhas?
How can one skillfully come to know this meaning?
If one can understand the meaning of correspondence, this is precisely what is called abiding in bodily discipline.
If one observes that which is signless— that all things are selfless, entirely empty and non-existent—
such a person is not called one who lacks discipline, for they cultivate and study the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Observing all that exists as non-existent, this person constantly dwells at the limit of non-existence;
having no attachment to anything that exists, this person is able to realize the concentration of signlessness.
If a person knows that dharmas are without self, That their own essence is empty, devoid of nature, and non-existent,
Such a person is not called one who lacks precepts, For they have already awakened to the certainty of reality;
If a person can know that the five aggregates are empty, And that all dharmas are quiescent and devoid of a personal self—
He is then called one who upholds the precepts, for his body no longer performs evil deeds.

There is no one who observes discipline by grasping at signs; those who harbor the notion of a self and cling with their minds, or who grasp at physical forms and cling to persons, give rise to craving and lack true discipline.
If one constantly cultivates and studies the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), this person ultimately realizes true and wondrous emptiness;
they will no longer give rise to craving and desire, nor will they fall into the evil realms due to a lack of precepts.
An ant might be able to move the void, and one might cause the firm and stable Mount Sumeru to shake;
yet if there is one who has well studied the true Dharma, the exquisite forms of the devas cannot move them.
One might paint the void with colors, or even grasp the great void with one's hand.
All Māras, with their cravings and desires, are unable to cause even the slightest agitation;
one might catch the sound of an echo, or make a great stone float upon the water,
but no one can know the mental intentions of one who trains thus in the precepts of the body.
All sounds whatsoever could be gathered and placed within a casket;
yet one who abides in such discipline of the body has no dwelling place that can be known.
All clouds, thunder, and flashes of lightning, as well as the brilliance of the sun and moon, could all be grasped; [but this cannot be done].
If there be one who abides in the precepts of the body, no one can know the intrinsic nature of that body;
Even if all the wind-circles in the four directions could be bound by nets and hooks,
If there be one who abides in the precepts of the body, no one can know the dimensions of that body.
Those who abide in the restraint of the mind are not within the realm of ordinary sentient beings;
those who are able to skillfully cultivate bodily precepts are like space, incapable of being defiled.
In the wind-paths of the four directions, even the tracks of birds in the sky may still be seen;
yet the dimensions of his body cannot be measured, and the movements of his mind are difficult to conceive.
If one abides in such bodily discipline, they will be free from all faults and evils and remain far removed from the entire mass of afflictions; by training in such bodily discipline,
they dwell in the pure and tranquil meditative absorption, and cannot be harmed by sword or fire.
No one is able to seize that body, because they have constantly practiced and studied the precepts of bodily conduct;
one who dwells thus is without fear, their mind is free from agitation and envy,
and they remain far removed from all calamities, because they have practiced and studied such precepts of bodily conduct.
They do not fear swords, staves, or poisons, nor do they dread the calamities of water or fire;
having distanced themselves from all misfortunes and hardships, this is because they have cultivated and studied such bodily discipline.
They do not fear rain, hail, or thieves, nor any of the various poisons and harms;
because they are free from all notions of self, and being free from such notions, they have no fear.
Having abandoned both dread and terror, their minds remain unshaken by the absence of fear.
With a mind unmoving and free from fear, hundreds of millions of māras cannot terrify them.
If one expounds, elucidates, and reveals this bodhisattva’s bodily precept,
and if there are those who train in this bodily precept, then hundreds of millions of māras will be unable to disturb them.
If one wishes to know the teachings of all Buddhas, One should know that they have no limit or boundary.
If there is one who cultivates and trains in bodily precepts, Such a person can become a stupa for the three realms.
If one wishes to know these Buddha-teachings, They are an inconceivable assembly of quiescence.
If one trains in such bodily discipline, their practice will be firm and they shall swiftly attain Buddhahood;
if there are those who wish to obtain the Dharma of the Great Sage and the inconceivable ten powers of a Buddha,
if they train in such bodily discipline, it will not be difficult for them to cultivate and attain these Buddha-powers.
The eighteen supreme, unique qualities in which all Buddhas and Tathāgatas abide—
if one trains in this bodily discipline, it will not be difficult for them to attain these dharmas;
nor will it be difficult to dwell within the jewels of the seven factors of enlightenment, as well as the bases of psychic power, eloquence, and so forth.
If there are those who cultivate and train in bodily discipline, it will not be difficult for them to attain that wondrous fruit;
regarding the Brahma-abodes, the four dhyānas, the three doors of liberation,
peaceful vitarka and vicāra, and cessation— it is not difficult for one who abides in bodily discipline to attain these.
The four foundations of mindfulness and the right efforts, the five faculties and five powers of the Great Sage,
as well as the Noble Eightfold Path— those who abide in the precepts of bodily conduct will attain these without difficulty;
as for all other dharmas possessed by the Buddhas, they are inconceivable and immeasurable.
It was not difficult for him to attain this Dharma, because he had trained in such bodily discipline.
Having heard of such bodily discipline, the king attained the supreme benefit;
filled with joy and leaping for delight, he then went forth into homelessness within that Buddha’s teaching.
Having gone forth for ten billion years, he practiced the most supreme and pure brahmacarya;
constantly cultivating the four brahmavihāras, he benefited all the devas and humans of the world.
Having thoroughly cultivated the pure Brahma-abodes, one then attains such supreme discipline of body;
furthermore, one beholds billions of Buddhas in the ten directions and practices such bodhisattva conduct.
Having gone forth into that supreme Dharma, he practices the most excellent, pure brahmacarya;
endowed with great learning and wondrous eloquence, he is called a wise and great Dharma-master.
Firmly upholding the prohibitive precepts without deficiency, The body of precepts is pure and free from blemish;
That which is called the noble precept, the outflow-free precept— One should know that the noble precept is eternally abiding.
"O youth!
In the past, when I was cultivating bodhi, I then manifested as King Viśeṣacintin. Do not harbor doubts that he was another person; you should know that he was indeed my own self."
"O youth!
You should train yourself accordingly, dwelling securely in such supreme bodily discipline; you shall extensively proclaim it to billions of beings, and before long, you too shall become like me."
“O youth! For this reason, a bodhisattva should practice pure bodily action. Why is that?

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice pure deeds do not fear falling into the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, or Yama; nor do they fear the eight difficulties or the sufferings and calamities of the five destinies. Furthermore, they do not fear water, fire, the five weapons, poisons, kings, thieves, lions, tigers, leopards, jackals, wolves, rhinoceroses, elephants, bears, brown bears, or any other malevolent beasts, venomous insects, or carnivorous creatures. They likewise do not fear the perils posed by humans or non-humans.

“O Youth! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who has cultivated pure conduct of body, wishing to lift up this trichiliocosm with his palm—whether to a height of one tala tree or even ten tala trees—can lift it entirely according to his desire.”
“O youth! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who purifies their physical conduct can reach the ultimate further shore of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

By the power of the merit obtained through retribution and the faculty of psychic travel (*ṛddhi*), they are able to embrace and enter all those meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) that are secluded, compliant, untainted, and quiescent.”
By relying on this concentration, one achieves the untainted state and attains the unimpeded eye regarding all worldly phenomena.
What is the basis of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*)?

It refers to the ability to exercise sovereign mastery and understanding without obstruction according to one's recollection; because it can be accomplished at will, it is called the basis of supernormal power.

"Furthermore, youth! A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who dwells in the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) is able to perform various miraculous transformations (*vikurvita*). That is to say: he can make one into many and many into one; he is sovereign in appearing and disappearing; he passes unimpeded through stone walls and mountains as if walking through space; he sits cross-legged in mid-air like a flying bird; he treads upon water as if on land; he emerges from and sinks into the earth without difference from being in water; his body emits smoke and flames like a great mass of fire; and though the sun and moon possess great majesty and power, he is able to touch them. Desiring to assume a vast body, he does so with sovereign ease and without obstruction, even up to the Brahma-heaven."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"With sovereign supernormal powers, they travel throughout the ten directions; Through stone walls and mountains alike, they pass through at will without obstruction."
Like a bird flying with the wind, they tread upon the great earth as if it were water; They appear and disappear with ease, unimpeded by anything;
They walk upon water without sinking, as if treading on solid ground;
A single body can manifest as a thousand bodies, and immeasurable many bodies can become one.
According to their will, they can manifest various forms; for the sake of ferrying sentient beings across, the wise ones travel through the air like soaring birds.
Their bodies emit smoke and flames like a mass of fire, yet they can also cause their own bodies to flow forth pure, cool, and fragrant water.
The wise one sits upright upon this ground, Able to touch the sun and moon with his hand;
In a single thought-moment, he can go to the realm of Brahmā, And expound the supreme Dharma for the Brahmā hosts.
When the thousands of billions of Brahmā hosts have heard the Dharma, They joyfully seek the Unsurpassed and attain victory.
Furthermore, they are able to go to other superior celestial realms and expound the most supreme Dharma.
Whenever they desire to preach the Dharma, they can cause the great trichiliocosm to tremble,
and cause the subtle and wondrous sounds [of the teaching] to completely fill immeasurable billions of Buddha-fields.
“O Youth! For this reason, a bodhisattva should train in the purification of bodily conduct. Why is that?

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the purification of physical conduct attains the purity of the divine ear-element (*divya-śrotra-dhātu*) that surpasses that of humans, and hears sounds—whether from the realms of hell, animals, or the domain of Yama, or from among gods and humans, whether near or far—this is called the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra-abhijñā*).
“O youth! A bodhisattva should further cultivate and train in the pure conduct of the body. Why is this?
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices the pure conduct of body is always able to know the minds of others:
they truly know a mind with desire as a mind with desire, and truly know a mind without desire as a mind without desire;
they truly know a mind with hatred as a mind with hatred, and truly know a mind without hatred as a mind without hatred.
When there is a mind with delusion, he knows it as it truly is: "there is a mind with delusion"; when there is no mind with delusion, he knows it as it truly is:
"there is no mind with delusion. When there is a mind with grasping, he knows it as it truly is: "there is a mind with grasping"; when there is no mind with grasping, he knows it as it truly is:

"there is no mind with grasping. When there is a mind with inversion, he knows it as it truly is: "there is a mind with inversion"; when there is no mind with inversion, he knows it as it truly is: "there is no mind with inversion."
He knows a perverted mind as it truly is; he knows a small mind as it truly is when there is a small mind, and he knows there is no small mind as it truly is when there is no small mind;
he knows a great mind as it truly is when there is a great mind, and he knows there is no great mind as it truly is when there is no great mind;
he knows a radiant mind as it truly is when there is a radiant mind, and he knows there is no radiant mind [as it truly is when there is no radiant mind].
One knows as it truly is a mind that lacks clarity; one knows as it truly is an immeasurable mind as an immeasurable mind; one knows as it truly is a limited mind as a limited mind;
one knows as it truly is a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind; one knows as it truly is an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind;
one knows as it truly is a distracted mind as a distracted mind; and one knows as it truly is an undistracted mind as an undistracted mind.
He knows an undistracted mind as an undistracted mind, a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind,
and an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind; he knows a superior mind as a superior mind,
a non-superior mind as a non-superior mind, a liberated mind as a liberated mind, and an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind.
He knows an untrained mind as an untrained mind, and he knows a trained mind as a trained mind, exactly as it is.
Young man!
This is called a bodhisattva’s accurate understanding of the minds of other sentient beings.
"Furthermore, young man!
A bodhisattva should train in the purification of physical conduct.
What is the bodhisattva’s purification of physical conduct?
That is to say, he recollects and knows various matters of past lives:

whether one birth, two births, three births, up to ten births, twenty births, thirty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, ten thousand births, a hundred thousand births, a million births, ten million births, or even a hundred million births; furthermore—
He recollects and knows the events of one kalpa, a hundred kalpas, and even up to a thousand or ten thousand kalpas;

he knows the formation of kalpas, he knows the destruction of kalpas, and he knows both the formation and destruction of kalpas, even knowing the events of the formation and destruction of immeasurable kalpas;
and within those kalpas, he knows that there were sentient beings with such names, such surnames, and such [lineages].

He knows their place of birth, such food and drink, such long life, such short life, such long duration of stay, such exhaustion of the lifespan; he knows such suffering experienced, such pleasure experienced;
whether dying here and being born there, or dying there and being born here; and their such-and-such appearance.
To thus recollect and know such lands and such past events is called the bodhisattva’s supernormal power of knowledge of past lives.
"Furthermore, young man!
A bodhisattva should cultivate pure conduct of body.
What is the pure conduct of body of a bodhisattva?

It is that which possesses the purity of the divine eye-sphere, surpassing that of the human eye, by which they see all sentient beings coming and going through birth and death—whether of beautiful form or ugly form, whether proceeding toward a good destination or a bad destination, whether abiding in a good destination or a bad destination, whether in suffering or in happiness, whether superior or inferior—and knows them all exactly as they have performed their own karma.

Because these sentient beings have accomplished evil conduct of body, accomplished evil conduct of speech, and accomplished evil conduct of mind; because they have slandered the noble ones and held wrong views, by reason of such karmic causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, they fall into hell.

These sentient beings, however, if they have accomplished good conduct of body, accomplished good conduct of speech, and accomplished good conduct of mind; if they do not slander the noble ones and possess right view, by reason of such causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, they proceed to a happy destination and are reborn in the heavens.
"O Youth!

This is called the Bodhisattva’s divine eye-element, purified and surpassing that of the human eye, by which he sees all sentient beings coming and going through birth and death—whether they are of beautiful form or ugly form, whether they are heading toward a good destination or a bad destination, whether they abide in a good destination or a bad destination, whether they experience suffering or pleasure, or whether they are superior or inferior—he fully understands them all according to their own karma; this is called the supernormal power of the divine eye."
"Furthermore, young man!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the pure conduct of body, by means of wisdom corresponding to the three periods of time in a single thought-moment, should understand whatever is to be known, seen, attained, or realized—all of that he fully knows, fully sees, fully attains, fully realizes, and fully comprehends."

What are those phenomena? They are as follows: conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations; conditioned by volitional formations is consciousness; conditioned by consciousness are name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases is contact; conditioned by contact is feeling; conditioned by feeling is craving; conditioned by craving is clinging; conditioned by clinging is existence; conditioned by existence is birth; and conditioned by birth arise old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair.

In this way, the twelve links of dependent origination should be known, seen, attained, realized, and fully awakened to. Thus, through the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; through the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases;

through the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; through the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; through the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; through the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; through the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; through the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; through the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; through the cessation of existence, birth ceases; and through the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair—all these utterly cease. This is to know and see according to reality, to attain and realize according to reality, and to awaken to according to reality.
"To understand the Four Noble Truths as they truly are is called the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The Bodhisattva has already demonstrated The sequence of the supernormal powers."
Abiding in samādhi, they are able to go anywhere at will.
Having well cultivated their faculty of hearing, they attain the inconceivable divine ear;
with that ear, they are able to hear the Dharma preached by the Teacher.
He is able to know the minds of sentient beings— those with desire and those free from desire,
those with anger and those free from anger, those with delusion and those free from delusion.
He clearly understands the affairs of past lives and the places where they formerly dwelt.
Throughout billions of kalpas, his wisdom is able to illuminate and penetrate all.
Having well cultivated the faculty of the eye, he attains inconceivable divine vision;
with that eye he beholds sentient beings, dying here and being born there.
In a single thought-moment, one can fully know the thoughts of all sentient beings;
knowing them all in this way, that wisdom is inconceivable. "O Youth!
What is verbal discipline?

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes verbal discipline, they attain the sixty kinds of unimpeded, pure, and exquisite vocal sounds of a Buddha, which are inconceivable; this is called verbal discipline.
"Furthermore, young man!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is fully endowed with verbal restraint speaks, all people believe and accept what he says; this is called verbal restraint."

"Furthermore, youth! A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who is fully endowed with the precepts of speech attains the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and attains the ten powers of a Tathāgata—namely: the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible; the power of knowing the causes and effects of the past, future, and present karma of all sentient beings; the power of knowing whether various dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and meditative attainments are accompanied by afflictions or free from afflictions; the power of knowing the lifespans of others and the differences in the faculties of other sentient beings; the power of knowing the various and immeasurable desires of sentient beings; the power of knowing the various and immeasurable natures of sentient beings; the power of knowing the path leading to all destinations; the power of knowing past lives; the power of knowing the birth and death of all sentient beings; and the power of knowing the exhaustion of outflows."
"Furthermore, young man!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is fully endowed with the restraint of speech is able to attain the four fearlessnesses and the eighteen unique qualities, this is called being fully endowed with the restraint of speech."
"Furthermore, youth!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is fully endowed with verbal restraint attains the three gates of liberation and the four divine abodes, this is called being fully endowed with verbal restraint."
"Furthermore, youth!

To speak briefly, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is fully endowed with verbal restraint attains the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path; this is called a bodhisattva being fully endowed with verbal restraint."
"Furthermore, youth!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is fully endowed with the precepts of speech attains the Brahma-abode of great compassion, attains the Brahma-abode of great equanimity, attains the awakening of peace, and attains the awakening of cessation, this is called a bodhisattva being fully endowed with the precepts of speech."
"Furthermore, young man!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is fully endowed with verbal discipline, he attains freedom from false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech. He does not utter coarse words toward his parents or teachers, and the bodhisattva completely distances himself from all such words of fault and evil."

Regarding those verbal expressions, one understands them as they truly are—like an echo, like a dream, like a magical illusion, like a transformation, like a mirage, and like a reflection of light. Within these echoes up to reflections of light, there is nothing to be apprehended; there is no conceptualization, no grasping, no objective support, and no attachment. This is called a bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the precept of speech.
“O youth! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who maintains pure verbal discipline attains the speech of all buddhas, the supernormal powers of all buddhas, and the spiritual penetrations of all buddhas.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If one is endowed with the restraint of speech, These bodhisattvas will certainly obtain Unimpeded wisdom regarding all phenomena;
This is called being fully possessed of the restraint of speech."

If one is endowed with the restraint of speech, one attains the thirty-two marks of a great man, the ten powers of a Buddha, and the unique qualities; this is called being fully possessed of the restraint of speech.
If one is endowed with the restraint of speech, one is able to attain all the teachings of the Buddhas.
That I have thus spoken all the Buddha-dharmas is called being fully endowed with the restraint of speech;
if one accords with the restraint of speech, they can attain the Brahma-abodes and eloquence,
reaching the inconceivable and marvelous Dharma— this is called being fully endowed with the restraint of speech.

If one is in accord with the restraint of speech, one attains the four foundations of mindfulness and the right efforts, and is endowed with the four bases of power, the faculties, the powers, and so forth; this is called being fully possessed of the restraint of speech.
If one is in accord with the restraint of speech, one attains great equanimity and fearlessness.
Attaining the pure dwelling of great compassion—this is called being fully endowed with the precept of speech.
One who is in accord with the precept of speech can attain pure and secure awakening, as well as tranquil thought and reflection;
this is called being fully endowed with the precept of speech.
If one is endowed with the restraint of speech, one stays far removed from false speech and divisive talk;
furthermore, one abandons harsh speech and frivolous chatter—this is called being fully possessed of the restraint of speech.
If one is endowed with the restraint of speech, one never slanders the True Dharma.
Nor does one disparage the Tathāgata; this is called being fully endowed with the restraint of speech.
One who is in accord with the restraint of speech does not utter improper or harsh words toward their parents or teachers;
this is called being fully endowed with the restraint of speech.
If one is endowed with the restraint of speech, one will never give rise to any verbal transgressions;
being able to leave them all behind without exception, this is called being fully possessed of the restraint of speech.
If one is endowed with the restraint of speech, one understands that words are like echoes.
To realize that sounds are like a dream— this is called being fully endowed with the precept of speech;
To understand that there is no self and no life-span, and that dependent origination is false and like a dream—
to be able to know that speech is thus, this is called being fully endowed with the precept of speech.
The Truth of Cessation is unreal, like a dream; the essence of Nirvāṇa is like the nature of a dream.
When a Bodhisattva knows that words are thus, this is called being fully endowed with the precept of speech.
Since no other words can be apprehended, there is no conceptual differentiation and no attachment.
To be without mental clinging and without grasping— this is called being fully endowed with verbal discipline.
"Young man, what is meant by mental discipline?

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is fully endowed with the precept of mental discipline, they will attain all Buddha-dharmas, attain all supernormal powers, and their mind will attain the liberation of immovability; if a bodhisattva mahāsattva is fully endowed with the precept of mental discipline, they will attain the vajra-samādhi concentration—this is called the perfection of the precept of mental discipline.
"Furthermore, young man!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is fully endowed with the restraint of the mind attains a blazing radiance, this is called being fully endowed with the restraint of the mind;
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is fully endowed with the restraint of the mind attains sixty kinds of exquisite vocal qualities, this is called being fully endowed with the restraint of the mind."
"Furthermore, youth!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is fully endowed with the precept of mental discipline attains the thirty-two marks of a great man, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, and the eighteen unique dharmas, this is called being fully endowed with the precept of mental discipline."
"Furthermore, youth!
